verseByVerse.quote: And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four men carry a paralysed friend to Jesus and, unable to get through the crowd, dig through the roof and lower him down on his mat. Love for a needy friend refuses to accept a closed door, and is willing to make a mess to bring someone to Christ.

The roof. A Galilean roof was beams laid across the walls, branches and reed matting over them, then thick mud and straw packed on top and rolled flat — which is why every house had a stone roller up there. An outside stair led up, because the roof was usable space for drying figs or sleeping in summer. Getting a man up on a mat was heavy, awkward work for four, but possible.

Making a mess. Mark is blunt: they “removed the roof” and made an opening. Mud, straw, matting and branches came down on a packed room, with the preacher underneath. Luke, writing for city readers, puts it in tiles; Mark gives you the dirt.

The bed. Not a frame but a poor man’s pallet, a mat you could roll and carry. His whole world was a piece of matting and four friends.

Four nobodies. They are never named, say nothing, and never appear again. Their entire recorded contribution to the kingdom is that they wouldn’t accept a locked door.

Whose ceiling. If this is Peter’s house, a man who had just left his nets watched his own ceiling come down into his own front room, and Mark records no complaint from anyone. A man outside needed to get in; the roof was only a roof.

A test. What would you let be damaged — your dignity, your schedule, your reputation as a reasonable person — to get one person in front of Christ? These four are in the Bible forever because they were willing to make a mess. Who is the friend you need to carry this week?
verseByVerse.note: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. An opening could be dug through and repaired.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the friends’ faith, Jesus says to the paralysed man, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” Jesus honours the faith that brings others to him, and he goes first to a person’s deepest need — forgiveness — before the visible one.

Their faith. Not his. Mark tells us nothing of what the man believed — whether he asked to be brought, whether he was ashamed, whether he expected anything. What Jesus saw and honoured was the faith of the men on the roof.

Can my faith help someone else? Many read this with a face in mind: a child who has walked away, a spouse who won’t believe, a friend long past caring. Yes and no, and both matter. Yes: your faith can carry a person to where Jesus is, which is what intercession does. You can’t make anyone believe, but you can bring them again and again before the One who can — under the preached word, onto your prayer list, into the company of his people — and refuse to accept that the door is shut. And no: the man didn’t stay a spectator. He heard “your sins are forgiven,” rose and walked. No one was forgiven in his place; you can’t believe for another. Your part is the roof and the ropes; the rising is God’s to give and theirs to receive. Many believers today were once only a name on someone’s stubborn, seemingly unanswered prayer list. Don’t stop digging through the roof.

“Son.” A warm, family word, a father’s word. Lowered into a room of strangers and religious professionals, filthy from the ceiling, at the centre of attention, the first word he hears tells him where he stands.

Why forgiveness first? Why this, not the legs everyone was looking at? Not, most likely, because the paralysis punished a particular sin. Sometimes suffering is tied to sin — “Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you” (John 5:14); very often not — “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:3). The crowd saw a ruined body. Jesus saw the ruined man and went to his greatest need.

Which was the emergency. Hold the outcomes side by side. A paralytic who walked home that afternoon and died unforgiven forty years later would still be lost. One forgiven and never healed, carried on that mat to the end, would be eternally safe. Jesus heals the legs to prove he has dealt with the soul, but leaves no doubt which was the emergency. And the mercy: he begins with the thing you weren’t asking about, because he treats you as a person, not a case. A test: in your prayers, which need comes first?
verseByVerse.note: “Son” is a warm address, like “my child.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some scribes silently accuse Jesus of blasphemy: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” They are right that only God forgives sins — which means Jesus is either a blasphemer or God, with no comfortable middle option.

A silent verdict. The scribes were “sitting there” — seated, the posture of the qualified man who has come to assess rather than listen — “questioning in their hearts.” The argument begins unspoken.

Their theology was right. These aren’t fools or straw men. “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” is Isaiah: “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake” (Isaiah 43:25) — the doubled pronoun is the force of it. A priest could declare a healed leper clean; a prophet could announce God’s forgiveness; a rabbi could teach the way back. None ever stood before a man and forgave him, because every sin is finally against God, and only the one offended can wipe the account. David knew it with a murdered man’s blood on his hands: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4).

Beyond the Messianic hope. Israel hoped for a king who would reign and drive out Rome. No known Jewish writing before Jesus has the Messiah forgiving sins in his own name. This isn’t a Messianic claim made too loudly; it is a category the hope didn’t contain.

A death sentence. Blasphemy carried stoning (Leviticus 24:16). At the night trial the high priest will say, “You have heard his blasphemy,” and they will condemn him (14:64). The verdict that kills Jesus is reached silently in a crowded front room in Capernaum, twelve chapters early. Everything in between is the trial.

No middle position. Run their logic honestly, as Mark wants. Major premise, true: only God forgives sins. Minor premise, true: this man just forgave sins. There is no third conclusion. Either he is a blasphemer of the first order, or he is what the voice at the Jordan called him. What has never been available is the comfortable view that he was a fine moral teacher who would be appalled at his followers. Fine moral teachers don’t do this.

Right about God, wrong about Jesus. The sting for religious people. They had the doctrine of divine pardon in perfect order, and it was the very shelf on which they filed him as an enemy. You can hold every article of faith correctly and be undone by the Person the articles are about. A test: do your settled convictions about how God works have room for God turning up and working?
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: the same charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, "Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your bed and walk'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus perceives their unspoken thoughts and asks which is easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven,” or “Rise, take up your bed and walk.” Jesus reads hearts as only God does, and he deliberately stakes his invisible claim on a visible, testable sign.

He reads the silence. Before answering the objection, he answers one that was never spoken: “perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned.” Solomon prayed to the God who alone can do that: “you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind” (1 Kings 8:39). Jeremiah: “The heart is deceitful above all things… who can understand it? ‘I the LORD search the heart’” (Jeremiah 17:9–10). Two divine prerogatives in ninety seconds — forgiving sin and reading hearts — and the men best equipped to notice are the ones being read.

Easier to say. The exact wording decides the argument. “Your sins are forgiven” is the easy sentence: nothing visible changes, there is no test, and a charlatan could say it for a decade without being caught. “Rise… and walk” is the hard one: checkable in four seconds before a packed room, and if the man doesn’t move, you are finished. Every religious fraud prefers claims that can’t be tested.

Inviting verification. Jesus does the reverse. He hangs the invisible claim on a visible, immediate, public test, and announces in advance that he is doing so. He isn’t hiding behind mystery.

A faith that can be checked. That instinct runs through Christianity. Paul doesn’t tell Corinth to have an experience; he says, “if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:14), and lists living eyewitnesses to go and ask. The faith has always staked itself on things that could in principle be shown false.

A test. What would have to happen for you to conclude your faith isn’t true? If the honest answer is “nothing at all,” you may have a mood rather than a faith. Jesus didn’t ask this room to feel something about him. He asked it to watch, and draw the conclusion the evidence required.

verseByVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic— "I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, Jesus tells the paralysed man to rise, take his bed and go home. Jesus claims the divine authority of Daniel’s heavenly Son of Man, and he brings God’s forgiveness here and now, sending the forgiven home whole.

A broken sentence. Jesus speaks to the scribes — “that you may know…” — and then Mark inserts a stage direction: “he said to the paralytic.” The dashes mark the swivel. The point is aimed at the professionals; the command at the man on the floor. Jesus never finishes the sentence to the scribes. The finish is the man standing up.

On earth. Two words that relocate pardon. Not in heaven after you die, where you find out how it went; not ninety miles south in Jerusalem through priest, lamb, curtain and fee. Here — in a fishing village, in a room with mud on the floor, from a man you could touch, to someone who had brought no sacrifice and couldn’t have carried one. A test: are you waiting to find out someday whether you are forgiven? He gives it now.

The Son of Man. His first use of the title in Mark, and his settled way of speaking of himself to the cross. In ordinary Aramaic it could mean simply a human being. But Jesus reaches for Daniel 7, where thrones are set, the Ancient of Days sits, and “one like a son of man” comes “with the clouds of heaven” and is given “dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him” (Daniel 7:13–14). In the Old Testament, the one who rides the clouds is God. Daniel sees a figure truly human who is given what belongs to God, and Jesus puts that figure on. So when he says the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins — and later that he is “lord even of the Sabbath” — he claims the authority Daniel saw handed to that heavenly Man.

Veiled and plain. The title is veiled enough that no one can convict him on it in a hurry, plain enough that anyone with the Scriptures open can see what has been said. Before Mark ends, it will carry both his throne and his cross: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45).

Go home. Three commands, and the third is the tender one. Not to the temple or a rabbi or a lap of the town, but home, where someone — a wife, a mother, children who had learned to step around a mat — is about to see him in the doorway on his own legs, carrying what carried him. He doesn’t merely repair you and leave you in the road. He sends you home.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man gets up at once, picks up his bed and walks out in front of everyone, and all are amazed and glorify God. The crowd marvelled at the healing but missed what it proved — that Jesus can forgive sins — and many still want his power more than his pardon.

Immediately. Mark’s favourite word, used dozens of times, gives the Gospel its pace. Here it does real work: no convalescence, no gradual return of feeling. Command and walking are one instant, because this authority doesn’t wait for nature to catch up.

Before them all. Not done quietly in a back room. Jesus staked his claim on a public test, and it is settled publicly, before the scribes who had silently convicted him, the crowd parting to let a man walk out the door his friends couldn’t get him through. And he picked up his bed: what had been the emblem of his helplessness went home over his shoulder as evidence.

What they didn’t say. They were amazed and glorified God — better than the scribes managed. But no one said: then the other thing he said must be true. No one asked: if he can do that to a man’s legs with a word, what has he just done to a man’s guilt, and could he do it for me? They were handed the proof on Jesus’ own terms, and their astonishment stopped at the miracle and never reached what it was for.

Legs and sins. That isn’t only a first-century failure. You can be moved by God’s power and unmoved by his pardon — want him for what he might fix and never come for what he came to forgive. Much modern praying is this: we ask him about the legs; he is waiting to talk about the sins.

A test. Think of the last five things you asked God for. How many were about circumstances, and how many about your soul? There is no shame in asking for the legs; the four friends did, and he didn’t scold them. But if the whole list is legs, you have understood him about as well as the crowd — and they went home amazed and unforgiven. The man on the mat got both, and only one was still with him fifty years later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Levi, Sinners, and New Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Out again (vv. 13–14). Jesus leaves the house, teaches by the lake, and walks past a customs post. Sitting in it is Levi son of Alphaeus, a Jew collecting money for the occupying power, and the two words Follow me end his career in the time it takes to say them.

The dinner (vv. 15–17). Levi's first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party for his own disreputable network and put Jesus at the centre of it. The scribes of the Pharisees do not challenge Jesus; they go at him through his followers. His answer is one sentence about a doctor, and it sorts the human race into two categories with no third.

The fasting question (vv. 18–20). Why do John's disciples fast and yours do not? Jesus answers with a wedding, quietly takes for himself a role the Old Testament gives to God alone, and in the same breath drops the first shadow of the cross into the Gospel.

Cloth and wineskins (vv. 21–22). Two pictures from ordinary domestic life make one uncomfortable point: what he has brought cannot be sewn onto what you already have.
verseByVerse.theology:
The two little parables of vv. 21–22 are the theological hinge of the chapter, and they are more radical than they look. An unshrunk patch on an old garment does not merely fail; when it is first washed it shrinks, grips, and pulls away, and the tear is worse than it was before the repair. New wine still working gives off gas; a skin that has already stretched once and gone brittle will split. In both pictures the old thing is not attacked. It is simply asked to contain something it was never built to hold, and it fails.

Jesus is not offering a reformed Judaism, and he is not offering a reformed you. Religion, as everyone naturally practises it, is patchwork — an addition to a self that stays fundamentally in charge. That, he says, does not produce a better garment; it produces a worse tear, which is exactly why adding a little Christianity to an unchanged life so often makes a person more miserable rather than less.

And then the promise at the end, which is easy to read past: new wine is for fresh wineskins. He supplies the skin as well as the wine. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26); if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). He did not come to mend you. That is worse news, and far better news, than mending.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi cannot yet explain a doctrine, so he cooks. He gathers the only people he knows — the ones no synagogue wanted — and gets them into a room with Jesus.

Now: the newest Christian in your church, six weeks old in the faith, still knows every person from the old life; the man who has been converted thirty years often knows nobody outside the church at all. Levi's method needs no training course. Buy the food, make the call, and be in the room.

The harder half of the example is the one people skip. Jesus went to that table as the physician, not as a patient, and nobody left it unchanged — Levi, who had already left his booth to follow him, did not go back, and the meal did not end with Jesus agreeing with the guests. Both errors are live. One keeps a safe distance and calls it holiness; the other sits down at every table, says nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and calls it grace. The Pharisees would not go in. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the sea, Jesus sees Levi the tax collector at his booth and says, “Follow me,” and Levi rises and follows. Jesus calls the very person his society and religion had written off as beyond saving, and Levi leaves everything, with no way back.

He leaves again. Mark’s Jesus often leaves — synagogue, house, crowd, town. After the most spectacular thing yet seen in Capernaum, he walks along the shore, and passes a customs post.

Levi, called Matthew. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew (Matthew 9:9), probably the name he carried afterwards; Mark uses the old name. Matthew, writing of himself, adds “the tax collector” to his own name in the apostle list (Matthew 10:3), which no one else does. A forgiven man isn’t embarrassed by his file.

A licence to print money. Capernaum sat on the road from Damascus to the Mediterranean, at the frontier of Herod Antipas’s territory. A collector bid for the contract, paid up front, and lived on whatever he could extract above it. There was no published rate to appeal to; what he said you owed, backed by soldiers, you owed. So he was a thief with legal cover and a collaborator living off his own country’s occupation. His word was worthless in court, and respectable people shunned him and his money.

Beyond saving. Worse, the road back for a thief ran through restitution — repay what you took and add a fifth (Numbers 5:7; Leviticus 6:5). A tax collector couldn’t; he had defrauded hundreds over years and kept no list of who. His repentance was, by his own religion’s reckoning, mathematically impossible. That is the man Jesus stops for.

Two words. “Follow me.” No interview, probation or conditions, no requirement that he first put anything right. And Mark’s reply in six: “And he rose and followed him.”

No way back. Peter and Andrew left their nets, and the nets were still there; after the crucifixion they went back to them for a night (John 21:3). Levi stood up from a booth someone else would occupy by the afternoon. His was the one call in the Gospel that couldn’t be reversed, and he made it without a question.

For the one who thinks he has gone too far. If you have privately concluded you have done damage that can’t be undone or repaid, look at who is sitting in that booth. The man Jesus chose for the apostolic band, and for writing a Gospel, was the one man in town whose religion had already given up on him. Hear the same two words.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi holds a dinner, and many tax collectors and sinners recline at table with Jesus and his disciples, and the Pharisees’ scribes demand of the disciples why he eats with such people. By sharing their table, Jesus publicly welcomes outcasts — showing how to be among people far from God without either avoiding them or becoming like them.

A party. Levi’s first act as a disciple: “Levi made him a great feast in his house” (Luke 5:29). “Reclining” means a formal banquet on couches round a low table, lasting hours. And the room was full of the only people Levi knew.

Sinners. Not a general remark about human nature but a label: people whose trade or way of life put them permanently outside the purity system — collectors, their friends, everyone the establishment had written off. And “there were many who followed him”: Levi’s network was already moving.

Why it detonated. We eat with anybody. In that world a shared table was the sign of full acceptance, peace between those at it. You didn’t eat with a man you counted unclean, because you would be saying publicly there was nothing between you. That is exactly what Jesus was saying, and all Capernaum could read it.

Getting at the followers. The scribes don’t put the question to Jesus but to his disciples — new, unsure, easier to unsettle. An old tactic, still used: if you can’t get at the leader, make his followers feel foolish about the company they keep.

How do I keep real friendships with people whose lives I don’t agree with? Without either condemning them or quietly signing off on everything? Jesus answers by being at the table, not by drawing a line round it. But look how he is there. Not blending in hoping not to be noticed, not as a fellow patient. The host had given up his career that day, and the evening never ends with Jesus agreeing with the room.

A test. Think of the last evening you spent among people far from God. Did anything about how you were there make Christ visible, or were you indistinguishable? Did you go home more like them, or did any of them meet something in you they couldn’t account for? We fail in two directions. The Pharisees wouldn’t go in at all and called it holiness. Others go in, sit down, say nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and call it grace. Jesus went in — as himself.
verseByVerse.note: At a formal meal guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow — hence “reclined.” “Sinners” here means people known for ignoring the law.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” The only qualification for coming to Christ is knowing you need him; those who think themselves well never send for the doctor.

The gentlest, most terrible sentence. Jesus isn’t conceding that the Pharisees are healthy; he takes their self-assessment to its end. Very well — if you are well, you won’t want a doctor, and you won’t get one. As with real medicine: the man who won’t admit he is ill doesn’t take the treatment. The cure is on the shelf; he dies of something treatable, insisting nothing is wrong.

“I came.” No one says “I came” about being born. A man who says he came was somewhere before, and had business here.

The disqualification qualifies. “Not to call the righteous, but sinners” — and the room is the evidence. The only qualification for Christ is the disqualification. Not progress, not a clean stretch, not having the worst behind you. Sickness is the entry requirement; the ticket is the thing you have been trying to hide.

For the one who fears he is too far gone. If you fear that if your church knew what is in your history or your head it would be the end — read it slowly. He didn’t come for the respectable and take the odd sinner as an exception. He came to call sinners. You aren’t the awkward case; you are the stated purpose of the visit.

For the one who thinks he is all right. If your quiet position is that you are basically decent, churchgoing, never did much harm — this verse isn’t a comfort and isn’t meant to be. There is no third category: the sick who know it and the sick who don’t, and only one group sends for the doctor. The Pharisees went home from Levi’s with their theology, reputations and sins intact.

A test. When did you last tell God something specific and shameful about yourself, in plain words, without softening it — not a general “we all fall short,” but the actual thing? Someone who can’t remember doing that hasn’t yet gone to the physician, however long he has sat in the waiting room.

What it cost the Physician. Doctors keep their distance; they wash, wear gloves, go home. This one came into the ward, took the disease into his own body, and died of it so the patients would live. He wasn’t being broad-minded at Levi’s table. He was starting the treatment.

parallels.desc: “to seek and to save the lost”

verseByVerse.quote: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, "Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked why his disciples don’t fast like John’s and the Pharisees’, Jesus answers that wedding guests can’t fast while the bridegroom is with them — but the bridegroom will be taken away, and then they will fast. Jesus claims to be the divine Bridegroom whose presence is joy, foreshadows his death, and expects his people to fast now out of longing for him.

A fair question. An odd alliance asks it: John’s ascetic disciples and the strict Pharisees, agreed on little else, both bewildered — everyone serious fasts. The law commanded one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29); the Pharisees fasted twice a week, as the man in the parable boasts (Luke 18:12). A teacher whose followers didn’t fast wasn’t serious.

A wedding. Jesus doesn’t defend his disciples; he changes the category with a picture everyone had stood inside. A Jewish wedding ran seven days. “Wedding guests” is literally “sons of the bridechamber,” the groom’s closest friends, and the rabbis themselves released them from certain religious duties for the week, because you can’t mourn and rejoice at once. Jesus answers from their own law. Fasting now would be sitting in the corner of a wedding refusing the food, with the bridegroom in the room.

Who is the bridegroom? In the Old Testament, one Person: “your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name” (Isaiah 54:5); “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). Jesus takes the title without explanation, in an answer about diet — the chapter’s second enormous claim, and no one seems to notice.

What his presence is like. Not an examination or an inspection, but a wedding — the happiest week in a village’s life, food, wine, noise, and a groom who can’t stop smiling. If your religion feels nothing like that, ask whether you have understood who is in the room.

“Taken away.” Then the light goes out of the sentence. Bridegrooms aren’t removed from their own weddings. The first shadow of the cross in Mark, dropped into a cheerful answer in chapter 2, before any opponent has touched him. He knew how it ended.

Are Christians meant to fast now? Jesus plainly assumed so: not abolished, but its time coming. He taught “when you fast” (Matthew 6:16), not “if.” It isn’t a way to get God’s attention or pay something off. It makes the body say what the heart means: a few hours of real, insistent hunger reminding you every twenty minutes that there is a deeper hunger you have fed with everything except God. If you have never done it, start small: miss one meal this week, tell no one, and spend the time with your Bible open.

Homesickness with a date. We fast because the Bridegroom has been taken and we want him back. Not gloom, but homesickness with a date in it: he was taken on a Friday, and the wedding feast the others were rehearsing has been fixed (Revelation 19:9).
verseByVerse.note: A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

parallels.desc: the one yearly fast the law commanded
a Pharisee who fasted twice a week

verseByVerse.quote: No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one patches an old garment with unshrunk cloth or puts new wine into old wineskins; new wine needs fresh skins. What Jesus brings can’t simply be added onto an old life; he makes people new to contain it.

The patch. New cloth off the loom is unshrunk. Sewn onto a much-washed garment, it looks a decent repair — until it gets wet, pulls tight against worn cloth with no give, and rips away, taking the old fabric with it. “A worse tear is made.” The garment was damaged before; the repair ruined it.

The skin. Wine was carried in goatskins. Fresh wine still ferments and swells, so it went into a new skin with stretch left. An old skin has done its stretching and gone brittle; pour working wine in and it splits — and Jesus counts the cost twice: “the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins.” You don’t merely fail to gain the new; you lose what you had.

Not an improvement but a new kind. Neither picture attacks the old thing. The garment was a garment; the skin did its job in its day. They are asked to hold what they were never built for, and fail. What Jesus brings isn’t an improved version of what was there. It is different in kind.

Patchwork religion. Most of us instinctively approach faith as patchwork. We take the life we have, the self firmly in charge, and sew something on: church on Sunday, a habit of prayer, tidier vocabulary, a few things given up. Same garment; the patch is decoration. That is why a certain half-Christianity makes people more miserable than before, and why they are unfairly blamed for it. They aren’t insincere. They are living out a new patch on an old coat, pulling at the seams whenever life gets wet. Something keeps ripping, and they conclude faith doesn’t work, when what failed is the repair job.

A test. Is Christ an addition to your life — an important, costly one, but an addition to a self that still holds the deciding vote? Or has the self been handed over? The two look alike from outside for a long time and behave completely differently under strain.

He gives the skin. “New wine is for fresh wineskins” — the gospel in the last clause. He doesn’t leave you holding wine and a ruined skin, told to find a better container. He gives it: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26); “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). Making the vessel is his work, which is why it can be asked of you. He didn’t come to mend you — worse news than you wanted and immeasurably better than you hoped. Mending would leave the old coat and a lifetime of stitching. He intends to make you new. Ask him for it.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting and expanding; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The field (vv. 23–24). The disciples walk through standing grain on a Sabbath, pulling heads off as they go and rubbing them in their hands. The Law explicitly allowed this; the Pharisees are not accusing them of theft. They are counting it as harvesting, threshing and winnowing — three of the thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, in one mouthful of wheat. And somebody had to be out in that field, on a Sabbath, watching.

The precedent (vv. 25–26). Jesus answers with a story rather than a ruling: David, hungry and on the run, eating the consecrated bread that only priests were permitted to eat, and Scripture recording not a word against him. The parallel is not simply that need outranks regulation. It is that a king travelling in rejection with his men has been here before.

The verdict (vv. 27–28). Two sentences that reset everything. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath — the day is a gift, and they had turned it into a scoring system. And then: the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The Giver is standing in the cornfield being told off for letting hungry men eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (v. 28) is a claim of breathtaking scope, and it is easy to miss how far it reaches. The Sabbath is not a national custom that a rabbi might reinterpret. It is stitched into the fabric of creation — God rested on the seventh day and made it holy before there was an Israel, a Sinai or a Jew (Gen. 2:2–3) — and it was afterwards written into the covenant by the finger of God (Exod. 20:8–11). To be lord of it is to be lord of the created order and of the covenant together.

And the day was always pointing past itself. Israel entered the land and never really entered the rest; centuries later Scripture can still say there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Every seventh evening for fifteen hundred years the nation rehearsed a rest it did not yet possess.

Put Mark's two sentences side by side and see what has happened. The Sabbath was made for man — so it is a gift. And the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath — so the Giver is standing in the field. The rest the day rehearsed turns out not to be a square on a calendar but a Person, and he is the one being scolded. They were defending the gift against the Giver.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: hungry men pulling grain on a walk, and religious experts who had positioned themselves in a cornfield on a Sabbath in order to observe an infringement.

Now: the same instinct wherever the keeping of a form has become more important than the person the form was given to serve — the church where a visitor's clothes are noticed before his face is, the family where the standard is enforced and the child is not enjoyed. The institution that crushes the person it was designed to serve has inverted its own purpose, and it usually does so while feeling unusually devout.

The practical half of the day is worth taking as seriously as the doctrine of it. A modern reader does not break the Sabbath by working in a field; he breaks it by never stopping — by carrying the office in his pocket to bed. Stopping for a day feels like negligence, and it exposes precisely what a man believes about who is holding the world together. It keeps turning without you. That is the humiliation, and it is also the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a Sabbath the disciples pluck grain as they walk, and the Pharisees object that this is unlawful on the Sabbath. The issue isn’t theft but rule-keeping that had lost sight of people; it is possible to be scrupulous about a rule and hard toward a person.

Not stealing. Almost everyone reads this as theft, and it isn’t. Paths ran between unfenced fields; the disciples pull off heads of wheat, rub them in their palms, blow away the chaff and eat. The law expressly allowed it: “If you go into your neighbor’s standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor’s standing grain” (Deuteronomy 23:25). God had legislated for hungry travellers. The Pharisees don’t allege theft. Their objection is the day.

Three kinds of work in a mouthful. Tradition around the fourth commandment listed thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, and the disciples touched three in one mouthful: plucking was reaping, rubbing was threshing, blowing away the husk was winnowing. A man could be a farm labourer for a harvest in the time it takes to eat a handful of wheat.

How did they see it? They were there — on a Sabbath morning, out on a path through the fields, at a carefully calculated distance so as not to exceed the permitted Sabbath walk themselves — in position, watching working men to see whether any would put out a hand. Someone planned that walk. “Look” is almost a shout. They had been waiting.

Faithfulness that is hard as flint. The same energy lives in every generation, and it always dresses as faithfulness. You can be scrupulous about a rule and hard as flint about a person; notice at a glance everything out of place in someone’s life and never notice he is hungry. Their Scriptures had told them what to see: “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

A test. Think of the last time you were sharply critical of another Christian — how he raises his children, spends money, uses his Sundays. Did you know what was actually going on in that house? Or were you at the edge of the field with a clear view of the rule and none of the man?
verseByVerse.note: The objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work.

parallels.desc: picking grain by hand was allowed

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers with David, who in need ate the holy bread of the Presence, lawful only for priests, and gave it to his men. Human need outweighed a ceremonial rule, God did not object — and the disciples, like David’s men, are with God’s anointed King.

A story, not a ruling. 1 Samuel 21: David, anointed but not yet on the throne, flees Saul with a few hungry men to the sanctuary at Nob. The only food is the bread of the Presence — twelve loaves set before God each Sabbath, the old loaves eaten by priests alone as a most holy portion (Leviticus 24:5–9). The priest gives it to David and his men, and Scripture records not one word of criticism from God or the narrator.

The rule gave way. First point: where genuine human need collided with a ceremonial regulation, the regulation gave way and heaven didn’t object. The rule was never the ultimate thing. A test: are your rules serving people or using them?

The anointed King. Second, sharper: Jesus doesn’t choose any story about hunger. He chooses the anointed king — rejected, unrecognised, on the road with his men — fed from the holy table. The disciples in that field are the men of a King the country hasn’t enthroned. If David’s men could eat holy bread because of who was with them, the Pharisees should be asking a much larger question.

Why does Jesus say Abiathar, when 1 Samuel names Ahimelech? An honest reader with a reference Bible will notice: 1 Samuel 21 names the priest Ahimelech; Jesus says “in the time of Abiathar the high priest,” and Abiathar was Ahimelech’s son. The church has discussed this openly for centuries, and there are two good answers. First, the Greek can mean “in the passage about Abiathar” — the very construction Mark uses later: “in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush” (12:26). With no chapter numbers, a teacher located a text by its most famous figure, and this stretch of 1 Samuel is Abiathar’s section: he escapes the slaughter at Nob a chapter later and becomes David’s priest for life. On that reading Jesus gives a reference, not a date. Second, naming an era by its best-known figure is how everyone talks about the past, and Abiathar was the celebrated high priest of David’s reign. Nothing in the argument depends on it. Jesus rests his case not on who was on duty but on what God didn’t say when hungry men ate holy bread — and the Pharisees, who knew that chapter far better than we do, didn’t raise the objection.
verseByVerse.note: On the name Abiathar (1 Samuel 21 names the priest Ahimelech), see the commentary.

parallels.desc: the bread of the Presence, eaten by priests

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” God gave the Sabbath as a gift of rest, not a burden — and Jesus claims to be its Lord, the true rest to which it always pointed.

Made for man. Given, and given long before there was a Jew to keep it: God rested on the seventh day and blessed it at creation (Genesis 2:2–3), centuries before Sinai. Not national custom, but part of the architecture of the world, like marriage, work, day and night.

A kindness. A day when the ox is unhitched, the servant off, the slave resting — when the poorest labourer gets what only rich men could buy, a day that is his. Egypt had given Israel no such day, and Deuteronomy attaches the memory of slavery to the command (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Not man for the Sabbath. They had taken a day designed to lift a burden and turned it into one — thirty-nine categories to track, a day you could fail. The gift had become an examination.

Lord of the Sabbath. If the day was made for man, then the Man in whom humanity is summed up, the one Daniel saw given dominion, is its lord. He isn’t proposing to relax the rules. He tells experts in a cornfield that the day belongs to him.

Must Christians keep a Sabbath — is Sunday a rule? Christians who love the Bible differ. Some hold that the fourth commandment, rooted in creation and written in the Ten, still binds one day in seven, now kept on the resurrection day. Others take Paul’s words — “One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike” (Romans 14:5); “let no one pass judgment on you… with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath” (Colossians 2:16) — to mean the shadow is fulfilled in Christ and the day is a matter of freedom. The more likely reading is the second (Colossians 2:16–17; cf. Acts 20:7), though neither side may judge the other.

What no one disputes. The day is a gift, not a scoring system, and someone who never stops hasn’t understood the God who did. Do you stop? Not slow down — stop. Is there a stretch of time in your week when the work is genuinely down, the phone isn’t checked under the table, and you aren’t quietly earning your right to exist? Most of us break the Sabbath in a way the Pharisees wouldn’t recognise: not by putting a hand to grain, but by never taking a hand off anything.

Why stopping frightens us. If you stop, things carry on without you; you discover you weren’t holding the world up. That is the humiliation in it, and the rest: “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Rest is a weekly confession that you aren’t God and aren’t needed to be. A test: plan one real stretch of rest this week, and keep it.

The rest walked through the grain. The Sabbath always pointed past itself: “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). For fifteen hundred years Israel rehearsed something it didn’t yet have. Then, on a Sabbath morning in a Galilean field, the rest itself walked through the grain with hungry men — and was scolded by those guarding the rehearsal. He is still the rest: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28) — given at the cost of a Friday on which he had no rest at all.

2.theology:
Chapter 2 opens the conflict that ends at the cross. The scribes and Pharisees are not villains in a simple morality tale — they are serious people defending serious religious commitments, and on the doctrine of forgiveness they are exactly right. Their error is not that they take the law too seriously; it is that they have not recognised the one the law was pointing to. When the fulfilment arrives, the categories built to anticipate it can no longer contain it, which is precisely the burden of the new wine and the old skins.

Four demonstrations, then, of why Jesus could not simply be absorbed into the religious system as constituted: he forgives sins directly rather than through the temple; he receives the excluded at his own table rather than at the end of a purification process; he calls his own presence a wedding rather than a fast; and he claims lordship over the creation ordinance of the Sabbath itself. Not because he is lawless, but because he is the law's Lord.
2.examples:
The Pharisees' discomfort at Jesus eating with sinners deserves sympathetic treatment before it receives critique. Their instinct toward purity was not irrational; it was a serious attempt to guard the holiness God had commanded, in a land under pagan occupation where the pressure to blur every line was constant. Their error was a category error: they had equated association with endorsement. Jesus's presence among sinners was not approval of their sin but the physician's presence among the sick, and the cure requires proximity. The model is the incarnation itself — the holy God does not deal with human ruin from a safe distance but comes into it to heal from within, and finally takes the disease into his own body on a cross.

Then: Pharisees keeping a careful distance in order to stay clean, while the one man in Capernaum who actually was clean reclined at a tax collector's table. Now: any form of Christianity that has quietly confused holiness with non-exposure — and, on the other side, any form of it that sits down at every table and never says who it came with.

3.title: By Whose Power?
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. <sup>2</sup>And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. <sup>3</sup>And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” <sup>4</sup>And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” But they were silent. <sup>5</sup>And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. <sup>6</sup>The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. <sup>7</sup>Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea <sup>8</sup>and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. <sup>9</sup>And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, <sup>10</sup>for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. <sup>11</sup>And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” <sup>12</sup>And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. <sup>13</sup>And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. <sup>14</sup>And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach <sup>15</sup>and have authority to cast out demons. <sup>16</sup>He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); <sup>17</sup>James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); <sup>18</sup>Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot, <sup>19</sup>and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>20</sup>Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. <sup>21</sup>And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” <sup>22</sup>And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and “by the prince of demons he casts out the demons.” <sup>23</sup>And he called them to him and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? <sup>24</sup>If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <sup>25</sup>And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. <sup>27</sup>But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>28</sup>“Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, <sup>29</sup>but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin”— <sup>30</sup>for they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” <sup>31</sup>And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. <sup>32</sup>And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” <sup>33</sup>And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” <sup>34</sup>And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>35</sup>For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is where the opposition hardens into a decision and the alternative community is formed. It opens with a trap in a synagogue and closes with a redefinition of family, and between the two everything about Jesus is contested. The Pharisees and Herodians — parties who agreed on nothing — walk out of a Sabbath service together to plan his death (v. 6). His own family concludes he is out of his mind and comes to take him home (v. 21). A delegation of scribes travels ninety miles from Jerusalem and pronounces him possessed (v. 22). Three verdicts, and all of them wrong.

Against that, Jesus does two constructive things. He appoints twelve men — a number no Jew could hear innocently — so that they might be with him and be sent out (vv. 13–15); and he tells the room what the kingdom actually is: a break-in. A stronger man has entered the strong man's house, tied him up, and is carrying out his property (v. 27). Every healing and deliverance in this Gospel is loot from that raid. The chapter ends by naming who now belongs to him, and the criterion is neither blood nor pedigree but doing the will of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Withered Hand and the Widening Response
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–2). Jesus walks into a synagogue where two things are waiting for him: a man with a ruined hand, and a row of men watching to see whether he will touch it. They are not curious. They are collecting evidence.

The question nobody would answer (vv. 3–4). He puts the man in the middle of the room and asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or doing harm, saving life or killing. It is unanswerable, and they know it, so they say nothing.

The anger (v. 5). The one place in Mark where Jesus is said to look on people with anger — and in the same breath, grieved. Then a command to a man who cannot obey it, and a hand made new.

The verdict (v. 6). Two parties who despised each other walk out together to plan a murder, and it is still the Sabbath.

The crowds (vv. 7–12). He withdraws, and a hundred-mile radius follows him to the shore. He asks for a boat to keep from being crushed, and silences the only voices in the crowd that know exactly who he is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 raise a question every attentive reader hits sooner or later: the demons keep saying true things about Jesus, and he keeps shutting them up. Why refuse free advertising from witnesses who cannot be wrong?

Two reasons converge, and the second is the one that touches the reader. The first is timing. In Galilee in that decade, to be publicly proclaimed Son of God meant one thing to a crowd — a nationalist king who would clear out the Romans. Jesus refuses to be crowned before he is crucified, because a title accepted on those terms would have to be unlearned at the cross. He will let the word be said out loud when it can be defined by his death (15:39, on the lips of the officer at the foot of it).

The second is more searching. What the unclean spirits say is doctrinally perfect. You are the Son of God is exactly right, and it saves them from nothing. James makes the point without flinching: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder (Jas. 2:19). A creed can be entirely correct and entirely worthless. The spirits here fall down before him, which is more than the scribes did, and confess his identity, which is more than the disciples had managed — and they remain what they are. Right belief about Christ is not the same as belonging to him, and this chapter will end by saying who does belong.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man with a shrivelled hand told to stand up in the middle of a watched synagogue, before anything had been healed, in front of the men who had come to build a case.

Now: every act of obedience that makes a person visible and vulnerable before the outcome is assured — the first time you say in an office that you are a Christian; the apology you make with no guarantee it will be received; the sin confessed to one other believer when it could have stayed hidden for life. He was asked to be conspicuous first and healed second, and he had no way of knowing the order in advance.

And notice what the same scene did to the watchers. They had come to see whether a rule would be broken, and they saw a crippled man made whole, and it did not move them an inch. It is possible to sit in a room where God is plainly at work and be entirely occupied with whether it is being done properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue on the Sabbath is a man with a withered hand, and the Pharisees watch Jesus closely to see whether he will heal him, so they can accuse him. Religion detached from love can look at a suffering person and see only a test case.

Again. The last time Jesus was in a synagogue on a Sabbath, a demon screamed and the town talked for weeks (1:21–28). He knows what happens when he walks into these buildings, and goes in anyway.

No back row. A Galilean synagogue was small: stone benches round the walls, the congregation facing inward, everyone able to see everyone. That decides the scene, because a man is about to be told to stand up in the middle of it.

A wrecked livelihood. “Withered” suggests a hand dried up — wasted, shrunken. Luke the doctor notes it was the right hand (Luke 6:6), in a world of manual labour the difference between a tradesman and a beggar. He wasn’t dying; no one could call it an emergency that couldn’t wait a day — which is exactly why the Pharisees kept him. A borderline case makes the better trap.

Watched. The verb is for keeping something under observation — watching sideways, as you watch a man you have already decided about. By chapter 3 they had no doubt he could heal. They were watching whether he would. “So that they might accuse him” is courtroom language. They aren’t gathering understanding but evidence, and they have brought a man’s disability into a service and used it as bait.

When religion detaches from love. There is a human being in that room with a ruined livelihood, and the most religious men present see an opportunity. Not usually by a dramatic collapse into wickedness — these men would have been horrified to be called wicked — but by degrees, until a suffering person in your own congregation registers mainly as an issue to be handled. A test: have you been more interested in whether something was done correctly than in the person it was done to?

Two withered things. A man with a withered hand, and men with withered hearts. Only one knew he needed healing.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. Healing a condition that was not life-threatening could wait a day — which is why they watched.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the man with the withered hand, "Come here." And he said to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" But they were silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls the man to stand in the middle and asks his critics whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save life or to kill; they say nothing. Jesus openly shows what the Sabbath is for, and makes clear that refusing to do good when we can is itself doing harm.

In open court. He could have healed the man quietly at the door, and the trap would have closed on nothing. Instead: “Come here” — up into the middle, where the room can see. If the healing is to be treated as a crime, it will be committed openly. Jesus isn’t caught breaking the Sabbath; he chooses the moment, venue and audience.

The man exposed. He didn’t ask for this. He came as he had for years, the hand hidden in his cloak. Now he stands in the middle with it on display, before neighbours who have known all his life and officials who are visibly hostile — exposed first, healed second, with no way yet of knowing the second is coming.

What is the day for? They were braced for an argument about categories of work — whether healing counts, whether the case is urgent. Jesus refuses the frame. He doesn’t ask whether healing is permitted but what the day is for.

Was healing on the Sabbath actually forbidden in the law? No. Moses forbade work, but nowhere forbade healing. The ban came from scribal rules built round the law, which allowed treatment only when life was in danger. Jesus wasn’t breaking Moses; he was breaking the fence the teachers had built round Moses. For Christians today the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, its Lord (2:28), and no day binds the conscience (Colossians 2:16–17); but his question stands over every day of the week.

No neutral option. On any day you are either doing good or harm, saving life or destroying it. To have the power to do good and withhold it is itself a choice: “whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17). A test: what good is within your reach this week that you are quietly withholding?

To kill. A blade in the question. Who is killing anyone? Not yet — but by v. 6 these men will spend the Sabbath planning a death. Jesus says it before they have said it to each other. The Sabbath on which he restores a hand is the Sabbath on which they plot murder, and only one of those is work.

Their silence. Not ignorance; these men could argue any point of law for an afternoon. They are silent because the question has one honest answer and it costs them the case. Most of us have used that silence: not denying what was said, not acting on it either. It feels safe. It isn’t. Someone who says nothing hasn’t stayed neutral; he has decided, and avoided the cost of saying so. Two verses later that silence walks out and starts making arrangements.

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looks around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and tells the man to stretch out his hand; he does, and it is restored. Jesus shows holy anger that grieves rather than gloats, and his power works as we obey his word, not before.

Anger. The only place in Mark where Jesus is said to look at a group with anger. He swept the room face by face. Matthew and Luke record the healing and omit this; Mark, carrying Peter’s memory, keeps it. Many carry a picture of Jesus in which this can’t fit — endlessly mild, never provoked. That picture isn’t from the Bible. The Jesus of the Gospels was angry here, made a whip and cleared the temple courts (John 2:15), and called men “whitewashed tombs” to their faces (Matthew 23:27) — and never sinned.

Angry and holy. “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26) isn’t a contradiction but a command with a boundary. How do you tell the two apart? Mark answers in the same sentence: “grieved.” The anger and grief are one motion. He is cut to the heart over what these men have become. “Hardness” is the word for a callus, or a broken bone healing into something stony — once soft, thickened at the point of injury until it can’t feel.

A test. Sinful anger enjoys itself. It wants the other person diminished, rehearses the argument in the shower, and would be quietly disappointed if they repented, because then there would be nothing to be right about. Righteous anger grieves; it hurts to feel; it wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and would be delighted to be made unnecessary. Run that on the last thing you were angry about: did you want the person changed, or beaten?

An impossible command. “Stretch out your hand” — exactly what the man couldn’t do; he had likely tried a thousand times. And Mark gives no interval: he stretched it out, and it was restored. He obeyed, and in the obeying the power was there.

The order of the Christian life. He didn’t stretch out a hand already healed; the stretching is where the healing happened. Faith isn’t the feeling of confidence you wait for before you move; it is moving on his word while you still feel as incapable as a minute ago. That answers the believer stuck on “I would obey if I had more faith.” You will find you had the faith in the doing. Make the phone call. Say the sentence. Open the Bible at six when nothing in you wants to. The strength comes in the stretching, never before.

Two pairs of hands. One withered hand held out at his command and made new; and his own sound workman’s hands stretched out one Friday on wood and ruined, so that the ruined might be restored. He healed with a word what would cost him nails.
verseByVerse.note: Mark alone records Jesus’ anger and grief here; Matthew and Luke do not mention them.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees leave and immediately plot with the Herodians how to destroy Jesus. Hardened hearts that reject God’s plain work will even unite with old enemies against him — and correct doctrine detached from love is no safeguard.

They walked out. An undeniable miracle in front of them, in a room they know, on a man they had seen every week for years — and they leave the service. Nothing is said about the hand; no one congratulates the man. “Immediately”: no going home to think and pray. The decision is made on the spot.

Unbelievable allies. A first-century reader would have found this almost incredible. The Pharisees were strict separatists devoted to Israel’s purity, who despised collaboration with Rome and saw Herod’s family as half-Edomite puppets. The Herodians were exactly that party: courtiers of Herod Antipas, worldly, political, invested in the arrangement with Rome. On religion, politics, money and nationhood they agreed on nothing. Within minutes of the healing they agree at once.

A shared hatred of the light. Men who can’t agree on one positive thing cooperate beautifully on a negative one. Luke notes drily that Pilate and Herod “became friends with each other that very day” — the day they both had a hand in trying Jesus (Luke 23:12). One of the ugliest reliable facts of human nature, on display a fifth of the way into the Gospel.

Destroy. Not discredit, out-argue or discipline. And it is still the Sabbath. Accused of violating the day by restoring a hand with a sentence, Jesus’ accusers spend the rest of the holy day organising a killing. They wouldn’t have carried a bed; they will carry a cross to the authorities. That is a hardened heart from inside: convinced it is defending God, with murder in the diary. No one in that meeting thought himself wicked. They thought themselves serious.

Orthodoxy is not a preservative. A sober word for anyone who takes doctrine seriously, as we should. These were the orthodox party: they believed in the resurrection, Scripture’s authority, the coming Messiah and the moral law — and left a service where God had visibly acted to plan his death. The safeguard was never doctrine alone, but whether it was still attached to love for God and pity for people. A test: does your theology make you more tender toward people, or only more correct?

Already decided. Chapter 3 of sixteen, and his death is already decided. From here he walks with his eyes open toward a verdict already reached — and heals someone in nearly every chapter on the way.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family’s rule — unlikely allies for the Pharisees.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdraws to the lake, and great crowds come from every region — Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, Tyre and Sidon — having heard what he was doing. Opposition only widens his reach, and the crowd from every direction previews the worldwide church, though many came for his power more than for him.

Withdrawing, not escalating. He doesn’t confront the men who have just decided to kill him or stay in the synagogue to make a point. He goes to the lake, and the ministry grows. The leaders’ opposition didn’t thin the crowd; it thickened it, pushing him out of a room that held eighty onto a shore that could hold thousands.

A map. Mark rarely lists addresses; here six regions in two verses. Galilee is home. Judea and Jerusalem are eighty or ninety miles south — the better part of a week’s walk. Idumea is old Edom beyond the southern desert, the descendants of Esau, forcibly converted a century before and barely counted Jewish — Herod’s own people. Beyond the Jordan is the east bank, Gentile-mixed. Tyre and Sidon aren’t in Israel at all but pagan Phoenician ports to the north-west, the cities of Jezebel’s father.

The coming church in miniature. The list runs outward in every direction — Jew, half-Jew, Gentile. Mark shows a crowd that looks like the church to come: everyone from everywhere, drawn to one man, most nowhere near understanding him. It rehearses old promises: to Abraham, “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3); to the Servant, “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). By the Gospel’s end a Roman soldier will say the true thing the crowd didn’t (15:39), and by Acts the list will keep going to Rome.

Why they came. Be honest: not for teaching. They “heard all that he was doing.” A crowd assembled by reports of power, and within chapters most will be gone; the day comes when he says something hard and “many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (John 6:66).

A test. What brought you to Christ, and what is keeping you? Some walked a hundred miles to that shore for what they had heard he could give; some for who he was. The shoreline looked identical either way, and only one survives a hard winter.
verseByVerse.note: Idumea (old Edom) lay south of Judea; Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities on the coast to the north. The crowd came from every direction.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has a boat kept ready so the crowd won’t crush him, because the many he had healed and all the sick were pressing to touch him. The Son of God accepted human limits and took practical precautions, and he received desperate people even with mixed motives.

An escape route. A small fishing boat kept just offshore — a platform and a way out, “lest they crush him,” the verb for a mob pressing a man against a wall. This wasn’t an audience but desperate, sick, frightened people who had heard that touching him worked. There were children in that crowd; people got hurt in crowds like that. And Jesus, who could have stilled them with a sentence, asked his friends to get a boat.

He did not despise the means. The Son of God, in a real human body with real exhaustion, took an ordinary precaution. He didn’t stand and let himself be trampled to prove something about faith.

Permission to be finite. Tired Christians rarely give themselves permission to hear this. Jesus didn’t meet every need that presented itself or stay available every hour people wanted him. He withdrew (v. 7). He slept in boats (4:38). He went before dawn where they couldn’t find him (1:35). He let a crowd stand on a beach while he pushed out a few yards. If you are the one everyone comes to — in a family, church or job — take the boat. Being finite isn’t a character flaw; it is how you were made, and the Lord worked within it. The needs around you are infinite and you are not, and pretending otherwise isn’t devotion. It is a slow way of becoming useless to everybody. A test: where do you need to keep a boat ready this week?

He healed many. Not a handful of cases; so many the beach became dangerous. And Mark doesn’t tidy up the afflictions; they had worn people down for years.

Mixed motives received. This crowd had no theology, invitation or understanding of who he was — just people in pain mobbing him so hard he needed an exit. He didn’t lecture them about motives first. He healed them. Remember that when you come to him with mixed motives and a bad attitude, wanting relief far more than him. He has never turned anyone away for coming badly. Come as the crowd came, and let him sort out your motives once you are near enough to reach.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, "You are the Son of God." And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever unclean spirits see Jesus, they fall down and cry, “You are the Son of God,” and he strictly orders them not to make him known. Correct words about Jesus without love for him are worthless, and Jesus would not let his identity be announced by his enemies or before it could be rightly understood.

The only exact theology. In that whole crowd from six regions, apostles included, the only voices saying anything theologically exact belong to demons.

They fell down. The posture of worship — not willingly, but because in his presence they can do nothing else. A small, involuntary rehearsal of the day when “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10). Every knee, including these. The only question any creature decides is whether it bows now in love or later in ruin.

A word-perfect, worthless creed. “You are the Son of God” — what the voice said at the Jordan (1:11), more than the disciples have managed. And it does the demons no good at all. That dismantles something many rest on. “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!” (James 2:19). These spirits have better Christology than most of the crowd; they fall down, which the Pharisees didn’t; they confess him aloud, which Peter hasn’t yet — and remain what they are.

A test. Could you tick every box on a statement of faith and still be, in your heart, at a distance from the Person it describes? The difference between the demons’ confession and a Christian’s isn’t accuracy. One says “You are the Son of God” and means “Keep away from me”; the other says the same words and means “Have me.” Mark ends this chapter by saying which you are: not by what you can recite, but whether you do the will of God (v. 35).

Why silence true testimony? Partly timing. In Galilee in that decade, “Son of God” shouted over thousands from six regions would have been heard as a call to arms — a king to drive out Rome. He won’t be crowned before he is crucified; a title taken on those terms would have to be unlearned at the cross. He lets the words stand at last on a Roman officer’s lips at the foot of it (15:39), where no one can mistake what kind of King he is. And partly the messenger: the truth about the Son of God won’t be carried on the tongue of the father of lies. That commission belongs to a fisherman, a tax collector, a Zealot — and to you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–35 — The Twelve, the Accusation, and the True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 13–19). Jesus goes up, calls whom he wants, and constitutes twelve men — a number nobody in Israel could hear innocently. The stated purpose comes in two halves in a deliberate order: that they might be with him, and that he might send them out. The list ends on a name that ruins it.

The two accusations (vv. 20–22). Back at the house the pressure is such that they cannot even eat, and two verdicts arrive from opposite directions. His family says he is out of his mind and comes to take him home. A delegation from Jerusalem says he is possessed and works by the prince of demons. Both agree something is badly wrong with him; they differ only on whether he is mad or evil.

The answer (vv. 23–27). Jesus takes the charge apart with cold logic and then turns it round: the reason demons are leaving is that a stronger man has broken into the house, tied up the owner, and is carrying out his property.

The warning and the family (vv. 28–35). The widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel, with one terrible exception attached — and then his mother and brothers arrive outside, and he looks round at the people sitting on the floor and calls them his family.
verseByVerse.theology:
The strong man of v. 27 is the hinge of the chapter and of the Gospel. Jesus concedes the scribes' premise that there is a real kingdom of darkness with a real ruler and a securely held house. What he denies is which side of the door he is on. He is not an agent of the owner. He is the burglar.

And the order in the picture is exact: the binding comes first, the plundering after. You cannot carry off a strong man's goods while he is loose. Every exorcism in Mark, every healing, every sinner set free, is loot being carried out of a house whose owner has already been tied up. This is why the New Testament can speak of Christians as people delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13) — transferred is a word for moving property.

Then ask when the binding happened, and the answer is the surprise at the centre of the faith. He bound the strong man by being bound himself. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in him — in the cross (Col. 2:15). The strong man was tied up by a stronger man who let himself be tied up first, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men appointed so that they might be with him — and only then be sent out. A long season of watching him pray, eat, weep, touch lepers, sleep in boats, before they were first sent out to preach (6:7-13).

Now: the order is still not negotiable, and it is still the thing we reverse. It is entirely possible to be extremely busy for God and scarcely ever with him — to run a rota, lead a group, defend the faith online, and go months without an unhurried hour in his company. The activity is not the problem; the sequence is. Ministry that does not flow out of being with Jesus becomes performance, and performance eventually becomes exhaustion or pride, and often both.

The plainest way to test it is the calendar. Look at last week honestly. How much of it was doing things for him, and how much was being with him? If the first number is large and the second is near zero, you have inverted verse 14, and no amount of usefulness will make up for it — because the sending was never meant to be the source of the strength.

And there is comfort in the same verse for the person who cannot do much at all: the first calling on every disciple is one that illness, age and obscurity cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the mountain Jesus calls those he wants, and they come; he appoints twelve to be with him and to be sent out to preach with authority over demons. Christ chooses his people by his own will, reconstitutes Israel around himself, and makes being with him the first calling of every disciple, before any work.

Up the mountain. In the Bible, going up a mountain to constitute a people isn’t neutral travel; Moses went up and came down with a nation ordered around twelve tribes. Luke adds that Jesus spent the whole night there in prayer before choosing (Luke 6:12).
