Five thousand well-fed men on a hillside in an occupied country is a rebellion looking for a leader — and twelve disciples who had spent the evening handing out miraculous bread, one a Zealot, were in no state to resist the mood. So he breaks it up: men onto the boat, and the crowd dealt with himself.

A crown without a cross. What he refuses is a crown offered freely, by acclamation, without a cross — the shortcut the devil laid before him in the wilderness (cf. Matthew 4:8–9). He won’t take a kingdom on those terms, because a king who feeds you isn’t the same as a king who saves you.

Prayer with the first free hour. He has had no rest; the retreat was ruined; he has taught for hours, fed thousands, defused a political crisis, and personally dismissed a crowd of that size — a whole evening in a subordinate clause. And with the first free hour he climbs a hill in the dark to pray.

Three prayers alone. The second of three times Mark shows him praying alone, and their placing is the sermon: before dawn at the height of his popularity (1:35); here, on the night the nation tried to crown him; and in Gethsemane, the night they came to arrest him (14:32–39). Success, the offer of glory, the approach of death — handled the same way. That quietly exposes us. Most of us pray hardest at the third kind of moment and hardly at the first two. Prosperity is treated as needing no prayer, and it is the season in which people are most often lost. A test: when things are going well, does your praying increase or fade?

Separated in the dark. A boat somewhere in the dark, a man alone on the mountain. They are separated and can’t see him; night has come down between them. That is how a hard stretch feels from inside the boat — and the next verse changes everything.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees the disciples straining at the oars against the wind, and in the fourth watch of the night he comes to them walking on the sea, meaning to pass by them. While we struggle in the dark, Christ sees and prays for us, comes at his own right time, and reveals himself as God who treads the waves.

He saw them. Perhaps the most comforting clause in the chapter. Middle of the night, he on a mountain ashore, they three or four miles out on the lake (John 6:19). Whatever kind of seeing it was, he watched them the whole time. They didn’t know it. From inside the boat there was only wind, black water, and an empty horizon; every fact available said they were alone.

Tormented rowing. “Making headway painfully” — literally tormented in the rowing, the root of the word for torture. Not a storm threatening to sink them as in chapter 4, but worse in its way: hours of grinding, unrewarded effort. They row and the shore gets no closer. And “the wind was against them” — and they are out there because he sent them. Obedience put them in the wind.

The shape of much Christian experience. You are where he put you, pulling as hard as you can; nothing moves; he seems somewhere else entirely; and it is dark. The verse tells you what you can’t know from inside the boat: he is watching, and was all night, and praying while he watched. Verse 46 has him praying on the mountain; v. 48 has him seeing them from it. Those belong together and are still true: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). A test: in your long, hard rowing, do you remember who is watching and praying?

The fourth watch. Between three and six in the morning. They set out in the evening and have been at the oars perhaps nine hours. He came not at the first hour when it got hard, nor at midnight, but in the last watch, when men have stopped talking and are simply pulling. He is never early, as we would arrange it. He has never been late.

Passing by. “He meant to pass by them” sounds as though he would leave them to it. He didn’t. “Passing by” is the Old Testament’s language for God making himself visible. To Moses: “while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand” (Exodus 33:22). At Elijah’s cave: “And behold, the LORD passed by” (1 Kings 19:11). Most exactly, Job says God alone “stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8), and three verses later, “Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not” (Job 9:11). Trampling the waves and passing by, in one passage, about God. This isn’t a man taking a shortcut past a struggling boat but a self-revelation: coming to them in the dark on the water, doing what Job says God alone does, in the language of every appearance of God in their Bible. He wasn’t passing them by but passing before them, so they could see who had been watching from the mountain.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch was about 3 to 6 a.m. “Pass by” recalls God “passing by” Moses and Elijah to show his glory.

parallels.desc: I will make my goodness pass before you

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing him walking on the sea, the disciples think he is a ghost and cry out in terror, but at once he says, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” Christ sometimes comes in ways we first fear, and his comfort rests not on changed circumstances but on who he is — the great “I am.”

A ghost. Of course they cried out. Between three and six in the morning, hours into a headwind, wet, exhausted, frightened — and a figure moving on the water beside the boat. The word is “phantasma,” an apparition; in that world a shape on the sea at night was an omen of death, and every sailor had grown up on such stories.

Coming as what we dread. The fair thing first: the Lord of glory came in the exact form of their worst fear, and they didn’t recognise him. Not stupid — human. The one thing that could save them looked, in the dark, like what was most likely to kill them. That is often how it is. God has a way of coming to his people in the shape of what they most dread. Joseph’s brothers didn’t recognise their salvation in the man who had them arrested. What is bearing down on you out of the dark this year may be the Lord, and you may not know it at the time.

All of them. “They all saw him and were terrified.” Mark rules out one man’s imagination or a trick of light. Twelve men, four of them fishermen who had spent their lives on that water at night, saw the same thing.

His voice first. “Immediately he spoke to them.” The moment they cry out, he speaks — before the wind drops or he gets into the boat. Before anything about their circumstances changes, he tells them who he is. That is still the order in which he deals with frightened people.

“It is I.” Literally “I am.” In ordinary speech, how you identify yourself in the dark: it’s me. But these are the words God gave Moses at the bush — “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14) — and they run through Isaiah on God’s lips: “I am he. Before me no god was formed” (Isaiah 43:10). Spoken here by a man standing on water, having crossed a sea that Scripture says God alone tramples.

The whole of Christian comfort. In order: “Take heart” — courage now, before anything changes. “It is I” — the reason, and the reason is a Person, not the weather, with the name from the bush. “Do not be afraid” — following only from the middle phrase. No argument: he doesn’t say the wind will drop or the night is nearly over. He tells them who is with them and treats that as enough. It is enough — spoken from the middle of the water they feared. A test: what are you waiting to change before you take heart? Take heart now, because of who he is.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gets into the boat, the wind stops, and the disciples are utterly astounded, for they hadn’t understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened. Even devoted disciples can fail to learn from God’s past goodness and grow hardened — yet Christ does not give up on them but comes alongside them.

He gets in. After nine hours of rowing and a night of terror, an almost domestic ending: a man climbs over the side and sits with them, and the wind stops. Mark doesn’t even say he rebuked it. It simply stops, because he is aboard.

A verdict no church would invent. “They did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.” This is the Gospel’s verdict on the Twelve, from a man whose information came from their chief, circulated while most were alive. And the connection isn’t the one we would expect: the walking on water astonished them because they hadn’t understood the loaves. The bread was the lesson. That afternoon they had carried food from his hands to five thousand and come back with twelve baskets, and drawn no conclusion about who he was. Had they understood the loaves, a man on the water wouldn’t have been a horror; it would have been the same Person doing the same kind of thing.

Past mercies as evidence. God’s past dealings with us are meant to be evidence. A new trouble often knocks us flat because we drew nothing from the last deliverance — relieved, grateful for a fortnight, and filed it as something that happened rather than something we learned about him. A test: what past mercy of God should be shaping how you face today’s trouble?

The word for his enemies. “Hardened” — the same term Mark used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and walked out to plan a murder (3:5). These aren’t enemies but apostles, mid-mission, fresh from casting out demons in his name, described in his opponents’ vocabulary. So hardness isn’t only an unbeliever’s disease, and it doesn’t announce itself. It isn’t disbelief — they believed much. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected, the state in which the same truths arrive and produce nothing, in which someone can carry the bread and never taste it (cf. 8:17–21).

Not final. Mark says it without despair, because we know what these men became. The hardening was real and not final. He kept them, taught them, corrected them; was betrayed and denied by them; and after the resurrection fed them breakfast on a beach and sent them out — and the man whose memory this Gospel preserves had denied him three times. He doesn’t give up on hard-hearted disciples. He gets into the boat with them.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Landing at Gennesaret, Jesus is recognised at once, and people carry their sick from everywhere and lay them in the marketplaces, begging to touch even the fringe of his garment, and all who touch it are healed. Desperate need that sets aside pride reaches Christ, and one person’s testimony can stir a whole region to come to him.

Blown off course. Gennesaret is the fertile plain on the north-west shore, a few miles of rich farmland Josephus praised. They had been sent to Bethsaida (v. 45); the night put them somewhere else, as nine hours against the wind will.

No rest again. The boat touches shore and it starts. Word spreads, and people start carrying — not helping the sick walk but carrying them on their pallets from villages and farms, chasing a moving target: “to wherever they heard he was.” He walks; the beds are carried after him all day by relays of neighbours and relatives. Whole communities mobilised, and not a word about any of them wanting anything for themselves.

In the marketplace. The open square where everything happened — shops, courts, gossip, day-labourers waiting for work — and the sick laid in rows in the middle of it, in public, in everyone’s way. These people have stopped caring how it looks. A desperation that has burned through embarrassment is the only kind that ever gets anywhere with Christ. A test: what is pride or embarrassment keeping you from bringing to him?

The fringe. The tassel every observant Jewish man wore at the corners of his cloak, as a reminder of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). The request has a one-chapter history: a woman with twelve years of bleeding said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well” (5:28), reached from behind, and was healed and called Daughter. Now a province does what she did. That is what one healed woman’s story did when it got out — as one healed madman’s did across the lake (5:20). Mark keeps showing the same mechanism: someone tells what happened to them, and a district comes. Whom could your story bring?

All of them. “As many as touched it were made well.” No qualification, no theology corrected first. Their understanding was thin and probably half superstitious, as hers had been. He doesn’t lecture them about the tassel; he heals them.

Nazareth and Gennesaret. The chapter that began with a village refusing him because they knew him too well ends with strangers running across a plain with beds. Nazareth had every advantage and wouldn’t stretch out a hand; Gennesaret had almost no understanding and grabbed the hem of his coat. The difference isn’t intelligence, opportunity or information. One town thought it already knew him. The other only knew it needed him.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

6.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 should not be softened — Mark wrote he could do no mighty work there, where Matthew writes did not do many (Matt. 13:58). But the exception clause settles the sense: he healed a few sick people that afternoon, so it was no failure of power. The impossibility is moral. In a village that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been spectacle, and he does not do spectacle — he refuses a sign to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and stands silent before Herod, who wanted to watch one (Luke 23:8–9). Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons. Unbelief does not disable God; it makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is not a shortcut past a struggling boat. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible: while my glory passes by (Ex. 33:22), behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). Most exactly, Job says of God that he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea, and three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11). Trampling the sea and passing by, in one passage, about God. And when they scream he answers with egō eimi — it is I, the ordinary words for identifying yourself in the dark, and the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14).

And their hearts were hardened (v. 52) is said of the apostles, in the very word used of the men in the synagogue who watched a hand restored and left to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only. It is not disbelief — the Twelve believed a great deal. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected, the state in which a man can carry the bread and never taste it.
6.examples:
Herod is the most searching portrait in the chapter, because he is not a scoffer. He feared John, knew he was a righteous and holy man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. He sent for him. He came back for more. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace: real interest, real feeling, real pleasure, and no root.

Everything was there except the one thing John was actually asking for. Herodias stayed. And a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to — it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

Then: a king who kept his oath and killed a prophet, because of his oaths and his guests. Not conscience — he had already lost that argument. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

Now: almost nobody does the worst thing they ever do because they wanted to. They do it because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable — the joke laughed at, the thing gone along with once the room had turned, the stand not taken because of who would have seen. Peter is eight chapters from exactly this, in a courtyard, in front of a servant girl. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25), and it walked a king with an army into a murder he did not want to commit.

So the test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether you can name one thing it has actually cost you this year.

7.title: What Really Defiles a Man
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. <sup>3</sup>(For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, <sup>4</sup>and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) <sup>5</sup>And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?” <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>7</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ <sup>8</sup>You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.” <sup>9</sup>And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! <sup>10</sup>For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>11</sup>But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban”’ (that is, given to God)— <sup>12</sup>then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, <sup>13</sup>thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” <sup>14</sup>And he called the people to him again and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: <sup>15</sup>There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” <sup>17</sup>And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. <sup>18</sup>And he said to them, “Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, <sup>19</sup>since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?” (Thus he declared all foods clean.) <sup>20</sup>And he said, “What comes out of a person is what defiles him. <sup>21</sup>For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, <sup>22</sup>coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. <sup>23</sup>All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.” <sup>24</sup>And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. <sup>25</sup>But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. <sup>26</sup>Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. <sup>27</sup>And he said to her, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>28</sup>But she answered him, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” <sup>29</sup>And he said to her, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” <sup>30</sup>And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. <sup>31</sup>Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. <sup>32</sup>And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. <sup>33</sup>And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. <sup>34</sup>And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” <sup>35</sup>And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. <sup>36</sup>And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. <sup>37</sup>And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes down a wall, and then walks through the gap.

It opens with a delegation from Jerusalem who have travelled ninety miles to raise the matter of unwashed hands. Jesus does not defend his disciples; he quotes Isaiah at the delegation, and then proves the charge with a single devastating example. Corban was a vow that could put a man's money beyond his parents' reach by declaring it dedicated to God — and the tradition would not merely permit it but forbid him to change his mind. A rule invented to honour God had become a device for robbing your father, with a straight face and in God's name.

Then he calls the crowd over and says the thing that changed everything: there is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him. Mark, writing down Peter's preaching years later, adds six words in a bracket — thus he declared all foods clean — and the boundary between clean and unclean peoples, kept for fifteen centuries, is gone.

And having dissolved it, he crosses it. The second half of the chapter is two healings on Gentile ground: a Phoenician mother who takes his own hard word and finds the door in it, and a deaf man in the Decapolis brought by friends, taken quietly aside, and given his hearing with one Aramaic word. The crowd's verdict is bigger than they know — he has done all things well is the sentence pronounced over the finished creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The complaint (vv. 1–5). A delegation arrives from Jerusalem — the second one in this Gospel — and what they have come ninety miles to raise is that the disciples do not wash their hands before eating. Mark stops to explain the custom, which tells you he is writing for people who have never heard of it.

The answer (vv. 6–8). Jesus does not defend his men. He quotes Isaiah at the delegation and calls them hypocrites: lips near, heart far, and human rules taught as though God had given them.

The example (vv. 9–13). Then he makes it concrete with a case anyone can follow. A man could put the money owed to his aged parents beyond their reach by pronouncing one word over it — and the tradition would back him. That is not a lapse in the system. That is the system working.

The principle (vv. 14–23). He calls the crowd over and says the most subversive thing in the chapter: nothing that goes into a man can defile him. Mark, writing years later with Peter's memory in his hand, adds a parenthesis that changed the church — thus he declared all foods clean — and then Jesus tells the disciples in private where defilement actually comes from, and lists thirteen of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? Look down the page and the numbers run 15, 17. Nothing has been lost and nothing has been hidden.

The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark do not have a verse 16. Later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said, and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23). What almost certainly happened is that a scribe, copying by hand, felt the sentence belonged after v. 15 and wrote it in the margin, and a later copyist took the margin note for part of the text.

The verse numbering itself is not ancient — it was added in the sixteenth century, long after the manuscripts. So when translators went back to the earliest copies and found the sentence absent, they could not renumber the whole New Testament; they simply left the number empty and put the words in a footnote.

That is worth a plain word of reassurance to any reader who finds a gap like this unsettling. Nothing has been taken out of your Bible. The opposite has happened: we now have older and better copies than were available in 1611, and where those copies show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you so in the margin rather than quietly leaving it in. A faith that will not look at its own manuscripts has something to hide. This one publishes the workings.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Corban — a rule invented to honour God, turned into a device for robbing your parents, with a straight face and in God's name.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. It is the man so committed at church that his mother has not had a visit in four months. It is the giving that goes to the building fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. It is any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been placed in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be quietly dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So here is a test you can actually run, and it is the one this passage supplies. Take any tradition you hold — a practice, a standard, a way of doing things — and ask whether keeping it is currently costing somebody else something God told you to give them. Not whether it is in the Bible; a good many decent traditions are not, and need not be. Whether it has begun to displace a commandment.

Jesus does not attack tradition as such. He attacks tradition that has been promoted — set level with Scripture, and then used against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem notice that some of Jesus’ disciples eat with ritually unwashed hands. Religious leaders who had seen his mighty works fastened instead on a man-made rule — showing how good human traditions can bury God’s word.

A second delegation. The first came from Jerusalem in chapter 3 and concluded he was possessed (3:22). These men made the same ninety-mile journey, and “gathered to him” as a committee gathers. They aren’t here to learn.

The disproportion. Trained theologians have travelled at real expense to Galilee, and what they found to raise is that some of the group didn’t rinse their hands before a meal. Before a man who cleansed a leper, raised a dead girl, fed a district from five loaves and stilled a storm, they have taken notes on his catering.

Fair to them. First, it isn’t about hygiene. “Defiled” is the word for common, profane — the opposite of holy. No one is worried about germs; this is ritual purity. Second, their intention was honourable. The law required priests to wash before handling holy things (Exodus 30:19–21). Wanting the whole nation to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), the Pharisees extended the priestly rule to every Jew and every meal: every table an altar, every family a priesthood. Devout, not contemptible.

Not fair to them. God never asked for it. Washing before ordinary food is nowhere in the law of Moses. It was a good human idea that had hardened into an obligation with the force of a commandment, and people were being judged by it.

How it always happens. No one sets out to replace Scripture. A wise practice is adopted for good reasons. In a generation it is “the way we do things.” In two, it is how serious Christians do things. In three, someone who doesn’t is thought unsound, and no one can say which verse required it. The Pharisees didn’t steal the Bible; they buried it under good ideas (cf. Luke 11:37–38). A test: which of your church’s customs do you treat as if they were commands of God?
verseByVerse.note: The washing in question was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: (For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark explains the Jewish washing rules for his Gentile readers, and the Pharisees ask why the disciples don’t walk according to the tradition of the elders. They openly appeal to human tradition as their authority, a danger for any believer who can’t tell God’s word from inherited custom.

Written for outsiders. Mark stops the story for two verses to explain the custom — something no Jewish reader needed, like explaining a kettle to an Englishman. He writes for Gentiles, almost certainly the church in Rome: he translates Aramaic, converts money into Roman coins, uses Latin loanwords. The oldest Gospel was written for people outside the covenant — quietly relevant to a chapter that ends with a Gentile woman and a Gentile deaf man.

The tradition of the elders. Alongside the written law, Israel developed a vast body of oral interpretation — rulings on what the commandments meant in practice, passed down for centuries and written down around AD 200 as the Mishnah. There is a whole tractate on hand-washing, specifying the quantity of water, the position of the hands, the number of rinses. And the Pharisees held — the crucial point — that this oral tradition had itself been given to Moses at Sinai, with equal authority. That is what Jesus is about to deny.

Cups, pots and couches. Mark’s list is faintly comic, probably on purpose: cups, pots, bronze vessels, the furniture you eat on. Rules for all of it, and men had spent their lives mastering them.

The framing gives it away. “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders?” They don’t ask why the disciples break God’s law. They name exactly which authority is contravened, and are confident it settles the matter. That is the position of someone who can no longer feel the difference between what God said and what his tradition says God meant. He would sincerely say Scripture is supreme; but when a real question arises, he reaches for the tradition, because that is where practical authority has quietly migrated (cf. Colossians 2:8; Galatians 1:14).

A test. Ask, without cynicism, where the practical authority sits in your convictions. When challenged about something you think a Christian should or shouldn’t do, what do you reach for first — the text, or the settled instinct of the people who formed you? The second isn’t always wrong. But someone who can’t tell which he is using has already made the Pharisees’ mistake.
verseByVerse.note: Mark explains Jewish customs for readers who did not know them — likely Gentile Christians, perhaps in Rome. The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law.

parallels.desc: zealous for the traditions of my fathers

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls them hypocrites, quoting Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me… teaching as doctrines the commandments of men,” and says they leave God’s commandment to hold to human tradition. Outward religion can be maintained while the heart is far from God, and worship that rests on human rules is empty.

Past the complaint to the men. He doesn’t answer the question, defend the disciples, or explain. He goes straight to the men making the complaint, opening with the prophet they revered.

Hypocrites. From the Greek theatre: an actor, a man in a mask speaking lines. Not necessarily conscious pretence — which matters, or the charge slides off us. Jesus isn’t merely saying they lie. He is saying there is a gap between performance and person, and the performance has taken over.

Lips near, heart far. Isaiah 29:13 was spoken to a scrupulously religious generation — not idolaters who had abandoned the temple, but people keeping it all up. That is what makes it lethal. And the diagnosis is a measurement of distance: the lips are close; the heart is far. Both true at once, and the first makes the second hard to detect.

How would you know? A concrete answer rather than a shudder. One test: what happens to your religion when no one is watching? The lips are by definition the public part. Prayer only in company, a Bible opened only where seen, generosity that is known — none wrong, all maintainable by a heart gone elsewhere. Subtract the audience and see what is left standing. Another: when did you last enjoy God — not a service, sermon or Christian company, but him? A distant heart can keep every observance and has usually stopped finding pleasure in the Person they are about, and stopped noticing it stopped.

In vain. Worship offered to the right God that achieves nothing — sobering for anyone who assumes attendance is acceptance. And the reason is precise: “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.” Not having human customs — every church must — but teaching them as if they came from God.

Leave and hold. “You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” — a man with both hands full who must drop one thing to pick up another. No one in that delegation thought he was abandoning God’s commandment; each would say he was defending it. That is why Jesus must prove it, and next he does, with one devastating example.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother'; and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sarcastically says they have a fine way of rejecting God’s commandment to establish their tradition, and cites “Honor your father and your mother” and the penalty for reviling parents. God’s plain command includes practical care for aging parents — a concrete test of whether religion is real.

Withering irony. “You have a fine way” — beautifully done, expertly managed: a man watching skilled work he despises. And note the direction: not that they neglect the commandment while pursuing tradition, but reject it in order to establish tradition. Setting it aside isn’t a side effect; it is the mechanism.

Immovable ground. He chooses the fifth of the Ten Commandments, written by the finger of God, the first with a promise (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). No one could plead ignorance or call it disputed.

Honour means support. We have sentimentalised it. “Honor your father and your mother” isn’t chiefly about small children’s manners. In that world it was mainly an economic obligation, understood as such. No pensions, no state provision; ageing parents were kept alive by their sons. To honour your father meant to feed him when he could no longer work.

A capital matter. He adds Exodus 21:17: treating parents with contempt was punishable by death. That is how seriously God took it. Two immovable stones: God commanded care of parents and attached the severest sanction to its contempt. Next he will show a device, taught by their own school, that let a man walk away from both and feel devout doing it.

A middle-aged man paying his mother’s bills. Jesus’ chosen example of real obedience isn’t a spiritual exercise but that — whether the old people in your family are being looked after. That is where the New Testament keeps landing when it tests a religion: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27); “if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). A test: are your parents, or the older people God has put in your care, being honoured in practical ways this month?

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, 'If a man tells his father or his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban"' (that is, given to God)— then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus exposes the Corban vow, by which a man declared money “given to God” so he no longer had to support his parents — making void God’s word by their tradition, and many such things. Religious devotion can be used as a cover to escape plain duties God has commanded, and God rejects any such exchange.

“But you say.” Three words carrying the whole indictment. God said one thing; you say another.

The mechanism. Mark leaves “Corban” untranslated and glosses it, a technical term. To pronounce something Corban was to declare it dedicated to God, as though laid on the altar, no longer for ordinary use; the scribes taught such a vow was binding and couldn’t be revoked. Now watch it worked. A man has ageing parents; the fifth commandment obliges him to support them, and the sum is real and calculable. He doesn’t want to part with it and can’t simply refuse without disgrace. So he says the word: “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban.” Now his hands are tied by piety. The money is holy; a vow may not be broken; everyone agrees his hands are tied.

Repentance made illegal. “You no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother.” The tradition doesn’t merely allow it; it forbids him to change his mind. The system has made repentance illegal. And the vow made the money unavailable to his parents without necessarily making it unavailable to him; he could keep its use, shielded from his duty by a holy word. So an old man goes hungry, his son is thought devout, and religion has produced exactly what God’s commandment existed to prevent (cf. Numbers 30:2).

Making void. The word for annulling a will. And “many such things you do”: Corban isn’t the disease, just the clearest symptom.

In modern clothes. The shape survives perfectly and is almost never dishonest. The man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother hasn’t had a visit since March. The money given to a fund while a brother in the same congregation can’t pay his heating bill. Any arrangement in which something genuinely religious is set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so the duty can be quietly dropped without anyone feeling wicked (cf. 1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

A test. In one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing someone else something God told me to give them? That is Corban, whatever it is called, and there is no version of it God accepts.
verseByVerse.note: Property declared Corban — dedicated to God — could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the people to him again and said to them, "Hear me, all of you, and understand: There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls the crowd and declares that nothing going into a person from outside can defile him; what comes out of a person defiles him. The food laws were a picture now fulfilled; true defilement comes from the heart, not from what we eat.

A deliberately public word. He turns from the Jerusalem scholars, raises his voice, and calls over the ordinary people at the edge of the argument. He is about to say something the experts won’t like, and says it to everyone. “Hear me, all of you, and understand” — not just attention, but thought.

The blast we hardly feel. Hear it as a Jew in that crowd would. Their national life was organised around the distinction he has just erased. Leviticus 11 lists at length what may and may not be eaten — pork, shellfish, rabbit, camel, birds of prey — and contact with a corpse, a leper or a discharge was unclean. It ran through every meal, kitchen, market and dealing with a Gentile neighbour. Not a dietary preference but the boundary marker of God’s people; men had died in the Maccabean persecution rather than eat pork. And he says nothing that goes into a man from outside can defile him. Either an outrage, or the arrival of what the whole system pointed to. No third option — presumably why he said “understand.”

A picture fulfilled. The food laws were always a picture: a daily, physical lesson in clean and unclean, drummed into a nation three times a day for fifteen centuries, so they would know in their bones that holiness matters and not everything is acceptable to God. A picture isn’t abolished when what it pictured arrives; it is fulfilled and put away. What it taught all along is that defilement is real — and he is about to say where it lives (cf. Romans 14:14).

Does this mean it doesn’t matter what I take in — what I watch, read or drink? No. Jesus is speaking about the food laws, not everything that enters through eyes and ears. Sin comes from the heart, but what we feed the heart matters: “Keep your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23). The lustful look is adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28), and Paul says, “I will not be dominated by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). A test: what are you feeding your heart through your eyes and ears this week?

The missing verse 16. Your Bible runs 15, then 17. Nothing has gone missing. The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no v. 16; later copies add “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear,” which Jesus certainly said and Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 23). A scribe likely wrote it in the margin, and a later copyist took the note into the text. Verse numbers came only in the sixteenth century; when translators found the earliest copies lacked the sentence, they couldn’t renumber the New Testament, so they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote. Nothing has been removed. We have older, better copies than four centuries ago, and honest translators tell you in the margin where a sentence crept in. A faith that hid its manuscripts would have something to hide; this one prints its workings at the bottom of the page.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 16: “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. And he said to them, "Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?" (Thus he declared all foods clean.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Privately the disciples ask about the saying; Jesus, sighing at their slowness, explains that food enters the stomach, not the heart — and Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean.” Christ abolished the food laws of Moses for his people, and even an apostle like Peter took years to absorb what he had plainly been taught.

The pattern of chapter 4. Public saying, private explanation, given to those who stayed and asked. They call it a parable — they knew something large had been said and had no idea what. “Then are you also without understanding?” There is weariness in it. But he answers; rebuke and explanation come together, as in 4:13. He doesn’t withhold teaching from slow disciples; he sighs and teaches them.

Stomach, not heart. The argument is almost crude, deliberately. Food doesn’t travel to the soul; it goes to the stomach, does its work and leaves the body. Whatever route moral corruption takes into a person, it isn’t that one. He distinguishes what the system had blurred: ceremonial uncleanness, about ritual standing, and moral defilement, about what a person actually is. The Pharisees spent so long on the first they treated it as the second — and ended up ceremonially spotless and robbing their parents.

Mark’s parenthesis. “Thus he declared all foods clean” isn’t Jesus’ sentence but Mark’s, an inspired comment drawing out the meaning. And Mark, by every early account, is writing down Peter’s preaching.

Are Christians free to eat any food? Yes. The food laws of Moses no longer bind anyone in Christ: Peter was told, “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Acts 10:15), and Paul says “everything created by God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4). Love may still limit that freedom: a Christian shouldn’t insist on his rights in a way that wounds a weaker believer (Romans 14:13–21; 1 Corinthians 8:13), and those who keep kosher out of conscience or for the sake of witness to Jewish friends are free to do so. What no one may do is make food a condition of standing with God (cf. Colossians 2:16–17).

Peter’s slow confession. Peter was in that house and heard this from the Lord himself. Years later on a rooftop in Joppa, God let down a sheet of unclean animals and told him to eat, and Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean” — and it took three times (Acts 10:9–16). Then he was called before the Jerusalem church to explain eating with Gentiles, and later Paul rebuked him publicly at Antioch for pulling back from Gentile tables (Galatians 2:11–14). So v. 19’s parenthesis is the note of a man who finally understood what he was told to his face long before.

Comfort for slow learners. You can be taught a truth clearly, by Christ in Scripture, and go years without it landing — then have it land in a way that reorganises everything. That isn’t proof you were never taught; it is what learning looks like in creatures like us. Peter needed the sermon, a vision, a Gentile household, a church council and a public rebuke, and he got there. A test: what truth have you known for years that God may be pressing home now?
verseByVerse.note: The food laws of Leviticus 11 had marked Israel off from the nations; Mark draws out that Jesus set them aside.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "What comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says what comes out of a person defiles him, for from within, out of the heart, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride and foolishness. Sin springs from the human heart, not merely from circumstances, so what we need is not better surroundings or stricter rules but a new heart from God.

The location is the doctrine. “From within, out of the heart of man.” Not from circumstances, upbringing, company, poverty, culture, or the food on the plate. From within — and the heart in the Bible isn’t the seat of emotions but the control room: what you love, choose, decide and are.

Thirteen items. Read them one at a time. Evil thoughts — first, because everything after starts here. Sexual immorality — the whole range. Theft, murder, adultery — three commandments named flatly. Coveting — the desire to have more, the engine under much of the rest. Wickedness. Deceit. Sensuality — shamelessness, the loss of the capacity to be embarrassed. Envy — literally an evil eye, the look you give what belongs to someone else. Slander. Pride. Foolishness — moral senselessness, the state of one who has stopped thinking straight about God.

No grading. Murder sits with envy, adultery with pride, theft with foolishness. We would have graded them. Jesus doesn’t, because he isn’t ranking behaviours by social damage; he is naming what comes from one source (cf. Galatians 5:19–21).

Against our culture. The modern account of human trouble is almost entirely external: people go wrong because of what was done to them, what surrounds them, systems, pressures, pasts. Some of that is true, and Scripture is fierce about oppression and tender about wounds. But the modern remedy follows the modern diagnosis: change the environment and what is underneath will come right. And the counsel: trust yourself; follow your heart. Jesus says the heart is where it comes from: “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9).

A test. Look at the thirteen and find the ones you would quietly exclude from your account of yourself. Most of us can manage the first few from a distance. Try coveting. Try envy — the small drop in your stomach when a colleague does well. Try slander, which needs no lie, only a true thing said to lower someone. Try pride. If they are in you — and they are — they didn’t come in from outside, no change of circumstances will remove them, and no washing of hands will touch them.

The only remedy. Not a better system, nor a stricter one. God promised the only remedy that reaches this deep: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). That is what the man before them came to do. Not to clean the outside of the cup, but to make people new — by being “made… to be sin” for us though he “knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that what comes out of a human heart can at last be something other than this list. Ask him for that new heart today.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — Two Healings Beyond Israel’s Borders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Tyre (vv. 24–30). Having just dismantled the boundary between clean and unclean, Jesus walks across it. He goes north into pagan Phoenicia, tries to stay hidden, and fails within hours — because a woman with a demonised daughter has heard he is there. What passes between them is the hardest exchange in the Gospel and one of the greatest lessons in prayer anywhere in Scripture.

The Decapolis (vv. 31–37). Then a long looping journey back down the eastern side of the lake — through Gentile country the whole way — and a man is brought to him who is deaf and can barely speak. Jesus takes him away from the crowd, uses touch instead of words because touch is the only language the man can receive, looks up, groans, and says one word.

The two halves belong together and the order is not accidental. The teaching cleared the ground: nothing outside a man defiles him. The healings show what that means in practice — a Phoenician mother and a Gentile deaf man, both of them outside every boundary Israel had, both of them served.

And the crowd's verdict at the end is bigger than they know: he has done all things well.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was Jesus being cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? It is the first question any honest reader asks, and it deserves a straight answer rather than an embarrassed one.

Three things take the sting out without softening the difficulty. The word first (v. 27) is the hinge: let the children be fed first. That is not a refusal; it is an order of service, and it implies a second course. Paul states the same order without apology — to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16). The dogs are under the table (v. 28), and the picture is domestic: not the scavengers of the street but the household pets under the table while the family eats. They are inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants what she asks, immediately, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28).

He was not insulting her. He was handing her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find the door. She did, in one sentence, and it is the only exchange in the Gospels where someone answers Jesus back and he says they are right.

And the deaf man's healing is the new creation beginning. The crowd's he has done all things well echoes Genesis 1:31 — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. And he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah's sign of the age of the Messiah: then... the ears of the deaf unstopped... and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isa. 35:5–6). They meant only that this healer was impressive. They were quoting the first page of the Bible and the promise of the last days in the same breath.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who could not hear, brought by friends who could — because he could not hear the news, could not ask, and could not have explained what he needed.

Now: every person who is carried to Christ by somebody else. It is the four on the roof in chapter 2 all over again, and it is worth noticing how often in this Gospel the person healed did not get there under their own power.

And look at how he handles him. He takes him aside from the crowd privately. A deaf man in a jostling crowd is a man being stared at and unable to follow a word of it. Jesus removes him from the audience before he touches him — which is a rebuke to every way of helping people that requires the helped to be visible.

Then he uses touch, because touch is the only language the man has: fingers into the ears, saliva on the tongue, a look up to heaven to say where this is coming from. It is not a ritual; it is a conversation conducted in the only vocabulary available. He tells the man what is about to happen to him in signs he can read.

And he sighed. Standing in front of one ruined pair of ears, the Creator groans — as Paul says the whole creation is making, and we with it, waiting for redemption (Rom. 8:22–23). He is not indifferent to what has been done to his world. He feels it, in the body he took, over one man nobody has named.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to the Gentile region of Tyre and Sidon and tries to stay hidden, but a Syrophoenician woman whose little daughter has an unclean spirit falls at his feet, begging him to cast it out. Jesus crosses the boundaries he has just dissolved, and a complete outsider comes to him in desperate faith.

Over the border. Tyre is a Phoenician port on the Mediterranean, thirty-odd miles north-west of Galilee — pagan territory, the country of Jezebel’s father (1 Kings 16:31), denounced by the prophets (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28), a place a devout Jew wouldn’t go without reason. And the placing is deliberate: having said nothing from outside can defile, he walks straight over the boundary he has dissolved.

He couldn’t be hidden. He enters a house and doesn’t want anyone to know — the rest that never happened in chapter 6, attempted by leaving the country. “Yet he could not be hidden” has a double bottom. His reputation crossed the border ahead of him. And it simply isn’t possible for this Person to be concealed; whatever room he enters, he is what he is.

What she overcame. “Little daughter” — the tender word Jairus used (5:23) — and the mother at his feet. A woman approaching a male Jewish teacher, uninvited, in a private house, for a child not present: every convention in the region is against it. And her daughter has an unclean spirit, so she has already tried everything Tyre offered.

Every kind of outsider. Mark makes sure we know what she is: a Gentile — literally “a Greek,” Greek in language and culture; “Syrophoenician,” a Phoenician of the Syrian province. Matthew calls her a Canaanite (Matthew 15:22), the ancient name for peoples Israel was commanded to drive out. Not Jewish by blood, religion or language, and descended from the nations under the ban. There is no category of outsider she doesn’t occupy. A test: who do you think is too far outside to come to Christ?

Was Jesus sent only to Israel? Matthew records Jesus saying, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). That was the shape of his earthly ministry: “Christ became a servant to the circumcised” (Romans 15:8), and the nations would be reached after the cross (Matthew 28:19). His word “first” in v. 27 shows the Gentiles weren’t excluded but were to come in their turn. This woman is an early firstfruit of that harvest (cf. 1 Kings 17:8–16, Elijah and the widow near Sidon).

She kept asking. She went on begging; Matthew records the disciples’ reaction, entirely in character: “Send her away, for she is crying out after us” (Matthew 15:23). Into that scene — a foreign woman on the floor of a borrowed house, asking again and again for a child left at home — comes the hardest sentence Jesus speaks to anyone in this Gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a Gentile port city on the coast north-west of Galilee. “Syrophoenician” means a Phoenician from the Roman province of Syria; Matthew calls her a Canaanite.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Israel was to be fed first, but Jesus’ words hold a door open for Gentiles, and he tests faith in order to draw it out, not to crush it.

No use pretending. The saying that makes readers wince, and a commentary that hurries past isn’t worth reading. First, the picture: a family at a meal, bread on the table, children being fed, and dogs — in this house under the table, not in the yard.

Children, bread, dogs. The children are Israel, God’s own word for the nation: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). The bread is what he has come with; Mark’s readers have just watched five thousand fed from five loaves. The dogs are Gentiles, and bluntly it was a term of contempt in Jewish speech. That must be admitted, not explained away. Three things change the sentence.

“First.” One word that is a door standing open. A man who says “first” has a second course in mind. Not a refusal but an order of service — the order the New Testament states without embarrassment: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). She isn’t told there is no place for her, but about the timing.

Household dogs. The word is a diminutive: not the pariah dogs of the street that ran in packs outside the town, but the household dog under the table. That matters enormously: the animal in his picture is inside the house. He has drawn a scene in which the outsider is already in the room.

What he actually does. He grants her request, at once, at a distance, and Matthew records what he said of her: “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matthew 15:28). That is the loudest commentary on the tone of v. 27, and not that of a man who has just insulted someone.

A picture with a door. So what was he doing? Handing her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find it. Everything she needed was in his own sentence: “first,” and a dog under the table, not in the street. He gave her the material to argue with, and waited. He tests faith to bring it out, not to break it — as he kept Jairus standing in the street while a woman told her story. The testing is never the withholding.

From the floor. Be honest about how it felt. She had no Matthew or commentary — a hard sentence and a sick child. What she did with it next is why we still know who she was. A test: when God’s answer sounds hard, do you walk away, or listen for the door in it?
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table. “First” implies the Gentiles’ turn will come.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first and also to the Greek

verseByVerse.quote: But she answered him, "Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman answers, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” Faith humbly accepts its unworthiness and pleads instead God’s own generosity and words — and such persistent prayer within God’s purposes is honoured.

The answer he praised. The only place in the Gospels where someone answers Jesus back in an argument and he says they are right. Take it clause by clause.

“Yes, Lord.” She doesn’t fight the picture, call it unfair, claim as much right as anyone, or take offence. She concedes the framework: yes, the children come first; yes, I am not one of them. That isn’t weakness but the opposite. She stops arguing about her standing, which she could never win, and argues about his generosity, which no one has ever lost.

Standing on his word. “Yet even the dogs under the table” — she picks up his own word, the household dog inside, and stands on it. He put the animal under the table; she simply points to where he put it.

The overflow. “Eat the children’s crumbs.” Nothing is taken from the children; feeding a dog under the table deprives no child of a mouthful. She isn’t asking for the meal to be reassigned but for the overflow — and she grasped by instinct that where he is there is always overflow. Mark’s readers have just counted twelve baskets of it (6:43).

Arguing with Jesus from Jesus. Not from her rights, her need, or her daughter’s suffering, though all were real, but from his own words and character. That is the difference between persevering faith and mere nagging. She met what looked like a closed door. She didn’t take offence and leave, nor stand outside pleading louder to wear him down. She listened to the very word that sounded like refusal, took hold of it, and pressed in. Her confidence rested not on her persistence but on his goodness — which is why she could hold on through an apparent no.

A method for unanswered prayer. If you are praying into silence, or into what looks like no, learn her method rather than merely admiring her. Don’t read the delay as the final verdict. Take God at his revealed character and promises and press into them. Plead the crumbs. Plead his word back to him — you said, you promised, you are the God who. That isn’t impertinence; it is how every great prayer in Scripture is built, from Abraham at Sodom to Moses on the mountain.

Within his purpose. Hold it with Scripture’s balance. This isn’t a technique for bending God to your will. The Lord himself in Gethsemane, praying with perfect faith, said, “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (14:36), and the cup didn’t pass. Her persistence was answered because it was within his purpose, not against it. So pray like her, refusing to let go — and trust like him, that the Father’s no, when it comes, is as wise and loving as his yes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter." And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her that because of her answer she may go, for the demon has left her daughter; she goes home and finds the child lying in bed, the demon gone. Christ’s word is effective at any distance, and faith goes home trusting his word alone.

Her sentence moved him. “For this statement” — the one she made out of his own. Matthew adds: “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire” (Matthew 15:28). The two great commendations of faith in the Gospels fall on this woman and a Roman centurion (Luke 7:9) — neither Jewish, neither raised on the Scriptures, both in the Lord’s judgment ahead of anyone in Israel.

Already done. “The demon has left your daughter” — past tense, done at a distance, in a house she can’t see, to a child she hasn’t been able to help. He doesn’t go with her, lay a hand on the girl, or speak to the spirit — unusual in Mark, whose exorcisms are close, physical and noisy. Here, a sentence in one house and a quiet room in another.

Prayer at a distance. Most of our praying is at a distance. Those we are most desperate about are usually not in the room: the child in another city, the friend in a hospital we can’t reach, the person who won’t see us. Nothing here requires nearness. He said it where she was, and it was true where the child was. A test: who far away should you bring to him today?

Going home on the word. “And she went home” — four words, the last act of her faith, easy to miss. She had a sentence and nothing else — no sign, no proof — and walked back, quite possibly a long way, on what he said. That is what faith always finally looks like: going home on the word.

Lying in bed. Beautifully understated. A child who had been thrown about by an unclean spirit — chapters 5 and 9 show what that looked like — lying quiet, resting. Her mother came in and found her asleep.

The crumbs were enough. A Phoenician woman with no covenant, Scriptures, synagogue or standing got what she asked from the God of Israel because she believed he was generous and wouldn’t stop saying so. The children were fed first. But the crumbs were enough to cast out a demon — and the second course, when it came, would be the nations of the earth sitting at the table.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus returns by a long route through Gentile territory to the Decapolis, where people bring him a deaf man with a speech impediment and beg him to lay his hand on him. The ground prepared by one man’s testimony welcomes Jesus, and those who cannot come to Christ themselves depend on others who will bring them.

The long way round. Trace it on a map. Tyre is on the coast; Sidon is twenty-five miles further north, the wrong direction; from there he comes down to the Sea of Galilee and into the Decapolis on the eastern side. A long, looping, inefficient journey, possibly months, and almost every mile of it Gentile ground. He has left Israel and is taking the long way round through the nations.

Ground made ready. The Decapolis is where he met the man among the tombs, where the townspeople begged him to leave, and where he left a restored madman with a story and no training, who “began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him” (5:20). Now Jesus comes back, and instead of being asked to go he is met by people bringing their sick. Mark doesn’t connect the dots; he needn’t. One man told one district what happened to him, and when the Lord returned the ground was ready. A test: whose ground might your story be preparing?

Brought, not coming. He doesn’t come; he is brought. He is deaf — he had never heard the reports about Jesus, couldn’t have overheard where he was, couldn’t ask. Whatever he knew, someone had to get it across to him without words. His speech is affected too; Mark’s rare word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 35:6, in the passage about what happens when God comes to save. Not likely an accident.

Carried by others. “They begged him to lay his hand on him” — they ask on his behalf, because he can’t. It is the four on the roof again (2:3–5), one of this Gospel’s most frequent patterns: someone who couldn’t get to Jesus, and someone who wouldn’t let that be the end. If you are carrying someone like that — praying for a person who can’t or won’t pray, doesn’t understand enough to ask, has no idea you have been at it for years — this is the man in the Bible for you. No one recorded the names of those who brought him. They are simply “they,” and without them he would have died deaf.
verseByVerse.note: Going from Tyre through Sidon to the Decapolis is a long loop through Gentile territory.

parallels.desc: the healed man proclaims in the Decapolis

verseByVerse.quote: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes the man aside privately, puts his fingers in his ears, spits and touches his tongue, looks up to heaven, sighs, and says “Ephphatha” — “Be opened.” Jesus cares for the dignity and understanding of the one he helps, grieves over the ruin of his creation, and restores it by his word.

Taken aside. There is always a crowd, and Jesus walks him out of it. Think what a jostling crowd is like for someone who can’t hear: faces turned toward him, mouths moving, people pointing — the object of attention and shut out of it at once. Whatever happens to him won’t happen before an audience. That rebukes every way of helping people that requires them to be put on show — the testimony extracted, the need described in public, the person made an occasion. A test: when you help someone, do you protect their dignity?

A conversation in signs. One of the most elaborate things Jesus does in any healing in Mark, odd to modern readers until you ask: how do you tell a deaf man what you are about to do? You can’t say it, so he says it in the only language available. Fingers into the ears: this is what I am dealing with. Saliva on the tongue — widely thought to heal, so it would read to him as treatment: this too. Looking up to heaven: and this is where it comes from. No power in the technique and no ritual; a conversation conducted in signs with a man who has never heard a sentence (cf. 8:23; John 9:6). He could have healed him from where he stood, as he had just healed a girl miles away with a word. He took the trouble to be understood, by one man, in that man’s own language.

A groan. “He sighed.” Not exertion — the healing costs him nothing and takes one word — but grief. Before one ruined pair of ears and a tongue that can’t form words, he is looking at what has been done to his own creation; he made ears to hear. Paul says the whole creation groans — the same root — and we groan inwardly with it, “as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:22–23). Here is the Creator in a body, groaning over the wreckage. He isn’t indifferent to your body or anyone’s. He doesn’t treat the physical ruin of the world as a small matter to tolerate until souls are saved. It draws a groan from him, over a man whose name no one wrote down.

Ephphatha. Mark keeps the Aramaic, as with “Talitha cumi” (5:41). Both times a word spoken to someone helpless in a private place, remembered exactly, because Peter stood there and never forgot the sound. One word, to a man who couldn’t hear it — and heard it.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. “Ephphatha” is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke.

parallels.desc: spitting on the blind man’s eyes

verseByVerse.quote: And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At once the man’s ears are opened, his tongue released, and he speaks plainly; Jesus tells them to tell no one, but the more he charges them, the more they proclaim it. Christ’s healing is a new creation, and those freshly astonished by him can’t stop telling others.

Three things he saw. “His ears were opened” — the word Jesus used, and it happened. Imagine the first second: a whole life inside silence, and suddenly wind, voices, his own breathing, a crowd fifty yards off. “His tongue was released” — as though something tied had been untied. “He spoke plainly” — medically the strangest part. Someone who has never heard speech doesn’t simply produce it; you learn to speak by hearing. He opens his mouth and talks properly at once, with no learning curve — which shows this wasn’t a repair but a creation.

Tell no one — again. The reader may find it strange here, in Gentile territory far from crowds wanting to crown him. But the same logic holds wherever he is. He won’t have a following built on what he can do to a body. A healer’s reputation isn’t the truth about him; it is a fragment that can be believed enthusiastically by people who have understood nothing, and it makes the road to the cross harder. He manages the story until it can be told properly, and it can’t be told properly until there is a cross in it.

Cheerful disobedience. “The more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it” — a see-saw: every extra instruction produced an equal quantity of talk. It happened with the cleansed leper (1:44–45). The pattern is consistent: those commanded to speak are often slow, and those commanded to be silent can’t be stopped.

Why the news travels. These were people with no theology, covenant, Scriptures or commission — the opposite of twelve trained men sent to preach — and they couldn’t keep quiet. Why does the news travel so much more easily among those just astonished by Christ than among those who have known about him thirty years? Not information. No one has to be persuaded to talk about something that has just happened to them. A test: when did you last tell someone what Christ has done for you, simply because you couldn’t keep it in?

verseByVerse.quote: And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people, astonished beyond measure, say, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.” Without realising it, they echo creation’s “very good” and Isaiah’s promise that the deaf will hear when God comes to save — Jesus is the Creator come to make his world new.

Out of words. “Astonished beyond measure” — Mark has run out of ordinary words. And the crowd says more than it knows; both halves of its sentence are quotations it didn’t realise it was making.

“All things well.” It echoes Genesis 1:31: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” The crowd means something modest — this healer is impressive; everything he touches turns out right. What they have said is the verdict pronounced over the finished creation, when God looked at a world with nothing wrong in it. And that is what just happened on that hillside. The One who made ears has repaired a pair; the One who gave the tongue speech has given it back. Not a rescue operation bolted onto a ruined world, but the Creator returning to his own marred work and beginning, one person at a time, to make it good again.

Isaiah 35. “He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak” is Isaiah: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy” (Isaiah 35:5–6). Not a general promise of better days but what will happen when God himself comes: “Behold, your God will come… He will come and save you” (Isaiah 35:4). The sign that God has come has just been given, in a Gentile district, to a man whose name we don’t know, before a crowd that couldn’t have quoted Isaiah if paid.

How he works. From one end of this Gospel to the other. The scholars came ninety miles to raise unwashed hands and went home unmoved. A pagan mother took hold of one word and got her daughter back. A deaf man, carried by friends, heard his own voice. A test: are you more like the scholars measuring cups, or like those who brought their need to him?

“Be opened” over every grave. The chapter began with men measuring the cleanness of cups. It ends with the Creator groaning over one broken body and saying, “Be opened” — and one day he will say it over every grave ever dug, and it will be very good.

parallels.desc: the ears of the deaf unstopped, the tongue of the mute sings

7.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? The numbers run 15, then 17, and nothing has been lost. The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no verse 16; later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23) — almost certainly written first in a margin and then mistaken for text. The verse numbers themselves date only from the sixteenth century, so translators could not renumber the New Testament; they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote. Nothing has been removed from your Bible. We simply have older copies than were available in 1611, and honest translators tell you in the margin rather than quietly leaving something in.

Was Jesus cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? Three things settle it without softening the difficulty. The word first is a door standing open — let the children be fed first implies a second course, and Paul states the same order plainly (Rom. 1:16). And the dogs in the picture are under the table (v. 28): not the scavengers of the street but the household pets, already inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants her request at once, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28). He handed her a picture with a door in it to see whether she would find the door, and she found it in one sentence.

And the crowd at the end echoes two texts without knowing it. He has done all things well sounds like the verdict over the finished creation — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good (Gen. 1:31). He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah 35:5–6, the sign of the day when God himself comes to save.
