7.examples:
Then: Corban — the money owed to an old man, put beyond his reach by a holy word, while his son kept the use of it and his reputation.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. The man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother has not had a visit since March. The giving that goes to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. Any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So take the test the passage supplies, in one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them?

Note that Jesus does not attack tradition as such — every church has customs and must. He attacks tradition that has been promoted: set level with Scripture, and then used against it. And note what he reaches for when he wants a case anybody can measure. Not prayer, not fasting, not the temple. Whether the old people in your family are being looked after — which is exactly where the New Testament keeps landing (Jas. 1:27; 1 Tim. 5:8).

And one more, from the parenthesis in v. 19. Peter was in that house and heard the explanation with his own ears — and years later needed a sheet let down from heaven three times before he would eat with a Gentile (Acts 10:9–16), and a public rebuke from Paul after that (Gal. 2:11–14). It is possible to be taught a truth plainly by Christ himself and go years before it lands. That is not proof you were never taught. It is what learning looks like in creatures like us — and Peter is the one who tells us he had been told all along.

8.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, <sup>2</sup>“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. <sup>3</sup>And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away.” <sup>4</sup>And his disciples answered him, “How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?” <sup>5</sup>And he asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.” <sup>6</sup>And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. <sup>7</sup>And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them. <sup>8</sup>And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. <sup>9</sup>And there were about four thousand people. Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.” <sup>13</sup>And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side. <sup>14</sup>Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. <sup>15</sup>And he cautioned them, saying, “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” <sup>16</sup>And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? <sup>18</sup>Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? <sup>19</sup>When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They said to him, “Twelve.” <sup>20</sup>“And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” And they said to him, “Seven.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?” <sup>22</sup>And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. <sup>23</sup>And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?” <sup>24</sup>And he looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees, walking.” <sup>25</sup>Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. <sup>26</sup>And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even enter the village.” <sup>27</sup>And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” <sup>28</sup>And they told him, “John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” <sup>29</sup>And he asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” <sup>30</sup>And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. <sup>31</sup>And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. <sup>32</sup>And he said this plainly. 8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the hinge of Mark, and everything in the book turns on it. The first half asks who Jesus is; the second half walks to Jerusalem to die.

It is built around sight. Four thousand Gentiles are fed on a hillside and the disciples learn nothing from it. The Pharisees, days after a district was fed from seven loaves, ask for a sign — and he groans, refuses flatly, and gets back in the boat. Then twelve men who have twice carried the surplus away in baskets sit worrying about having one loaf between them, and Jesus asks eight questions in five verses, ending with do you not yet understand?

So Mark puts a blind man next, and has him healed in two stages — the only such healing in the Gospels. I see people, but they look like trees, walking. Not blind. Genuinely seeing. Seeing wrong shapes. It is a picture of exactly what happens next.

At Caesarea Philippi — beneath a cliff of pagan shrines, in a city named for Caesar — Peter gets it right: You are the Christ. And immediately Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise, and Mark notes that he said it plainly, the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to correct him and is called Satan. Then the crowd is called over and told the terms: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Four Thousand Fed, a Sign Refused, and the Leaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second hillside (vv. 1–10). A crowd of four thousand has been with him three days in an empty place, and some of them have a long walk home. Seven loaves, a few small fish, and seven hampers of scraps at the end. It is not a retelling of chapter 6 — Jesus himself will insist on the difference in verse 19.

The demand (vv. 11–13). The Pharisees arrive and ask for a sign from heaven, days after a hillside was fed from a basket. He groans, refuses flatly, gets back in the boat and leaves them.

The boat (vv. 14–21). A warning about leaven is heard as a comment about catering, and Jesus asks eight questions in five verses. The list of what they have seen is read back to them, with the numbers, and it changes nothing.

Everything in this half of the chapter is about seeing — a crowd fed and not understood, a sign demanded by men who have had a hundred, and twelve men in a boat with the bread-maker, worrying about bread. Which is exactly why the next thing Mark records is a man who could not see at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Are the two feedings one story told twice? It is the standard suggestion, and Mark closes it off himself. In vv. 19–20 Jesus makes the disciples recite both, with the figures — five loaves and five thousand and twelve baskets; seven loaves and four thousand and seven baskets — as two separate events they were present at.

The settings differ too. The five thousand were Jews on the green grass of Galilee, seated in ranks of hundreds and fifties like Israel in the wilderness, with twelve baskets over. The four thousand are in the Decapolis, on Gentile ground, with seven — and some of them have come from far away, which is how the Old Testament speaks of the nations (Isa. 60:4; Josh. 9:6). Twelve is the number of the tribes. Seven is the number of fullness. He fed Israel and had a basket for every tribe; he fed the nations and there was more than enough.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men in a boat, worrying about having one loaf between them, having twice watched thousands fed out of nothing.

Now: exactly the same, and the comedy of it is uncomfortable rather than funny. We have documented evidence of God's provision — the job that came, the diagnosis that was not what we feared, the money that arrived, the marriage that held — and the next shortage finds us doing arithmetic as though none of it had happened.

Note where Jesus locates the failure. Not in their circumstances and not even in their fear. Do you not remember? The problem is memory. They had the facts; they had carried the baskets themselves; and the facts had not been converted into knowledge of the Person who supplied them.

So the practical remedy is unglamorous and it works. Keep a record. Write down what God has actually done, with dates, so that the next crisis meets a list rather than a mood. The disciples could still produce the numbers when they were asked — twelve, seven — and had drawn nothing from them. Israel was commanded to build cairns of stones in the Jordan so that children would ask what they meant (Josh. 4:6–7). We are people who forget, and God has never treated that as a small problem.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When another great crowd has been with Jesus three days without food, he says he has compassion on them and won’t send them away hungry lest they faint on the way, some having come from far away. Jesus notices and cares about people’s physical needs, and his compassion reaches the Gentiles who have come “from far away.”

Gentile ground. “Again” tells us we have been somewhere like this before. But this isn’t Galilee. Chapter 7 left Jesus in the Decapolis (7:31), and nothing brings him home. This is most likely a largely Gentile crowd on Gentile ground.

He speaks first. In chapter 6 the disciples raised the problem and he handed it back; here no one has raised anything. He looks at the crowd and does the arithmetic himself. The same compassion as before (6:34) — not a policy but what happens inside him when he looks at people.

Three days. That changes the picture. These people didn’t come out for an afternoon. They stayed three days in a desolate place, sleeping rough, listening to a Jewish teacher whose language and religion weren’t theirs, and whatever they brought ran out long ago. And he noticed. In the middle of teaching thousands, he kept track of how long they had been there and what they had eaten.

The walk home. “If I send them away hungry… they will faint on the way.” Not the sermon or the response, but the walk home: people going light-headed on a hot road with miles to go, children, the old. He pictures it.

From far away. A clause easily read past, doing two things. Plainly, pastoral care: some have the furthest to travel, and he has factored that in — not an average, but the ones at the back with the longest road. And underneath, “from far away” is how Scripture speaks of the nations coming in: “they all gather together, they come to you; your sons shall come from afar” (Isaiah 60:4); “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). He is worried about their legs, and Mark is telling you who they are.

For Gentile readers. Most of us are. The first thing recorded of him on the day the nations were fed is that he noticed how far they had come and didn’t want them collapsing on the way home. A test: do you believe he notices your ordinary, physical needs as closely as that?
verseByVerse.note: This crowd, in the Decapolis, was probably largely Gentile.

verseByVerse.quote: And his disciples answered him, "How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?" And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples ask how anyone can feed so many in a desolate place, and Jesus asks how many loaves they have; they say seven. Even after seeing Jesus feed thousands, his disciples leave him out of their calculations — and he patiently asks what is actually in their hands.

Worse this time. The same objection as chapter 6, and worse, because last time they hadn’t seen it done. Before enjoying their failure, look at the sentence’s shape. “How can one feed these people?” is impersonal — not “how can you,” which would at least have put the problem where it belonged. They survey a situation and report inadequate resources, entirely correctly, and the Person beside them doesn’t appear in the calculation.

A very old sentence. When Israel wanted meat in the wilderness, Moses asked, “Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?” (Numbers 11:13), and God answered with a question that could be printed over this chapter: “Is the LORD’s hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not” (Numbers 11:23). The disciples stand in a wilderness before a hungry multitude saying what Moses said.

The same method. “How many loaves do you have?” He doesn’t argue with their arithmetic or lecture them about faith. He asks what is actually in their hands. A habit worth taking: the mind faced with something too big produces a paralysing survey of the gap. He turns it round — never mind the gap; what have you got? Count it. Bring it. A test: what do you actually have in your hands for the need in front of you?

“Seven.” One word, and what is missing is the point. No one says, “Lord, last time you did this with five.” No one looks up. They produce the number like a stock figure and wait — not obstructive, just ordinary. And that is what Mark wants you to see: the first half of this chapter is about people with all the evidence and none of the sight, and it ends with a man who can’t see at all being led out of a village by the hand.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has the crowd sit, gives thanks for the seven loaves, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to distribute, then blesses a few small fish as well. Christ provides through thankful prayer and through his disciples’ hands, and nothing brought to him is too small for his care.

Different crowd, different shape. Last time the green grass of a Galilean spring (6:39); here just “the ground.” And no seating in hundreds and fifties: that was Israel in the wilderness, drawn up as Moses drew them. These are Gentiles, and Mark doesn’t impose the pattern.

Thanks. The four verbs again — took, gave thanks, broke, gave — to be done once more in an upper room over bread he calls his body (14:22). One word differs: in chapter 6 “blessed,” here “having given thanks,” the word from which the church took “Eucharist.” Mark uses both of the same act, a small lesson in itself: not a formula, but a man thanking his Father for food plainly not enough.

Discovered in the distributing. Mark says it twice in one verse: he gives to the disciples; the disciples give to the crowd. The multiplying happens in their hands, out in the rows, as before — the men who just said it couldn’t be done find out it can by carrying it. That is how he has always worked with his church. He seldom rains provision directly on the needy; he gives it to ordinary, unconvinced servants to distribute, and sufficiency is discovered in the distributing. You won’t settle whether there is enough by standing at the front doing sums. You settle it on the fourth row. A test: what is he asking you to start giving out before you can see it will be enough?

A few small fish. Mark handles the fish as an afterthought: separate sentence, separate blessing. A very human detail — someone remembered halfway through there were also some fish; no legend-maker includes that. And it says something about him: he blesses the small fish too. The scraps aren’t beneath his notice; nothing brought to him is handled carelessly.

verseByVerse.quote: And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four thousand eat and are satisfied, seven baskets of leftovers are gathered, and Jesus sails to Dalmanutha. A second, distinct feeding shows Christ’s abundant provision for the nations as well as Israel.

Filled. The same emphatic word as chapter 6 — fed to the point of stopping. Not a token or a taste.

Two events, not one told twice. Twelve baskets then, seven now; five loaves then, seven now; five thousand then, four thousand now. When Jesus makes the disciples recite both (vv. 19–20), he keeps every figure apart. That isn’t a story told twice and mistakenly recorded as two. Mark has two because there were two.

Twelve and seven. The numbers do work. Twelve is the number of the tribes: he fed Israel, with a basket for every tribe. Seven is the Bible’s number of fullness and completion — the week, the finished creation. He has fed the nations, and there was more than enough. The baskets here are a different, larger kind — the word used for the basket Paul was lowered in (Acts 9:25).

Dalmanutha. No one knows where it was; the name appears nowhere else in ancient literature, and copyists already substituted familiar places (Matthew says Magadan). A small point in the account’s favour: an inventor sets his story somewhere the reader has heard of.

Back to a reception committee. What matters is the direction: back to the Jewish side, having fed the Gentiles across the lake — and the first thing waiting at home is a delegation asking him to prove himself. A test: do you take his past provision as reason to trust him for the next need?
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets differs from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand and could mean a large hamper. Dalmanutha’s location is unknown; Matthew says Magadan.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation." And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees come demanding a sign from heaven to test him; Jesus sighs deeply and declares no sign will be given to this generation, then leaves. Unbelief that keeps demanding proof is not lacking evidence but willingness, and Jesus refuses to perform on demand.

A sign from heaven. The boat has barely touched shore. They aren’t asking whether he can heal — settled for chapters. They want something in the sky, on demand, like Elijah’s fire on Carmel. Healing could always be explained away; fire from heaven, they thought, couldn’t.

To test him. Mark gives the motive: the verb used of Satan in the wilderness (1:13). Not enquiry but an examination set by men who have already marked the paper. And the timing: behind him four thousand are walking home fed; before that five thousand; before that a leper, a paralytic, a withered hand, a legion, a dead girl, a hurricane. They want a sign.

A deep groan. An intensified word for groaning, found nowhere else in the New Testament. Mark used the simpler form when Jesus stood before the deaf man and groaned over his ruined creation (7:34). The same sound twice: over a body that can’t hear, and over men who won’t see. The second is deeper. Not irritation but grief.

The most emphatic refusal. “No sign will be given to this generation” — in Greek a Hebrew oath form, blunter than English: if a sign shall be given — with the curse left unspoken.

Didn’t Jesus promise the sign of Jonah? Matthew and Luke add, “except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew 12:39). There is no contradiction. Jesus refuses the sign they demand, a proof on request. The one sign he will give is his death and resurrection, “three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40), and Mark is about to have Jesus announce it plainly (v. 31).

Not refusing evidence. He has given evidence continuously and will give more. He refuses a miracle produced on demand as a condition of belief — because faith manufactured that way isn’t faith but a calculated response to a demonstration, and because these men have already shown what they do with the evidence they have. “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31). Exactly right: someone did rise, and those who heard first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:12–13).

If you wish God would do something undeniable. Settle it in the sky where no one could argue — this passage is a kindness, though it doesn’t feel like one. The problem was never the quantity of evidence. Every man in that conversation had watched things that couldn’t be explained, and it moved them not an inch, because the trouble was never in their eyes. A test: is your hesitation about Christ really about evidence, or about what believing would cost?

He left. He doesn’t argue or stay to win. He gets back in the boat. The third time he walks away from people who don’t want him — the Gerasene town (5:17), Nazareth (6:6), now Dalmanutha. He never forces himself on anyone, and there is no more frightening fact about him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. And he cautioned them, saying, "Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With only one loaf in the boat, Jesus warns, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod,” and the disciples think he is talking about their lack of bread. Unbelief disguised as rigour and religion compromised by worldly power both spread silently, and even disciples can miss Christ’s warnings by focusing on trivial concerns.

One loaf. Precise and slightly comic: they pushed off in a hurry and no one did the shopping — one loaf, thirteen men. Mark places it carefully: one loaf in that boat, the disciples worried about it — and one Person in that boat who has twice this month fed a district from a basket.

Leaven. Not a sachet of yeast but a lump of last week’s dough kept back and going sour, worked into the new batch. Everywhere in Scripture the point is that a small quantity silently changes the whole mass from inside: “A little leaven leavens the whole lump” (Galatians 5:9; 1 Corinthians 5:6). A warning about something that gets in unnoticed and works.

The leaven of the Pharisees. Fresh in mind: the demand for evidence from men who have all they will ever get. Unbelief dressed as rigour — a mind that keeps asking for one more proof because it means to yield to none.

The leaven of Herod. Chapter 6 gave sixteen verses on Herod so we would know: he feared John, knew he was righteous, protected him, heard him gladly — and killed him because of his oaths and guests. That leaven is accommodation to power: religion kept as an interest, conscience overruled whenever it collides with what the room expects.

Two ways people are lost. One is too clever to believe; the other believes well enough and won’t pay. And Jesus warns his own disciples about both, so neither is only an outsiders’ danger (cf. Luke 12:1). A test: which leaven is more likely to be at work in you?

A domestic grievance. “They began discussing… that they had no bread.” He warned them of a spiritual infection that destroys from inside, and they concluded he was making a pointed remark about the catering. They turned the deepest warning of the chapter into a domestic grievance. Before laughing, notice how easily it is done. You can sit under a sermon that names what is quietly killing you and spend the drive home discussing the length of the service, the temperature of the building, or whether an illustration was fair. The mind reaches for the manageable subject every time, and the smaller subject is always more comfortable.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through a whole lump; it pictures a corrupting influence. Herod stands for worldly power and its politics.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing their discussion, Jesus asks why they talk of having no bread, whether they still don’t perceive or understand, whether their hearts are hardened, whether having eyes they don’t see and ears they don’t hear, and whether they don’t remember. Even close followers of Christ can lose the capacity to be moved by him, and he lovingly asks them to examine themselves.

The sharpest words to the Twelve. He isn’t told; Mark keeps noting that he knows what is inside people (2:8), this time his own men. Eight questions in five verses, no pause for answers until the end.

“Not yet.” “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread?” holds up the absurdity: in a boat, with me, discussing a bread shortage. “Do you not yet perceive or understand?” — “yet” is the painful word. Eight chapters: a leper, a paralytic, a hurricane, a legion, a girl raised, five thousand fed, a man walking on water, four thousand fed. Yet.

Hardened hearts. The sentence that should stop any Christian reading comfortably. The third time Mark uses this word: of the men in the synagogue who saw a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5); of the disciples after the walking on water (6:52); and now to their faces. The word is for a callus — soft tissue thickening until it can’t feel. Not disbelief; these men believed much, had left everything, and had been casting out demons in his name. It is the loss of the capacity to be affected. A hardened heart can carry the bread and never taste it. And it is a question, not a verdict — the mercy in it. He asks them to check.

The outsiders’ text. “Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear?” — Jeremiah to a rebellious nation, “who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not” (Jeremiah 5:21; cf. Ezekiel 12:2), and behind it Isaiah 6, which Jesus applied to outsiders in 4:12. He applies the outsiders’ text to the inner circle. Those given the secret of the kingdom are described in the language of those who weren’t.

Proximity isn’t immunity. That is the warning, not for the world but for people long near Christ. You can hold correct doctrine, attend the right church, do genuine work in his name, and be steadily losing the ability to be moved by him — and the loss is undetectable from inside, which is why he must ask. A test: when did a truth about Christ last move you? Ask him to soften what has hardened.

“Do you not remember?” The last question turns a corner, because it has an answer, and it will be their own. He doesn’t tell them what they forgot; he will make them say it.

verseByVerse.quote: When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" They said to him, "Twelve." "And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" And they said to him, "Seven." And he said to them, "Do you not yet understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus makes them recall the twelve baskets left after feeding five thousand and the seven after feeding four thousand, then asks, “Do you not yet understand?” Knowing the facts of God’s past goodness isn’t enough; we must draw from them trust in the Person who did them.

An examination. He doesn’t preach; he makes them state facts they already know. “Twelve” — straight away; each of them had carried one. “Seven” — instantly. The data is intact; the filing system perfect. (And note what this does to the suggestion that the two feedings are one event told twice: he makes them recite both, with different loaves, crowds and baskets, and the men in that boat were at both.)

“Do you not yet understand?” The eighth question hangs there; Mark records no answer.

Remembered everything, understood nothing. The most useful thing in the chapter. He has shown they remembered everything and understood nothing. The facts weren’t missing; they could produce the figures on demand. What never happened was the step from the figures to the Person — from twelve baskets to “therefore the man in this boat won’t be defeated by a bread shortage.”

A common disease. Extremely common among long-time Christians. We are rarely short of information. Most of us could account for God’s dealings with us — provision that came, a door that opened, an illness that turned, a year we couldn’t have got through and did. Then the next difficulty arrives and finds us where the disciples were, doing sums in a boat.

Make yourself recite it. The remedy is plain and practical, and more or less what he does here. Not vaguely — with numbers and dates, as they answered him. Write down what God has actually done for you, and keep the list where you will see it when the next thing comes. That isn’t sentiment but a command running through Scripture. Israel piled twelve stones from the Jordan so that when children asked, the fathers would have to tell the story (Joshua 4:6–7). “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2) is a man giving orders to his own memory, knowing it won’t do it by itself. A test: start that list today.

Not put out of the boat. He asks, gets no answer, and takes them to Bethsaida — where the next thing that happens is a blind man led out of a village by the hand and given sight in two stages. Mark has put that story exactly there on purpose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — Two-Stage Sight and the Great Confession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The blind man (vv. 22–26). The only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages, and it is placed here on purpose. A man is led out of the village by the hand, sees people like walking trees, is touched again, and sees clearly. It is a picture of what is about to happen to the men in the boat.

The question (vv. 27–30). At Caesarea Philippi — at the foot of a mountain, beside a cave sacred to Pan, in a city named for Caesar — Jesus asks the question the whole Gospel has been building to, and Peter answers it: You are the Christ.

The correction (vv. 31–33). And immediately Jesus starts teaching them something they cannot bear: that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Mark says he said it plainly — the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to put him right, and gets the hardest sentence any disciple ever heard.

The terms (vv. 34–38). Then he calls the crowd over, so that nobody can say the terms were for professionals only, and states them: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

This is the hinge of the Gospel. Everything before it asks who he is. Everything after it walks to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why two touches? Not because the first failed. Mark places this healing between the disciples who have eyes and do not see (v. 18) and Peter's half-sighted confession, and it is an enacted parable of exactly that. I see people, but they look like trees, walking is a precise description of where the Twelve now stand: no longer blind, genuinely seeing, and seeing wrong shapes. Peter will name him Christ in verse 29 and rebuke him in verse 32.

And why "after three days"? Mark writes after three days (v. 31; also 9:31; 10:34) where Matthew and Luke have on the third day, and honest readers have wondered whether that requires a fourth day and breaks the Friday-to-Sunday timeline. It does not; it is simply the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole day. Scripture proves it on the spot: the chief priests remember this very prediction as After three days I will rise, and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64) — both phrases, of one morning, without a flicker of contradiction.

And why "Get behind me, Satan"? Not because Peter was demonic. Because the content of his objection was the wilderness temptation returning through the mouth of a friend: a kingdom without a cross. Jesus had heard it before (1:13), and he will hear it again from passers-by at the foot of the cross itself — save yourself, and come down (15:30). Peter meant it lovingly, which is precisely what made it dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing the words take up his cross, in a country where Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody in that crowd thought of a metaphor. They had seen men carrying the crossbeam through the streets, stripped, jeered at, on a walk with one destination.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth. A cross has become a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, walking away from everything he had.

And note who is being addressed. Mark says he called the crowd — not just the Twelve. This is not a higher path for the heroic few. It is the entry requirement, stated to the general public, by a man who knew exactly what he was asking because he was going to do it first.

So make it concrete rather than admiring it in the abstract. Deny himself is not going without sugar; it is the removal of the self from the throne — the decision, in a specific matter this week, that what you want is no longer the deciding vote. Name the matter. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, "Do you see anything?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Bethsaida people bring a blind man to Jesus; he takes him by the hand, leads him out of the village, spits on his eyes, lays hands on him, and asks, “Do you see anything?” Jesus personally and tenderly leads those who cannot see, and this healing in stages pictures the disciples’ own partial sight.

Bethsaida. The town of Philip, Andrew and Peter (John 1:44), on the north-east shore — and one Jesus later pronounces woe over for its unbelief (Matthew 11:21), which gives the end of this account its edge.

Brought. The pattern again: he didn’t find his way here; someone led him — like the paralytic through the roof and the deaf man in the Decapolis. A person who couldn’t get to Christ, carried by people who could.

Led by the hand. One of Mark’s tenderest sentences. The Lord of glory takes a blind man’s hand and walks him out of town. Not a word recorded: a man in the dark, holding on, going somewhere he can’t see, led by someone he has never met. It takes as long as it takes; no one hurries a blind man over rough ground. That is Christ’s whole disposition toward those who can’t see: he doesn’t shout directions from a distance; he comes and takes the hand. A test: is there someone in the dark you could walk alongside, rather than instruct from afar?

Why out of the village? Partly as with the deaf man (7:33) — away from a staring crowd. Partly, in this town, because of v. 26. The privacy is deliberate: at the Gospel’s hinge, the two great healings are done quietly, for one man at a time.

A physical Saviour. The saliva again, widely thought to heal, so it would register as treatment; and once more a way of communicating with someone who can’t follow what is happening. Nothing fastidious: he touches the man’s eyes with his own hands and saliva.

“Do you see anything?” The strangest sentence in the account, and why this healing has always puzzled people: Jesus asks, as if the outcome were uncertain, as if checking. He wasn’t. Nothing in this Gospel suggests he ever needed a second attempt; he had just fed four thousand and silenced a hurricane. He is doing something deliberate, and the next verse shows what.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip.

parallels.desc: Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked up and said, "I see people, but they look like trees, walking." Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his home, saying, "Do not even enter the village."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man sees people “like trees, walking”; Jesus lays hands on him again and he sees everything clearly, and is sent home, not into the village. Partial sight of Christ is real sight, but Christ keeps working until his people see clearly — as the disciples would only after the cross and resurrection.

Trees, walking. One of the most vivid sentences in the New Testament, which can only have come from the man himself: shapes, upright, tall, moving; without the movement they would be a wood. He is genuinely seeing — not blind — and genuinely not seeing properly; he couldn’t have crossed a street.

Seeing everything clearly. Mark piles three phrases where one would do — opened, restored, saw everything clearly — determined that no one should wonder whether the job was finished.

Why in two stages? Not because the first touch failed. Look where Mark put it. Six verses ago Jesus said to the Twelve, “Having eyes do you not see?” Five verses later Peter will say, “You are the Christ” — and three verses after that try to correct Jesus about the cross. That is a man seeing people like trees walking: not blind, genuinely seeing, seeing wrong shapes. The Gospel’s hinge is bracketed by a healing that took two touches, picturing what the disciples are going through: first sight at Caesarea Philippi, full sight only after a cross and an empty tomb.

For those who see dimly. Take it first as it stands, because many honest believers are this man. They see enough to know Jesus is real, the gospel true, that they belong to him — and so much is blurred: prayers that feel like talking to a ceiling, promises believed and not felt, a grasp of him more outline than face. Hear what this says: the same hand gave the first touch and the second. Jesus didn’t open his eyes halfway and walk off satisfied. He stayed, laid hands on him again, and didn’t stop until he saw everything clearly.

Keep coming for the second touch. Don’t despise a dim sight of Christ, or conclude from its dimness that you don’t truly see him; the man who saw walking trees was no longer blind. But don’t settle there as if blurred vision were all this life allows. Keep coming for the second touch — in the word, at the Table, on your knees, among his people — and know that clearing your sight is finally his work, not yours: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The day is coming when all who now “see in a mirror dimly” will see him “face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). He has never left a work of his half-finished.

Not into the village. Sent home rather than into Bethsaida. Given Jesus’ later words about that town’s unbelief (Matthew 11:21), it reads as mercy: a man with new eyes isn’t to be made a spectacle for people who won’t be changed by him anyway (cf. Isaiah 35:5).
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this two-stage healing; it sits just before the disciples see who Jesus is — but only in part.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that I am?" And they told him, "John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, and they report the popular views: John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the prophets. The world’s opinions about Jesus are respectful but always too small — because they cost nothing.

A chosen setting. Caesarea Philippi lay twenty-five miles north of the Sea of Galilee at the foot of Mount Hermon, where a source of the Jordan comes out of the rock. Beside that spring was a great cave sacred to Pan, the goat-god — the place was called Paneas — with niches cut into the cliff for idols. Herod the Great built a white marble temple there to the divinity of Augustus; his son Philip enlarged the town and renamed it after Caesar and himself. A cliff of pagan shrines, a temple to a man who called himself a god, and a city named for the emperor of the world. That is where Jesus stops and asks who he is.

On the way. It happens walking. Mark keeps saying “on the way” from here, and the way leads to Jerusalem.

The safe question first. “Who do people say that I am?” Anyone can answer; it requires nothing of the one answering. Report the opinions.

Nothing has moved. The same three answers as in chapter 6 when news reached Herod (6:14–15). Months of ministry, thousands fed, a district of healings, and the public verdict hasn’t moved.

Compliments, all too small. None is an insult. John — the greatest born of women, returned. Elijah — the prophet Malachi said would come before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). One of the prophets — a man who speaks for God. The largest categories available, and every one far too small. The crowd reaches for the biggest box it already owns rather than admit a new one is required.

Today’s versions. The same shape at a lower altitude: a great moral teacher, a revolutionary, a mystic, a good man. All respectful, all inadequate, all costing nothing — which is their appeal. You can admire a prophet from a distance. You can’t merely admire the Son of God; you either fall down or walk away. A test: which small box have you been keeping Jesus in?
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And he asked them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered him, "You are the Christ." And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks, “But who do you say that I am?” and Peter answers, “You are the Christ,” and Jesus strictly charges them to tell no one. Everyone must personally answer who Jesus is, and the right title — Messiah — must be understood by the cross before it is proclaimed.

The question in the second person. “But” is a hinge, and the weight falls on “you.” The question the Gospel has been walking toward, put personally after they have safely reported what others think. You can spend years discussing what people say about Jesus — what the church teaches, what your parents believed, the current arguments and objections — at a comfortable distance, committing to nothing. Then the question comes in the second person, and no one can answer for you: not a godly mother, a good church, or a tradition you respect. If you have never answered it in your own words, Christianity hasn’t yet asked you anything; you have only been informed. A test: answer it now, in your own words.

“You are the Christ.” Peter, as always, first and speaking for all. “Christ” is the Greek for the Hebrew “Messiah,” the Anointed — not a surname but a title carrying Israel’s whole hope: David’s son who would reign, restore the kingdom and put the world right. And it is correct. Jesus doesn’t qualify, correct or deny it.

What Mark leaves out. In Matthew Jesus answers with a blessing: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven,” and the promise of the rock and the keys (Matthew 16:17–19). Mark has none of it. This Gospel gives Peter’s finest hour in four words and his worst moment in full. And this is Peter’s own preaching: the man remembered the rebuke and let the commendation go.

What of the rock in Matthew’s account? Readers have taken it as Peter himself, as his confession, or as Christ (Matthew 16:18). The most natural reading is that Peter, as the first to confess Christ, is the rock in the sense that the apostles are the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20). But nothing in the text speaks of successors, and a foundation is laid once, not handed down; it gives no ground for a papacy.

Silenced at once. Why? Because “Christ” came with a national programme attached, and the programme was wrong. A Messiah in Galilee then meant a king who would raise an army and drive out Rome. Peter said the true word with a false picture behind it — and the next verse shows how false. Jesus accepts the title openly only before the high priest, on the night it kills him (14:61–62), when no one could mistake what kind of king he is.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah — the promised king. Popular hopes for a political Messiah may explain the command to silence.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus begins to teach plainly that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the leaders, be killed, and after three days rise again, and Peter takes him aside to rebuke him. The cross was not an accident but God’s necessary plan to save sinners, and even loving disciples can resist it.

A new beginning. “He began to teach them” marks a turn: something said for the first time that from now on is the burden of everything.

“Must.” One of the great words of the New Testament: it is necessary, bound to be — not resignation but a plan. Everything about the cross depends on this. What is coming isn’t a defeat, accident, miscalculation, or a good movement overtaken by enemies, but a necessity: “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23).

Why must he die? Because of sin. The Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45), to die in the place of sinners as the Servant of Isaiah 53 bears the sins of others. The “must” is God’s plan, foretold in the Scriptures, to save the guilty without denying his justice. A test: do you see the cross as God’s rescue planned for you, or as a tragedy that befell a good man?

Daniel’s figure suffering. “Son of Man,” his chosen title, comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom. Here Jesus does what no one had done: joins Daniel’s glorious figure to suffering and rejection.

The list. Suffer many things. Be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes — the whole Sanhedrin, named separately — not by the mob or Romans but by the official leadership of God’s people. Be killed — flat, no euphemism. And after three days rise again — the resurrection told with the death, in the same sentence, the first time he mentioned either. They won’t hear the second half; after the transfiguration they are still “questioning what this rising from the dead might mean” (9:10). But he said it from the first.

“After three days” or “on the third day”? Mark writes “after three days” here and twice more (9:31; 10:34), where Matthew and Luke say “on the third day,” and some wonder whether that demands a fourth day. It doesn’t. It is the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole: Friday, Saturday and Sunday are three days. And Scripture settles it: the chief priests, recalling this prediction, tell Pilate Jesus said, “After three days I will rise,” and in the same breath ask for a guard “until the third day” (Matthew 27:63–64) — both phrases for one morning, from men with every motive to be exact.

Plainly. A landmark. Until now everything was managed: demons silenced, the healed told to say nothing, crowds taught in parables. And the moment they get the title right, the lid comes off — and the first plain thing he says is that he will be killed. That shows what the secret was protecting: never that he was the Christ, but what kind.

Peter’s loving rebuke. “Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him” — a private, kindly meant word out of earshot, with the verb used of Jesus rebuking demons and wind. Three verses after confessing him as the Christ, Peter takes the Christ aside to correct him — out of love. He has just seen who this is and can’t bear what he heard. Matthew gives his words: “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16:22). The most affectionate sentence in the chapter, and it gets the hardest answer in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, "Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning and seeing the disciples, Jesus rebukes Peter: “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” Even well-meant human thinking that would avoid the cross becomes the devil’s argument, and the most dangerous opposition to God’s will often comes from those who love us.

Made public. Peter took him aside privately. Jesus turns away from Peter toward the others, looks at them, and only then speaks — publicly, because every man there is thinking it and the correction is for all.

Not a verdict on Peter’s soul. The hardest sentence a disciple ever heard, to the man who four verses earlier gave the best answer in the Gospel. Two things keep it from being what it first appears. First, it isn’t a verdict on Peter’s soul. Jesus doesn’t call him demonic or damned; he keeps walking with him, takes him up the mountain in the next chapter, and restores him on a beach after the resurrection. What is identified is the source of the objection, not the state of the man.

A familiar offer. Second, look at what Peter said: “This shall never happen to you.” A Messiah without a cross, a crown without a death, glory by a shorter road. Jesus had heard it before, when he was “tempted by Satan” in the wilderness (1:13), offered all the kingdoms of the world without Calvary (cf. Matthew 4:10). And he will hear it again at the cross: “save yourself, and come down from the cross!” (15:30). The same voice and offer three times — in a wilderness, from a friend, from a crowd at an execution.

Behind, not away. “Get behind me” isn’t “get away from me” but the language of position: get back where a disciple stands — behind. Peter got in front and started giving directions. He is told to resume following.

The things of man. The diagnosis names a category, not a sin. Peter wasn’t being wicked; he was thinking like a man. Every human instinct says suffering is to be avoided, a good plan doesn’t end in a grave, and if you love someone you get them out of danger. All decent, and all “the things of man” — and set against God’s declared purpose it becomes, whatever the intention, the devil’s argument.

The warning to take away. The most dangerous opposition to God’s will in your life won’t come from enemies but from people who love you, meaning it kindly, taking you aside for a quiet word — and from the reasonable, protective voice in your own head that says, “Surely not this. Surely there is another way.” Peter’s motives were good; Peter was wrong; both sat together in one man. A test: where are you, or someone who loves you, steering you away from a costly obedience?

verseByVerse.quote: And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling the crowd with his disciples, Jesus says, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.” Following Christ means dethroning self, accepting that the old life is under sentence, and walking behind him — the basic call to every believer, not an option for a few.

To everyone. Notice the audience. He could have said this to the Twelve; every instinct of religious management would keep the most demanding words for the committed. He gathers the public and states the terms aloud. That settles it: cross-bearing isn’t an advanced course for the heroic few while ordinary believers get an easier arrangement. It is the entry requirement, published to anyone considering him. “If anyone would come after me” — to walk behind someone, exactly where Peter was just told to return.

Deny himself. The verb used of Peter in the courtyard, where he denied knowing Jesus three times (14:68–71). That is its force: to say of yourself what Peter said of Christ — I don’t know this man; his claims have no authority over me; he doesn’t get a vote. Not self-improvement or asceticism; giving up sugar for a season isn’t this. Nor self-hatred; the Bible never asks you to despise a creature God made and Christ died for. It is removing the self from the throne. “What do I want?” stops being the question that decides.

Make it concrete. Name the matter this week where what you want and what he wants pull in different directions — the money, the relationship, the grudge, the ambition, the hour of the day. If you can’t name one, the denial is theoretical, and theoretical self-denial has never cost anyone anything.

Take up his cross. We have worn this phrase smooth; it needs its edge back. No one in that crowd heard a metaphor. Crucifixion was local and recent: after Herod the Great died, the governor Varus crucified two thousand Jews, within living memory of the older people there. They had all seen a condemned man carrying the crossbeam to the execution site, stripped, jeered at, walking one way only. So “take up your cross” doesn’t mean put up with a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a tiresome colleague. A man carrying a cross wasn’t a man with a burden but one already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life. The call is to accept that the old self is under sentence, publicly, and the walk goes one way. “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20) is Paul taking this call as his own.

And follow me. The third turns the first two from grim heroism into something else. You aren’t asked to carry a cross into the dark alone, but to walk behind Someone going first, who asks nothing he hasn’t accepted; within months he will carry the actual beam up an actual road. The whole difference between Christian self-denial and mere religious severity is in that last word. Not a discipline but a Person, walking ahead, whose back you can see.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? For what can a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses it for Christ and the gospel will save it; what profit is gaining the whole world and losing one’s soul, and what can be given in exchange for it? Clinging to ourselves shrinks and loses us, while giving ourselves to Christ finds our true life — and no price can buy back a soul except the ransom Christ paid.

An argument. He doesn’t say “because I say so.” He gives three “for”s, each an appeal to self-interest properly understood. “Life” is the same word rendered “soul” in the next two verses; English needs two words, Mark uses one, and the pun is the point: your life, your self, the thing that is you. Whoever wants to hold on to himself loses himself; whoever hands himself over, for Christ and the gospel, gets himself back.

Easily verified. Not a paradox invented to sound deep, but the most easily checked thing here. Look at people you know. Those who organised their lives around protecting themselves — comfort, reputation, options, feelings — have they become larger or smaller? A life curved in on itself narrows; what it can enjoy shrinks, its tolerance for inconvenience drops, and little is left that isn’t about them. And those who have genuinely spent themselves — on children, the sick, a church, God’s work in some obscure place — are almost always the ones with most life in them, the ones you go to in trouble. He isn’t asking for a sacrifice that leaves you poorer; he is telling you where the arithmetic comes out.

Is this salvation by self-sacrifice? No. Losing one’s life for Christ isn’t the price of salvation; it is the shape of the life faith produces. We are saved by grace through faith and created for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10). But the faith that saves is the faith that follows Christ, and following him costs everything (Luke 14:26–33). The verse isn’t only for martyrs but for every disciple who gives up the right to his own life (cf. John 12:25).

The whole world. The Gospel’s most quoted sentence, worn smooth; give it its teeth. “Gain the whole world” — not a good career but everything there is, with nothing left for anyone else; Jesus makes the best possible case for the other side: suppose you won completely. “Forfeit his soul” — a commercial word: to be fined, to suffer the loss. Assets acquired, price paid. And the sum doesn’t work even at the maximum: you would have paid too much, because what you paid over is what would have enjoyed it.

Smaller prices. Almost no one is offered the whole world. What people trade their souls for is always smaller: a promotion, a house in the right street, a relationship that couldn’t survive their being a Christian, the good opinion of a set of people, twenty more years of being left alone. If the whole world is a bad price, what is the price you are quietly considering?

No price can buy it back. “What can a man give in return for his soul?” What could you produce, having lost it, to get it back? The psalmist answers: “no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice” (Psalm 49:7–8). Nothing in the world is large enough. That is why this Gospel walks toward what it will say two chapters on: the Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). The price no one could pay was paid — not by the world, which was never worth it, but by him.

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is ashamed of Jesus and his words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will be ashamed of when he comes in his Father’s glory with the holy angels. Quietly hiding our allegiance to Christ to avoid social cost is serious, because the despised Jesus will return in glory as the Judge.

Ashamed. The last “for” moves from the sums to something more ordinary and likely. Not “whoever denies me,” though Peter will within months, but “ashamed” — not a decision or a moment but a temperature. And it covers “me and my words”: you can be content to be associated with Jesus generally and embarrassed by particular things he said, quoting some words easily and wishing others weren’t there.

An adulterous generation. Not primarily sexual sin but the prophets’ word for a people unfaithful to God, gone after other lovers (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3). He describes the surrounding culture’s pressure — the atmosphere in which being ashamed of him feels like good manners.

A thousand small silences. That is how it operates. Few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of denial. We face a thousand small pressures toward silence, each with a respectable name. The conversation at work that turns, and the sentence you don’t say. The qualifying phrase — “I mean, I’m not one of those Christians” — offered to buy distance. The dinner party where you let it be assumed you agree, and tell yourself it wasn’t the moment. The grace not said in a restaurant, the faith not mentioned to a colleague after four years, the Bible turned face down when someone comes in. None feels like betrayal. All of it is what this verse is about. A test: where has quiet shame about Christ crept into your week?

Settled shame, not a lapse. The answer is reciprocity: shame now, shame then. Don’t soften it, but understand what it measures. He isn’t threatening people for a failure of nerve in a hard moment — the man whose preaching lies behind this sentence failed exactly that, in a courtyard, three times, with oaths, and was forgiven on a beach and made the church’s leader. Settled shame isn’t a moment of cowardice, and the difference is what you do afterwards. He describes a life in which he was quietly kept out of sight because being known with him was judged too costly (cf. Matthew 10:33).

Who is speaking. A Galilean carpenter on a road near a pagan shrine, in an occupied province, with a few dozen around him, twelve of whom have just proved they don’t understand. He has said he will be arrested and executed by his own nation’s leaders. And he says, “when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.” That is Daniel’s vision, and he has told them he is that figure — “one like a son of man” coming “with the clouds of heaven,” given dominion and glory, all peoples serving him (Daniel 7:13–14).

A question of timing. So shame is finally about timing. There is a case for being embarrassed by him now: a provincial nobody facing crucifixion, and the world’s opinion of him hasn’t much improved. And a day is coming when the sky opens and the Son of Man arrives in his Father’s glory with heaven’s armies, and every person you were afraid of is looking at him. No one will be ashamed of him then. The only question is whether you were ashamed of him now, when it cost something — and whether on that day the one thing you want is to hear him say your name before the holy angels and not look away (cf. 2 Timothy 1:8).
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

8.theology:
Two feedings, not one story told twice. Jesus makes the disciples recite both with the figures (vv. 19–20): five loaves, five thousand, twelve baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, seven baskets. Twelve baskets for Israel, one for each tribe; seven for the nations, the number of fullness. And some of them have come from far away is how Scripture speaks of the Gentiles coming in (Isa. 60:4; Eph. 2:13).

Why no sign? Not because evidence is illegitimate — he had given a great deal and would give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as the price of belief, from men who have already shown what they do with the evidence they have. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31) — which proved exactly right, since somebody did, and the men who got the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matt. 28:12–13).

After three days. Mark's phrase (v. 31; 9:31; 10:34) against Matthew's and Luke's on the third day is not a discrepancy but the Jewish reckoning, in which any part of a day counts as a day. Scripture settles it: the chief priests recall this prediction as After three days I will rise and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64).

Get behind me, Satan. Not a verdict on Peter — Jesus takes him up the mountain in the next chapter and restores him on a beach at the end. It names the source of the objection. This shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22) is a kingdom without a cross, which is the wilderness offer (1:13) returning through the mouth of a friend, and it will come a third time from passers-by at the foot of the cross — save yourself, and come down (15:30).
8.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing take up his cross in a country where the governor Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody heard a metaphor. They had watched condemned men carry the crossbeam out through the streets, stripped and jeered at, walking in one direction only.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth and made a cross into a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life.

And deny himself is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard: I do not know the man, he is nothing to do with me. That is what you are asked to say about yourself — not self-hatred, and not going without sugar, but the removal of the self from the throne, so that what do I want? stops being the question that decides. Name the specific matter this week where that is in play. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

And the third word is what keeps this from being grim heroism: follow me. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark alone. You are asked to walk behind somebody whose back you can see, who is going first, and who within months will carry an actual beam up an actual road.

One more, from v. 38. He does not say whoever denies me — he says ashamed, which is not a decision or a moment but a temperature. Very few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures toward silence, each with a respectable name: the sentence not said when the conversation turned, the qualifying phrase offered up to buy distance (I'm not one of those Christians), the belief not mentioned to a colleague in four years. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what the verse is about.

9.title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power.” <sup>2</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, <sup>3</sup>and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. <sup>4</sup>And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. <sup>5</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>6</sup>For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. <sup>7</sup>And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” <sup>8</sup>And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. <sup>10</sup>So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean. <sup>11</sup>And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>12</sup>And he said to them, “Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? <sup>13</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.” <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. <sup>15</sup>And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. <sup>16</sup>And he asked them, “What are you arguing about with them?” <sup>17</sup>And someone from the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. <sup>18</sup>And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able.” <sup>19</sup>And he answered them, “O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.” <sup>20</sup>And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. <sup>21</sup>And Jesus asked his father, “How long has this been happening to him?” And he said, “From childhood. <sup>22</sup>And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for one who believes.” <sup>24</sup>Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” <sup>25</sup>And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again.” <sup>26</sup>And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, “He is dead.” <sup>27</sup>But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose. <sup>28</sup>And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>29</sup>And he said to them, “This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.” <sup>30</sup>They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, <sup>31</sup>for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, “The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise.” <sup>32</sup>But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him. <sup>33</sup>And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” <sup>34</sup>But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. <sup>35</sup>And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, “If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.” <sup>36</sup>And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, <sup>37</sup>“Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me.” <sup>38</sup>John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” <sup>39</sup>But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. <sup>40</sup>For the one who is not against us is for us. <sup>41</sup>For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward. <sup>42</sup>“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. <sup>43</sup>And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. <sup>45</sup>And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. <sup>47</sup>And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, <sup>48</sup>‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’ <sup>49</sup>For everyone will be salted with fire. <sup>50</sup>Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”
9.overview:
Mark puts the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his Gospel back to back, and the join is the point.

Six days after telling his disciples he must be killed, Jesus takes three of them up a mountain and stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him and — Luke tells us — discuss his exodus, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter, terrified, offers to build shelters. A cloud comes down and the Father says the only thing he commands in this Gospel: listen to him. Then the light goes, and they see Jesus only.

And they walk down into a shouting crowd, an argument with the scribes, nine defeated colleagues, and a boy convulsing on the ground. The father has been watching this since the child was small, has pulled him out of fires and out of water, and has just been let down by the disciples — which is where the if you can in his prayer came from. Out of him comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

The rest of the chapter is a road and a house. Jesus tells them a second time that he will be handed over and killed; they do not understand and are afraid to ask; and they fill the silence by arguing about which of them is the greatest. So he sits down, picks up a child, and redefines greatness — then warns them, in the most violent language he ever uses, about tripping up the little ones and about keeping anything that is taking them to Gehenna. The chapter ends: be at peace with one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Transfiguration and the Failure in the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 2–8). Six days after telling them he must be killed, Jesus takes three men up a high mountain and, for a few minutes, stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him. Peter, terrified, starts talking. A cloud comes down, and a voice says the one thing heaven has ever commanded about him: listen to him.

The descent (vv. 9–13). Coming down, he tells them to keep it quiet until the resurrection — and they go on down the hill privately trying to work out what rising from the dead could possibly mean.

The valley (vv. 14–29). And at the bottom: a crowd, an argument, scribes pressing their advantage, nine defeated disciples, and a father whose son has been convulsing since childhood and who has just watched the professionals fail. Out of his mouth comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

Mark has put the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his book back to back on purpose. The glory on the mountain is real. The failure in the valley is real. And the same Christ is in both.
verseByVerse.theology:
What actually happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — he was transformed, changed in form. And the point is not that something was added to Jesus but that something was, for a moment, no longer withheld.

Set it beside Moses. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone (Ex. 34:29–35), and he had to veil it — but that light was borrowed, reflected off a glory he had stood near, and it faded, which Paul says is exactly why he veiled it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes out from inside. His clothes go white because of what is underneath them.

So this is not a miracle done to Jesus. It is a brief withdrawal of the ordinariness he had been wearing since Bethlehem — three men allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

And why these two men? Moses is the Law and Elijah the Prophets; between them they are the whole Old Testament, standing on that mountain not to be admired alongside Jesus but to attend on him. Luke tells us what they were discussing: his departure — the word is exodus — which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Moses, who led the first one out of Egypt, is talking about the greater one with the man who will lead it, and the road out runs through a cross.

Then they are gone, and Mark writes the sentence the whole scene exists for: they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: three men who had seen the glory of God on a mountaintop, walking down into a shouting crowd, a public argument, and nine colleagues who had just failed in front of everybody.

Now: the come-down is the most ordinary experience in the Christian life, and Mark has built the chapter to prepare you for it. The conference ends. The retreat finishes. The Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday. And what is waiting at the bottom of the hill is usually not glory but a mess — the same marriage, the same diagnosis, the same argument, the same failure.

Two things to take from how Mark has arranged this. First, the mountain is not the point. Peter wanted to build shelters and stay, and he was told to come down and listen. The vision was given so that three men could go into the valley knowing who was walking beside them.

Second, Jesus goes down. He does not stay in the light. He walks into the shouting, asks what the argument is about, and takes charge of it — and the boy he lifts up off the ground is lifted by the same hands that had shone on the mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus promises that some standing there will not die before they see the kingdom of God come with power. Six days later three of them saw it on the mountain of transfiguration — a preview of glory given to carry disciples through the way of the cross.

A failed promise? At first glance it looks like one. Everyone standing there has been dead nearly two thousand years. Did Jesus say the kingdom would come in their lifetime, and was he wrong? No — and the answer lies largely in the next sentence.

The transfiguration. Mark’s arrangement points to it. The next words are “after six days,” and three of those standing there are taken up a mountain and see the Son of God in unveiled glory. Mark rarely gives precise intervals; he gives one here.
