The Lord’s doing. “This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” The builders weren’t thwarted by accident; what they meant as rejection was what God was doing — and Peter, standing there, quotes the verse in his preaching and his letter (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7). A test: is the stone the world rejects the one your life rests on?

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders want to arrest Jesus because they realise the parable was told against them, but they fear the crowd, so they leave him and go away. They understood exactly, and rejected him anyway — the problem was never lack of information but an unwilling heart.

They perceived. No misunderstanding. They knew they were the tenants, who the beloved son was, and what was said about their future. That removes the most convenient excuse ever offered for rejecting Christ. These men weren’t confused.

They acted out the parable. Told they are the men who murder the heir, they go away to arrange the murder of the heir. The warning becomes the occasion of the crime it warns about. That is what a hardened heart does with truth: it doesn’t soften; it uses the light to see by while it does what the light exposed.

Fear of the crowd. “But feared the people” — not conscience, not doubt whether he might be right, but crowd management. The city is full for Passover, the throng hears him gladly (v. 37), and a public arrest could start a riot. So fear of the crowd sets the timetable, which is why it will happen at night, in a garden, with a guide who knew where he prayed.

They walked away. “So they left him and went away” — the saddest clause in the chapter. They stood before the Son of God, who had told them, plainly enough to be understood perfectly, who he was, what they would do, and what it would cost. Nobody dragged them off; they lost no argument. They turned round and walked, and the next time they are in a room with him it will be at night with false witnesses.

The ordinary way of being lost. It is possible to understand the gospel completely — what it claims and what it requires — and walk away, not in rage or confusion but because it costs too much. That is the most ordinary way in the world of being lost. A test: is there something you know Christ is asking of you that you have walked away from because of the cost?

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and Herodians, sent to trap Jesus, flatter him and then ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar; seeing their hypocrisy, he asks for a denarius. Jesus sees through flattery and malice, and calmly takes control of a question designed to destroy him.

An unlikely alliance. The alliance from chapter 3 again (3:6): strict Pharisees, who resented Rome, and the party of Herod, whose power depended on it — agreed on nothing but this. Mark’s word for trap is a hunting word, to catch as with a snare. And they are sent: the council working through others, having found that direct confrontation failed.

Flattery as a technique. “We know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion… you are not swayed by appearances.” They praise him for independence and fearlessness — exactly what they need him to display in the next thirty seconds. They aren’t complimenting him; they are pointing him at a cliff. And every word is true. Flattery is rarely a lie. It is a true thing said by someone who wants something, and the tell isn’t the content but the timing: it arrives just before the request. A test: when someone praises you, do you notice what they want next?

Two lethal jaws. They ask twice — “Should we pay them, or should we not?” — to shut off any escape into generality. Say yes, and he loses the crowd: this was the tax imposed when Judea became a Roman province in AD 6, which provoked an armed revolt under Judas the Galilean and was hated as the badge of occupation. A Messiah who endorsed it was no Messiah. Say no, and the Herodians have a charge of sedition to carry to Pilate — which is what they will allege anyway: “We found this man… forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar” (Luke 23:2).

He names it. “Knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, ‘Why put me to the test?’” He isn’t taken in and says so aloud. He doesn’t pretend the flattery was sincere — a small lesson in dealing with people who come at you sideways.

“Bring me a denarius.” With that he takes control. He has no coin himself; he asks them for one — and they produce it. Someone among these scrupulous men has the emperor’s coin in his pocket, in the temple. The trap is already sprung on them, and they haven’t noticed.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks whose likeness and inscription is on the coin; they say Caesar’s, and he answers, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Christians owe government real obedience, including taxes, but God alone owns the whole person, because we bear his image.

The coin. A silver denarius of Tiberius carried the emperor’s head and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus; the reverse called him high priest. A coin, and a small metal blasphemy. Mark’s word for “likeness” is eikōn, image — and the second commandment forbade graven images. They produce one, in the temple courts, on request.

“Caesar’s.” There is only one answer, and by giving it they concede that they use his currency, travel his roads and live under his protection.

Give back what is owed. “Render” means to pay back, to return what is owed. The coin has his face on it; hand it back to him.

What bears God’s image. Then the second half, where the sentence detonates. If what bears Caesar’s image belongs to Caesar, what bears God’s image belongs to God — and that isn’t a coin: “God created man in his own image” (Genesis 1:27). He answers the tax question and then puts the questioners on the scales. Caesar gets the coinage; God gets the person — all of him, because no part of a human being is unstamped. And he doesn’t say how much belongs to Caesar; that varies with the government you live under. He fixes only the limit.

A real duty. The verse works in two directions, both legitimate. It establishes an obligation. Jesus doesn’t call the tax illegitimate or license defiance of government. Paul says the authority is God’s servant for ordering society, so pay taxes and honour the office (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). A faith that despises all earthly authority hasn’t read this verse. A test: do you pay what you owe — and speak of those in authority — as someone answerable to God?

A firm limit. It also bounds the obligation absolutely. Caesar may claim the coin, never the soul. When the state demands what belongs to God alone — worship, or breaking God’s plain command — the answer is no: “We must obey God rather than men,” the apostles told this council (Acts 5:29). The martyrs died on that line. They paid Rome’s taxes and prayed for its emperor, and wouldn’t burn the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that title was God’s.

They marveled. They came to trap him and went away astonished — the only recorded outcome.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, cite Moses’ law that a brother must marry his childless brother’s widow, and pose the case of seven brothers who had the same wife: whose wife will she be in the resurrection? They try to make the resurrection look absurd by imagining the next life as this one continued.

The Sadducees. Mark explains them for his Roman readers. They were the temple party — the priestly aristocracy, wealthy, conservative, politically pragmatic, running the establishment Jesus had just disrupted. They gave the five books of Moses the highest authority and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). A different opponent with a different objection, and the only time they appear in Mark.

Their ground. “Teacher, Moses wrote for us” — Moses, because his is the authority they accept. The question is designed to be argued on their own ground.

A mercy turned into a weapon. This is the law of Deuteronomy 25:5–6, and it was a kindness. In a world without pensions, where women seldom inherited, a childless widow was destitute and her husband’s name and land died with him. The brother married her so she was provided for and the first son carried the dead man’s name. A related duty of a near kinsman lies behind the book of Ruth. The Sadducees are about to make a joke of it.

A debating exercise. Seven brothers isn’t a real case but a puzzle built to make the resurrection ridiculous, with seven chosen for maximum absurdity. And notice the woman: seven men take her; she is passed along, widowed seven times, childless — and nobody in the conversation gives her grief a thought. A test: do you ever argue about doctrine in a way that forgets the people in it?

The joke. “Whose wife will she be?” isn’t really a question but a joke, the sort clever men use to embarrass a doctrine they have already dismissed. The logic: if the resurrection is real, heaven holds an insoluble domestic problem, so the resurrection is absurd.

The hidden assumption. Underneath lies the assumption Jesus will go straight for: they picture the life to come as this life continued — the same institutions, the same property law, running on forever. A great many people who have never heard of a Sadducee make the same mistake.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the Sadducees they are wrong because they know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power: in the resurrection people don’t marry but are like the angels. The life to come isn’t this life extended but transformed by God — and nothing good in this life will be lost there.

Two failures. He answers the joke with a blunt diagnosis, delivered to the professional custodians of both. They don’t know the Scriptures — not that they hadn’t read them, but they didn’t know what was in them, as verse 26 will show. Nor the power of God — the deeper failure. They had quietly settled that God couldn’t do what they couldn’t imagine. Unable to picture a resurrection life that isn’t this life extended, they concluded there is none.

Unbelief that sounds like realism. That second failure is common among religious people, and it doesn’t announce itself as unbelief. It sounds like realism: the settled assumption that God won’t act, that this marriage won’t change, this person won’t be converted, nothing much will happen — formed from experience, not Scripture, and then read back into Scripture. A test: what have you decided God cannot or will not do?

Not this age with the same furniture. “When they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.” He denies their premise.

For the bereaved. This verse needs gentle handling, because many live inside it. If you have buried a husband or wife and felt this sentence close on your chest, take the whole of it. He doesn’t say we become angels but are like them, in the point at issue: those who can no longer die no longer marry and bear children. He doesn’t say love ends, or that we won’t know one another. The fear that resurrection means less — thinner relationships, an impersonal eternity — is the Sadducees’ mistake in reverse, and the Bible never suggests it. Paul expects to see the Thessalonians as his joy and crown (1 Thessalonians 2:19); the disciples recognised Moses and Elijah on the mountain.

A signpost taken down. Marriage ends as an institution not because it was too small but because it was a signpost, and you take down the signpost when you arrive. Paul says the mystery of marriage refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32). What you had was a picture of the union about to be consummated in fact. So the honest word to a widow or widower is that nothing good will be lost — not the years, the knowing, or the love. It will be taken up into something larger, at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus proves the resurrection from Moses at the burning bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — and he is God not of the dead but of the living. God’s covenant bond with his people can’t be broken by death, so those who belong to him live to him and will be raised.

Their own ground. He could have quoted Daniel — “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2) — or Isaiah — “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise” (Isaiah 26:19). But the Sadducees gave Moses the highest authority, so he goes to the Torah, to the burning bush in Exodus 3, a passage every priest there knew well. “Have you not read?” — the second time in this chapter he asks professional readers that (v. 10).

The God of the patriarchs. “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (v. 26, quoting Exodus 3:6). When God speaks at the bush, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob have been dead for centuries, their bones in the cave at Machpelah. Yet God still names himself by them.

Not grammar but covenant. “He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” The argument doesn’t hang on a verb tense; it rests on what a covenant is. God had bound himself to Abraham personally, “to be God to you and to your offspring after you” (Genesis 17:7). A bond like that can’t be ended by the death of one party without God’s own word failing. If Abraham had simply ceased to exist, God would be naming himself by a relationship with no one — the God of a memory. He isn’t. He is their God still, which means they live to him, and the God who keeps covenant with the whole person will raise the body too. “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16). He put their names into his own title, and he isn’t the God of dust.

“You are quite wrong.” He began with “you are wrong” (v. 24) and ends more strongly — badly mistaken. Mark doesn’t soften it.

Hidden in a familiar text. The resurrection isn’t a late invention; it lay in the books of Moses, in one of the most familiar passages, and the men who read it constantly had never seen it. If you belong to Christ, the God who calls himself yours won’t let death end that. And there is more in your Bible than you have got out of it. A test: which passage do you think you know that you have never really read?
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The one honest question (vv. 28–34). After a day of traps, a scribe asks something he actually wants to know — which commandment is the most important. He gets the Shema and Leviticus 19, agrees warmly, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And after that, nobody dares ask anything at all.

The question he asks them (vv. 35–37). So Jesus asks one instead, and it is the deepest thing he says in public. If the Christ is David's son, why does David call him Lord?

The warning (vv. 38–40). Then a warning about the men in the long robes who love the greetings and the best seats, say long prayers for show, and devour widows' houses.

The widow (vv. 41–44). And he goes and sits down opposite the treasury and watches people give — and the last thing he does in this temple before he leaves it forever is point out a woman putting in two of the smallest coins in circulation.

Mark has put her immediately after devour widows' houses, and that is not an accident.
verseByVerse.theology:
Psalm 110 and the deepest disclosure in the Gospel. Jesus takes the most quoted psalm in the New Testament and asks a question nobody could answer.

Everyone agreed the Christ would be David's son — the promise ran through the whole Old Testament (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Isa. 11:1). And in Psalm 110, David writes: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand. The first LORD is God; the second is somebody David calls my Lord.

In that culture the point is unanswerable. Honour ran upward from son to father, never downward. A man does not call his own descendant his lord.

So: how can the Christ be David's son and David's Lord at once? Mark records no answer, and the crowd hears him gladly, and nobody says a word.

The answer is that both are true, and it takes the whole New Testament to say it. Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity.

And notice which verse of the psalm he quotes: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. He asks this in the temple, on the Tuesday, surrounded by the men who will have him killed on the Friday. They are the enemies in the sentence, and he quotes it to their faces.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God.

The scribe has answered magnificently. He has the doctrine of God right, the summary of the law right, and the priorities right — he even says out loud, as a temple professional, that love of God and neighbour outweighs the whole sacrificial system, which is a remarkable thing for such a man to concede.

And Jesus does not say you are in. He says not far.

Now: that is the most uncomfortable commendation in the Gospel, because not far is still outside, and it is the address of a great many people who have been in church all their lives.

The gap between near and in is not a gap in knowledge. This man's theology was better than the Twelve's. The gap is a Person. He was standing three feet away, and the question was never whether the scribe could give the right answer about the law but whether he would follow the man who was about to keep it for him.

So it is worth asking plainly: could you give the right answers, and never have come? Right doctrine is the beginning and it is not the destination. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it — and Mark never tells us whether this man did.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A scribe who has heard Jesus answer well asks which commandment is greatest, and Jesus answers with the Shema — the Lord is one, so love him with all your heart, soul, mind and strength — and then, love your neighbour as yourself. Love for the one true God, with the whole self, and love for others are the heart of God’s law, and no one has kept them except Christ.

At last, someone honest. Mark gives the man’s motive, unlike anyone else’s in this chapter: he has been listening, was impressed, and asks because he wants to know. Matthew’s account has a sharper edge — he asked “to test him” (Matthew 22:35) — so perhaps his motives improved as the conversation went on. Either way, Mark presents him as the one man all day who came to learn.

A live question. Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Law and debated which were heavy and which light. Asking a teacher to name the first was a way of finding out how he thought.

He begins with who God is. Jesus starts one line earlier than he needed: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4) — the Shema, recited by devout Jews morning and evening. He doesn’t begin with what you must do but with who God is. Because there is one God — not one among many, not a department of life — the love owed him can’t be partial. A rival would deserve a share. He has none.

All of you. Heart, soul, mind and strength aren’t a division into parts but a way of leaving nothing out. The heart is the control room: what you decide and want. The soul is your very life. The mind — added to Deuteronomy’s list — means God is loved with the intellect, and lazy thinking about him isn’t humility. Strength is the body, energy, money and hours. So it is concrete. Loving God with your strength is a question about your diary and bank statement; loving him with your mind, about whether you have taken the trouble to understand what you believe. A test: which of the four does God get least of from you?

And your neighbour. Asked for one, he gives two, and they can’t be separated: Leviticus 19:18, lifted from a chapter full of practical instructions about wages, gleanings, the deaf and the blind, and honest scales. “As yourself” isn’t a command to love yourself first; it takes the self-interest everyone already has as the measure. As carefully as you consider your own comfort, reputation and future — that much, for them. John draws the conclusion: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 4:20).

The command that convicts. No one has kept this for a single hour. It is the commandment that convicts everyone — and the man who quoted it is on his way to keep it perfectly for us, and to die for those who didn’t.
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribe agrees that God is one and that loving God and neighbour is far more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices, and Jesus, seeing his wise answer, tells him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” Right understanding brings a person close, but entering the kingdom means coming to Christ himself.

It went in. “You are right, Teacher.” He doesn’t argue; he repeats the answer back in his own words, which is what someone does when a thing has really gone in. And he adds a phrase of his own from Deuteronomy 4:35, “there is no other besides him.” He isn’t parroting; he is thinking.

A costly admission. Notice who is speaking and where: a scribe, in the temple courts, in Passover week, with the altar smoke rising nearby and the whole machinery of sacrifice running around him — saying that loving God and neighbour matters more than all of it. Not novel; the prophets had said it for centuries: “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6); “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). He had read his Bible and believed it, and said so in the one place where it cost something.

Not far. “You are not far from the kingdom of God” — genuine praise, and one of the most searching sentences in the Gospel. The man has the doctrine of God, the summary of the law and the priorities right, and is told so. And not far is still outside. Near the kingdom isn’t in it, and there is no third category.

The gap is a Person. The gap isn’t information; he knows more than many. The gap is a Person standing a few feet away. This whole chapter asks who Jesus is — the beloved son, the rejected stone, David’s Lord. The scribe can recite the greatest commandment; the question is whether he will follow the man about to keep it in his place. Mark never tells us. The account stops, and the man walks out of the Gospel one step from home.

Near or in? That leaves the question with the reader. You can give the right answers and never have come: hold sound doctrine, love a good sermon, defend the faith well — and be near. Being able to describe a door isn’t the same as walking through it. A test: have you only admired Christ, or have you come to him and trusted him yourself?

Silence. “After that no one dared to ask him any more questions.” Three parties have tried and been dismantled; the silence is the verdict.

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teaching in the temple, Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David’s son when David, inspired by the Spirit, calls him “my Lord” in Psalm 110. The Messiah is both David’s descendant and David’s Lord — truly human and truly divine, enthroned at God’s right hand.

He asks them. No one dares ask him anything, so he asks. It isn’t an attack on the doctrine. The Christ is David’s son; the promise runs through the Old Testament (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1), and Bartimaeus shouted it on the Jericho road and received his sight (10:47–52). Jesus asks whether it is the whole truth.

Two authors, one text. “David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared.” David himself — so the psalm is his; in the Holy Spirit — so it is also God’s. Two authors, one text, no tension. That is how Jesus read his Bible, and how he teaches us to.

Two Lords. “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet’” — Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New. The first “Lord” is God’s own name, printed LORD in our Old Testaments; the second is a title of rank, “my master.” So David, under the Spirit, records God speaking to someone David calls his Lord.

A father doesn’t call his son lord. In that culture the difficulty is total. Honour flowed upward: a son honoured his father, a descendant his ancestor, never the reverse. Yet Israel’s greatest king looks down the centuries at his descendant and calls him Master. Mark records no answer; nobody had one.

Both true. The answer is that both are true at once: God’s Son, “who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power… by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3–4). David’s son by birth, David’s Lord from eternity; the one who came from David’s line existed before David — “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). This is the deepest thing Jesus discloses about himself in public in Mark, given as a riddle, days before the cross, because stated flatly in the temple it would end the week early.

His enemies under his feet. Notice the line he chose: “until I put your enemies under your feet,” quoted to the faces of men who have resolved to kill him. The one they will crucify is the one God will enthrone. A test: do you treat Jesus as a great teacher of David’s line, or bow to him as Lord?

Heard gladly. “The great throng heard him gladly.” The professionals have gone silent; the crowd is delighted. Within days that same city will shout for his execution.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: And in his teaching he said, "Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns the crowd against scribes who love fine robes, public greetings and the best seats, who devour widows’ houses and make long prayers for show; they will receive the greater condemnation. Religious leaders who crave honour and exploit the vulnerable under cover of piety face God’s heaviest judgment.

Not a whole profession. He has just commended a scribe, so this isn’t a blanket condemnation of a profession but a warning about what religious office does to someone who lets it. And it is spoken publicly, to the crowd, about the most respected class in the community: “Beware” — keep your eyes open about your own religious leaders.

The appetite for honour. Four charges, and they build. They “like to walk around in long robes” — the robe of the scholar; not the robe but the strolling, the pleasure of being seen in a garment that says what you are. They like “greetings in the marketplaces” — public deference. “The best seats in the synagogues” — facing the congregation. “The places of honor at feasts” — nearest the host.

A portrait. Together they paint not a wicked man but one who has come to need deference. None of these is a sin in itself; a robe is a robe and a seat a seat. What is described is an appetite — the quiet, constant, unadmitted pleasure of being thought well of, which grows so slowly nobody notices it arrive. And it needs no robe today: there is a version in whose name gets mentioned, who is asked to pray, who is consulted, who is thanked from the front. A test: would you serve as gladly if nobody ever noticed?

Devouring widows. Then the charge turns from vanity to something far worse: “who devour widows’ houses.” Teachers of the law were expected to live largely on gifts, and devout households counted it a privilege to support a scholar; a widow with a little property and great respect for holy men was the softest target in the community. Whatever the exact means — gifts pressed, estates mishandled — Jesus’ word is devour. A religious profession is being used to strip the assets of the most defenceless people in the land.

Prayer as the instrument. “And for a pretense make long prayers.” The halves belong together: the long public prayer isn’t incidental to the exploitation but its instrument — what persuades the widow her money is safe with such a man.

Greater condemnation. Not merely condemnation, but greater. There are degrees, and the aggravating factor is the religious cover: to use God’s name as the tool of a fraud is worse than the fraud. “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1). And the very next thing Jesus does is watch a widow put her last two coins into the treasury those men administer.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sits opposite the temple treasury and watches people give; many rich people put in large sums, and a poor widow puts in two tiny copper coins worth a penny. Christ sees not only what we give but who we are as we give it — and the smallest gift does not escape his notice.

He sat and watched. Finished with the arguments, he crosses the court, sits directly opposite the treasury, and watches. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where, according to later Jewish tradition, thirteen collection chests stood with trumpet-shaped mouths, each for a different purpose. Coins rattling into metal mouths made a noise, and many coins made a great deal.

Christ watches giving. He sat and watched people give, deliberately, for some time. It is the plainest statement in the Bible that Christ watches giving — not the accounts or the total, but the people: faces and hands, on the last day he taught in that building. He still does. There is no anonymous giving; there is only giving other people can’t see. A test: if Christ sat opposite your giving this month, what would he see?

The rich gave much. “Many rich people put in large sums.” Mark doesn’t sneer at them, and neither should we. These were large gifts, genuinely given; the temple was maintained by them. Nothing says they were hypocrites. But they were noticed.

A widow. Two verses after “who devour widows’ houses,” that isn’t a coincidence. Mark lays the two side by side deliberately.

Two coins. Two small copper coins — lepta, the smallest coins in circulation; together they were a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage. And there were two. That is the quiet devastation of the story. She could have kept one; nobody would have known or blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice possible with two coins, and gave both.

A penny. “Which make a penny” — Mark converts it into Roman money, a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, so his readers in Rome feel how little it was. Dropped into the chest, it would have made almost no sound at all. But it was seen.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, with collection chests for offerings. Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called his disciples to him and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls his disciples and tells them the widow has put in more than all the others, because they gave out of abundance while she, out of poverty, gave all she had to live on. God measures a gift not by its size but by what it costs the giver and the trust behind it.

Look at her. He gathers the disciples, as he does when something matters. In the next verse one of them will say, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones” (13:1). He calls them to look instead at a woman with two of the smallest coins in the empire.

A different set of scales. “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing.” By every measure the treasury could apply, that is false: she gave a fraction of a penny, they large sums. He says she gave more than all of them — more than the total. He is using different scales.

What was left afterwards. “They all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.” The measure isn’t the amount but what was left afterward. They gave out of surplus — real gifts, honestly given — and nothing in their lives changed on the way home. She gave and had nothing left. The last phrase is literally “her whole life” (bios): she put her living in the box.

Both ways. The kingdom’s arithmetic cuts both ways. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And the gift you are embarrassed by — a little from a pension, an hour from someone with almost no hours, help from a person with nothing to spare — Christ counts larger than the endowment. A test: does your giving cost you anything?

Commending her or lamenting her? Mark places this right after the scribes who “devour widows’ houses,” and right before the temple is doomed (13:2). Both are true. He laments the system: the treasury she fills is run by men he has just denounced, and the building it maintains is finished. And he commends her without reserve. She didn’t give to a system; she gave to God, the only way she could, and he saw it and said so — and a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth.

Must the poor give everything? Jesus commends her heart; he doesn’t command the poor to give away their living. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not what he doesn’t have (2 Corinthians 8:12), and a believer must provide for his household (1 Timothy 5:8). And placed straight after the warning against devouring widows’ houses (12:40), the passage forbids any church or ministry to press the poor to give beyond their means.

He did the same. “The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). He sits in that court days from the cross, watching a poor woman give everything she had to live on — and he is about to do exactly that. She put her whole living into God’s hands with nothing held back; he is the only other person in the story who does the same, and he does it on Friday. Then he walks out of the temple and, in Mark, never goes back.

12.theology:
Render to Caesar cuts in two directions and both must be held. It establishes a real obligation — the coin bears his image, so give it to him, and Paul says the same (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy. And it bounds that obligation absolutely: Caesar may claim the coin, but what bears God's image belongs to God, and man bears it (Gen. 1:27). So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) was said to this same council. The martyrs paid every tax Rome levied and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord.

The Sadducees and the ground he chose. They were the priestly aristocracy who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied resurrection, angels and spirits alike (Acts 23:8). So Jesus does not quote Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19; they would have waved those away. He goes into the Torah, into the burning bush every priest knew by heart, and finds the resurrection in two words: I am the God of Abraham — spoken centuries after Abraham died. A covenant of that kind cannot be ended by the death of one party without God's own word failing. He wins the argument inside the fence they built themselves.

David's son and David's Lord. In Psalm 110:1 the first LORD is the divine name and the second is my lord, a title of superior rank. In that culture honour ran upward only; no man called his own descendant his master. So how is the Christ both? Mark records no answer, and the whole New Testament is the answer: descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity. And note the line he quotes — until I put your enemies under your feet — spoken in the temple to the men who would kill him on Friday.
12.examples:
Then: two lepta, the thinnest coins in circulation, dropped into a bronze trumpet-mouthed chest that made almost no sound.

And the detail that undoes you is that there were two. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known and nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Now: the measure is not the amount but what is left afterwards. The rich gave real gifts, honestly, and nothing in their lives changed on the way home. She gave and had nothing — all she had to live on.

That cuts both ways. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And the gift you are embarrassed by — the small amount from a pension, an hour from someone who has almost no hours — is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

Is he commending her or lamenting her? Both, and the passage is stronger for holding them together. He has just denounced the men who devour widows' houses, two verses earlier, and the building her money maintains has forty years left. He does not commend the machinery for taking it. And he commends her without a single qualification — she gave to God in the only way available to her, and because he said so out loud, a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth.

And note where he was sitting. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and he spent one of his last hours in that temple watching a woman put in everything she had to live on. She is the only other person in the story who does what he is about to do on Friday.

13.title: Stay Awake
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” <sup>2</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <sup>4</sup>“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus began to say to them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>7</sup>And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>8</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. <sup>10</sup>And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. <sup>11</sup>And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. <sup>12</sup>And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. <sup>13</sup>And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>15</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, <sup>16</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>17</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>18</sup>Pray that it may not happen in winter. <sup>19</sup>For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. <sup>20</sup>And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. <sup>21</sup>And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>22</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. <sup>23</sup>But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. <sup>24</sup>But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, <sup>25</sup>and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. <sup>26</sup>And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. <sup>27</sup>And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. <sup>28</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>29</sup>So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>30</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>31</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>32</sup>“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. <sup>33</sup>Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. <sup>34</sup>It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. <sup>35</sup>Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— <sup>36</sup>lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. <sup>37</sup>And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.”
13.overview:
They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the stonework — and he was right to. Herod's platform covers thirty-five acres; the largest block still visible weighs several hundred tons; Josephus says the gold front was too bright to look at in the morning sun. Building had been going on for some forty-six years when Jesus first spoke of it (John 2:20), and it was not finished until AD 63.

Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and seven years after the last workman went home it was gone.

Four disciples take him aside on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when and how they will know. What follows is the longest teaching in Mark before the passion, and its most striking feature is what it refuses to give. He describes signs and then says they do not mean what people will say they mean — the end is not yet. He describes the fall of Jerusalem in detail, and the flight, and the unequalled distress, and sets it inside a generation. And then, at v. 32, the discourse turns a corner: of his own coming there is no sign, no timetable, and no one knows the day — not the angels, not even the Son.

What is left, four times over, is a command. Stay awake — which the parable at the end defines not as scanning the horizon but as being found at your post, doing the work you were left. And in the next two chapters Mark walks his reader through all four watches of the night, and the disciples fail at every one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Signs, Perseverance, and the Abomination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stones (vv. 1–4). They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the masonry, and Jesus says that not one of those stones will be left standing on another. Four of them come to him privately on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when.

The age (vv. 5–13). His answer begins by taking away the thing they wanted. Deceivers will come; wars will come; earthquakes and famines will come — and none of it means what people will say it means. The end is not yet. The church will be beaten in synagogues and hauled before governors, betrayed by brothers and fathers and children, hated by everyone. And in the middle of the list, one line that is not a disaster at all: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

The crisis (vv. 14–23). Then something specific: an abomination standing where it ought not to be, and instructions so urgent that a man on his roof is not to go downstairs for his belongings. Forty years later, Roman legions came up the valley.

Notice what the discourse never gives them: a date. It gives signs that will be misread, warnings that will be needed, and one command repeated four times — stay awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and Jesus answers about the temple and about his own coming, and the seam between them is visible if you look for it.

Everything down to v. 30 is hedged with signs and set inside a timeframe: false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, unequalled distress — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of those things did happen, in the horror of AD 70, some forty years on. That is why the fig tree can say the season is near, at the very gates.

Then look at the hinge in v. 32: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. The but turns a corner. From here Jesus says the opposite of everything before — no sign, no timetable, nobody knows, it arrives like a householder in the night.

So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgement on Jerusalem, marked with signs and dated inside a generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date. Read this way — and it is the reading the seams of the text ask for — Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He said the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He said his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 10) — one bright, forward-driving line dropped into the middle of a catalogue of disasters.

It is the only item in the list that is not something to be endured but something to be done, and the little word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people.

Now: that turns the whole grim catalogue inside out. The wars and betrayals and floggings are not the church waiting helplessly for the end. They are the conditions under which the gospel travels — and often it travels furthest precisely by way of those dragged before governors and kings (v. 9). Paul reached Caesar's household because he was arrested. The persecution is not an interruption of the mission; it is one of its engines.

So the age between the resurrection and the coming has a task, and not merely a fear. Every tribe that hears is the clock of the world moving one turn closer to the dawn — which is why a Christian reading the news is not simply watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple marvels at its great stones and buildings, and Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. The most permanent-looking thing in their world was under God’s judgment and would fall — so we mustn’t build our lives on what is impressive but passing.

The last exit. He has just watched a widow give her last two coins (12:41–44), and now he walks out of the temple for the last time. In Mark he never enters it again.

Understandable wonder. “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” You can’t blame him. Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. The platform Herod built covers some thirty-five acres and is still there. Its retaining walls were dressed limestone blocks cut so precisely they needed no mortar; the largest, visible in the Western Wall tunnels, is over forty feet long and weighs several hundred tons. The sanctuary was faced with white stone and gold, and Josephus says that from a distance it looked like a snow-covered mountain. Work began around 20 BC and was finished only in the early 60s AD.

Not one stone. “Do you see these great buildings?” He grants it — yes, look. “There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” A few years after it was finished, it was gone: in AD 70 the Romans burned the sanctuary and, Josephus says, Titus ordered the city and temple razed. Why does the Western Wall still stand? It is part of the retaining wall around the platform, not the temple itself. Of the buildings Jesus pointed to, not one stone was left on another.

Blasphemy to their ears. We hear it as history; they heard it as blasphemy. This was the house of God, where atonement was made, the centre of Jewish life and the sign of the covenant. To say it would be levelled was unbearable. Jeremiah nearly died for saying less (Jeremiah 26:8–9), and a twisted version of this very saying will be used against Jesus at his trial (14:58).

What lasts. The disciple was admiring the most permanent-looking thing in his world — the biggest, most expensive, most obviously here to stay — and it had forty years left. What survived that generation wasn’t the masonry but twelve men, most of them poor, and a message. Everything you can point at and call impressive is on a clock. A test: what are you building your life with — things that fall, or the word of Christ that stands?
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with some stones many yards long. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the Mount of Olives, facing the temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew privately ask when these things will happen and what sign will show they are near. Jesus’ answer will refuse to satisfy curiosity about dates, because what his people need is not a timetable but readiness.

With the building in view. The Mount of Olives is the ridge across the Kidron valley, looking straight down onto the temple platform. So the whole discourse is given with the building in sight. He isn’t describing an abstraction; he is telling four men what will happen to what they can see.

A loaded hill. The place carries its own prophecy. Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave a defiled temple and stand “on the mountain that is on the east side of the city” (Ezekiel 11:23) — this hill. And Zechariah says of the day of the LORD, “On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). The glory left the temple and stopped on this ridge, and here he sits.

Four men, privately. Peter, James, John and Andrew — the first four called from their nets (1:16–20). The crowd that heard him gladly (12:37) is gone. This is the last long teaching in Mark before the passion, given to four men on a hillside.

Two questions. “When will these things be?” — a date. “What will be the sign?” — a warning visible in advance. And notice what they ask about: not the end of the world (Mark’s version has no such phrase) but “these things” — the stones. He said the temple would be flattened, and they want to know when, and how they will see it coming.

The refusal is the care. It is what any of us would ask, and the discourse won’t answer it in the form it was put. He gives signs, then warns that they don’t mean what people will be tempted to think; he gives a timeframe for the temple, then says that of his own coming no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son. And he ends with what they actually need: stay awake. That is a warning for the whole chapter. People come to Mark 13 wanting what these four wanted, and it was built to withhold it — not from secrecy, but because someone who knows the date prepares on the last afternoon, while someone who doesn’t must live ready every day. A test: are you more interested in when Christ will come than in being ready when he does?
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus began to say to them, "See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am he!' and they will lead many astray. And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns his disciples not to be led astray by those who come in his name, and not to be alarmed by wars, earthquakes and famines, which must happen but are only the beginning of birth pains, not the end. The great danger of this age is deception, not disaster, and believers are to meet world turmoil with calm, not panic or date-setting.

The first danger. They asked when; his first word is “See that no one leads you astray.” Before a single sign is described, he names the real danger, and it isn’t wars or earthquakes. It is being deceived, a warning he will repeat through the chapter (vv. 21–23).

In my name. “Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’” It happened almost at once. Josephus describes Theudas, who promised to part the Jordan, and an Egyptian who led crowds to the Mount of Olives promising Jerusalem’s walls would fall; Gamaliel mentions Theudas and Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36–37). The pattern has never stopped, and note its shape: they come “in my name” — not opposing Christ but claiming him, which is why the danger is to the church, not the world.

Don’t be alarmed. “When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed.” He isn’t saying the wars will be small; he is telling his people how to receive the news.

“This must take place.” The “must” is the word of divine necessity, used of his own suffering (8:31). History isn’t out of hand; what is coming doesn’t mean God has lost control. “But the end is not yet” — he deliberately disconnects calamities from the calendar.

Birth pains. Nation against nation, earthquakes, famines: every generation has had all three, and every generation has produced people sure theirs was the last. “These are but the beginning of the birth pains.” Labour pains are real agony, and they mean something is coming, but the early ones tell you almost nothing about how long. Paul uses the same picture: “the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). The world isn’t simply decaying; it is in labour.

Neither panic nor calculation. When the next catastrophe arrives, two responses are wrong: panic, anxiously scanning events for the pattern; and calculating excitement that treats disaster as a timetable, which has produced a long line of confident predictions and quiet retractions. Jesus forbids both. Read the news as someone told in advance what the age would look like, and get on with the work he gave you. A test: does the news make you anxious, or send you back to your work for Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

verseByVerse.quote: But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns that his followers will be handed to councils, beaten in synagogues and brought before governors and kings to testify; the gospel must first be preached to all nations; and on trial they needn’t worry beforehand what to say, for the Holy Spirit will speak. Persecution is the setting for the church’s mission, and Christ’s witnesses are not alone in the dock.

Coming to you. “But be on your guard.” The warning again, now specific: what is coming is coming to you.

Acts in advance. Read Acts with this verse open and it is a table of contents. Councils — Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5). Synagogues — Paul received the thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). Governors — Felix and Festus (Acts 24–25). Kings — Agrippa (Acts 26), and at last Caesar. And the first blows land in synagogues: persecution begins at home, among one’s own people. It usually does.

The dock is a pulpit. “To bear witness before them.” The purpose isn’t suffering but witness. Every trial put the gospel before an audience it would otherwise never have reached, as Paul wrote from prison: “what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12).

A task, not only a fear. “And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations” — the one item in the list that isn’t endured but done, with the same “must” as verse 7. Persecution isn’t an interruption of the mission but one of its engines; the gospel travelled farthest along roads that arrested men were dragged down. So a Christian reading the news isn’t watching the world fall apart but watching the field where the seed is being sown. A test: are you treating hostility to your faith as a reason to go quiet or as an opportunity to speak?

Does our success bring Christ back? In one sense this was fulfilled early: Paul could say before AD 70 that the gospel had been “proclaimed in all creation under heaven” (Colossians 1:23). In its fullest sense it goes on until the end. But Christ’s return isn’t triggered by our success, as though the church could finish a list and bring him back. The day is fixed by the Father (v. 32). Our part is to be faithful in the task.

A promise for the dock. “Do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say.” When a believer is dragged before a hostile court with no lawyer, no preparation and no idea of the charge, God undertakes to supply the words. Stephen’s face and speech are the fulfilment (Acts 6:15; 7), and so is the boldness of two uneducated fishermen that astonished the council (Acts 4:13).

Not an excuse for no preparation. It isn’t a licence for a preacher who hasn’t opened his Bible all week to expect the Spirit to make up the difference. Paul told Timothy, “Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15), and asked for his books and parchments in prison (2 Timothy 4:13). The unprepared sermon isn’t faith but presumption wearing faith’s coat.

Not alone. “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.” The believer in that courtroom isn’t alone, and isn’t finally the one on trial. Someone else is doing the speaking.
verseByVerse.note: The councils were local Jewish courts; synagogues had the authority to flog.

parallels.desc: Peter and John before the council

verseByVerse.quote: And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns that family members will betray one another to death and his followers will be hated by all for his name’s sake, but the one who endures to the end will be saved. Following Christ may cost even our closest relationships, yet God keeps his chosen people so that true faith endures.

The closest bonds. “Deliver over” is what he said would be done to him (10:33); now it is done to his people, by their own. And the sentence isn’t a general statement about hard times. It names the closest bonds in order: brother, the one you grew up beside; father, handing over his own child; children, rising against parents. It echoes Micah’s picture of moral collapse: “for the son treats the father with contempt… a man’s enemies are the men of his own house” (Micah 7:6). And it has happened in every century, and does now: there are believers today whose families reported them.

He knew it from inside. If your family regards your faith as betrayal — if you have lost a brother’s respect or a father’s welcome over it — your Lord said this would happen, and knew it from the inside: his own family came to seize him, saying, “He is out of his mind” (3:21). A test: are you willing to keep following Christ even if it costs you your family’s approval?

For my name’s sake. “You will be hated by all for my name’s sake” — not for being difficult, rude or politically awkward. Christians sometimes attract dislike for other reasons and then claim this verse. The promise is for hatred earned by belonging to him.

Must I hold on by my own strength? “The one who endures to the end will be saved” has kept anxious believers awake, so let it be answered straight. It isn’t salvation by stamina; we are saved by grace through faith, not the strength of our grip. It describes what real faith does: endurance isn’t the price of salvation but its evidence. The rocky ground in chapter 4 received the word with joy, had no root, and fell away when the heat came (4:16–17). The falling away didn’t cancel genuine faith; it revealed a shallow one.

The guarantee. And the guarantee is in this chapter. If you are asking, “Will I hold on?” — the right question — read on: “for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days” (v. 20), and the Son of Man “will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds” (v. 27). He doesn’t lose them: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The command is real and so is the promise, and they don’t compete. “Endure” is what you are told to do; “whom he chose” is why you will.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they see “the abomination of desolation” standing where he ought not, those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once, without going back for possessions. Jesus gives a specific warning about the coming desecration and destruction of Jerusalem — and a lasting lesson that when judgment comes, possessions are worth nothing.

The sign they asked for. The discourse turns from the general to the specific: this is the sign asked for in verse 4. The phrase is from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11): a desecration so vile it leaves God’s sanctuary desolate, using the Old Testament’s usual word for an idol. It had already been foreshadowed. In 167 BC Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up a pagan altar on the altar of burnt offering and swine were sacrificed in the temple. To every Jew the phrase meant the worst thing that ever happened, happening again.

A person. Mark’s grammar is deliberately odd: “standing where he ought not to be” — the participle is masculine though “abomination” is neuter. This isn’t only a thing set up in the holy place; it is somebody.

“Let the reader understand.” An aside from Mark to whoever reads this aloud in church: this is coded; be alert; when it happens, don’t stand about discussing it. A generation later Roman legions came carrying their standards — objects of worship bearing the emperor’s image — and Josephus records that when the temple fell, the soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and sacrificed to them.

Is this AD 70, or a future Antichrist? Many Christians, especially dispensationalists, expect a future ruler to enthrone himself in a rebuilt temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Revelation 13). But Luke gives Jesus’ words in a form his Gentile readers couldn’t miss: “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near” (Luke 21:20). The more likely reading is that this is AD 70, and the masculine “he” points to the Roman commander and his army. Paul’s man of lawlessness shows a final rebellion against God is still to come, but that isn’t what Jesus warns of here, where the remedy is to flee to the mountains.

Flee, don’t fight. Not defend the holy city — every nationalist instinct said the opposite, and the Zealots acted on it and were destroyed. Eusebius records that the Jerusalem Christians, warned (he says) by a revelation, left before the war closed in and settled at Pella beyond the Jordan. A church took its Lord’s warning literally and lived.

Don’t go back. Houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair: go down and keep going; don’t step inside for anything. A man working in the field left his cloak at the edge; it was costly, his blanket at night, protected by the law because the poor couldn’t do without it (Exodus 22:26–27). Leave it. Behind it stands another family told to leave a doomed city and not look back, and one who turned (Genesis 19:17, 26); in Luke, “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32).

The cloak. So this is tactical advice for a crisis in AD 70 — and a permanent picture of what judgment does to the value of possessions. A moment comes when the cloak isn’t worth the four seconds, and everything you own is that cloak. A test: what are you holding so tightly that you would turn back for it?
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple; it was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grieves for pregnant and nursing women in those days, tells his disciples to pray it won’t be in winter, and foretells unequalled distress — but for the sake of the elect God has cut the days short. Even history’s worst suffering is limited by God, who sets its bounds out of love for his people.

Tenderness in the terror. He has told them to run without stopping for a coat, and now he thinks of who can’t run. “Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days!” The Son of God, describing the fall of a city forty years away, pauses over the women nine months pregnant that week and the mothers with babies at the breast. He isn’t giving a strategic assessment; he is imagining particular people, and the word is a cry of grief, not a curse.

Pray about the timing. “Pray that it may not happen in winter.” Winter in Judea meant swollen streams, impassable tracks and cold nights in the open. So: ask God to arrange the timing of a judgment he has already determined, so the flight is survivable. That settles something about prayer. A thing can be fixed in God’s purpose and still be a right subject of prayer; his sovereignty over an event is no reason to stop asking about its details. Nothing is too settled to pray about, and nothing too small. A test: what have you stopped praying about because you think God has already decided it?

Unequalled distress. “Such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation… until now, and never will be” — the prophets’ absolute language for catastrophe beyond comparison (Daniel 12:1; Joel 2:2). What happened in AD 70 is hard to overstate. Josephus, an eyewitness, describes famine so severe that people chewed leather, a mother who ate her own child, and crucifixions outside the walls at hundreds a day until there was no room for crosses. He puts the dead at over a million; even a heavily discounted figure is a horror.

God set the limit. “If the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved.” Left to run its course, it would have consumed everyone; nothing human would have stopped it. “But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.” The tribulation is bounded — not by evil exhausting itself, nor by armies or the church’s strength, but by God. And Mark says it twice in one breath — “the elect,” “whom he chose” — so we don’t miss how deliberate it is.

Better than exemption. It doesn’t promise God’s people are exempt; they were in Jerusalem, and Christians have been in every horror since. It promises something better: they are the reason it stops. History isn’t a machine running until it wears out; behind the worst of it is a hand on the clock, set by love for particular people. So when you can’t see how something can go on and anyone survive it — the persecution in that country, the sickness in this house, the years taken — the promise isn’t that you will be lifted out. It is that there is a limit, fixed before it began, and fixed for your sake.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: And then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'Look, there he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns not to believe anyone who says, “Look, here is the Christ,” for false christs and false prophets will perform signs and wonders to lead astray, if possible, the elect; he has told them beforehand. Miracles don’t prove truth; God’s people are kept from deception by knowing and holding to what Christ has said.

Here or there. He ends the section not with the tribulation but with deception — the worst thing in the passage isn’t the siege. And notice its form: “here” and “there,” a location — someone has him somewhere and you must go and see. That is the mark of the counterfeit. The real coming will be “as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west” (Matthew 24:27); nobody will need to be told where to look.

The signs will work. “False christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders.” Jesus doesn’t say they will be tricks. The Bible is consistent: Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues (Exodus 7:22); Deuteronomy legislates for a prophet whose sign comes true and who then says, “Let us go after other gods” — don’t listen, for the LORD is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3); Paul warns of the lawless one coming “with all power and false signs and wonders” (2 Thessalonians 2:9). So the supernatural isn’t self-authenticating. That something works is never by itself a reason to follow anybody.

The test is doctrine. The test is never the power but the teaching beneath it: does this lead people to the Christ who came in the flesh and died on a cross, or away from him? John gives the same test (1 John 4:2–3). A test for you: do you judge teachers by their results and excitement, or by whether they bring you to the Christ of Scripture?

“If possible, the elect.” The elect are the target — not the world, which needs no deceiving, but the church, by people using Christ’s name. And “if possible” is a quiet reassurance, not a licence for carelessness: the attempt will be formidable, and God’s people won’t finally be lost.

Told beforehand. “But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.” That is how God protects his people from deception — not by making them incapable of being fooled, but by telling them in advance and expecting them to remember. Which puts a plain duty on a Christian who wants to be safe: know your Bible well enough that a false thing sounds wrong when you hear it. The forewarning protects only someone who has read it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The coming (vv. 24–27). Sun darkened, moon gone out, stars falling, the powers shaken — and then the Son of Man, coming in clouds with great power and glory, sending out angels to gather his people from the four winds. It is Daniel 7 arriving, spoken by a man three days from a public execution.

The fig tree (vv. 28–31). A lesson in reading signs, and the most argued-over verse in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. And then a claim no creature could make — heaven and earth will go, and his words will not.

The hinge (v. 32). But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows — not the angels, not the Son. Everything before this verse had signs. Nothing after it does.

The command (vv. 33–37). A householder goes away, leaves each servant a job, tells the doorkeeper to stay awake — and might come back at any of the four watches of the night. Stay awake, four times over, and the last words are addressed past the four men on the hillside to everybody.

And Mark's reader is about to walk through all four watches in the next two chapters, with the disciples failing at every one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against the deity of Christ. Arius built on it in the fourth century; it is still reached for today. If Jesus did not know the day, the argument runs, he cannot be God.
