Meant well, and wrong. “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” Entirely characteristic, meant well — and wrong. He accepts the prophecy for the others and exempts himself, in front of them: not only presumption about himself but a low estimate of his brothers, said in their hearing. Someone who thinks he alone will stand has already begun to fall, because he has stopped needing anyone.

The precise warning. “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” Not a rebuke but a specification, and Mark’s is the most precise of the four: this very night, twice, three times. It is the kind of detail only the man it happened to would remember so exactly, and this Gospel carries Peter’s preaching. He has preserved the sentence that broke him, numbers and all.

Twice or once? Matthew, Luke and John say “before the rooster crows”; only Mark says “twice.” The others give the general warning; Mark, from Peter’s memory, gives the precise form, with a first crowing Peter ignored and a second that broke him. There is no contradiction; one account is simply fuller.

He meant it. “If I must die with you, I will not deny you” — said emphatically. And he meant it. That is what makes the passage useful rather than merely a story about a boaster. Peter wasn’t lying; he loved him. Within hours he will draw a sword against an armed crowd, more than the others manage. He wasn’t a coward. He simply didn’t know himself.

All of them. “And they all said the same.” Mark won’t let Peter carry it alone: every one said it, and every one ran.

Untested strength. The practical lesson is aimed at anyone who feels reasonably safe. The danger isn’t that you might one day decide to abandon Christ; no one in that room decided anything. It is confidence in a strength that has never been tested — the quiet assumption that you would hold, would speak up, wouldn’t do what others did. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). A test: where are you trusting your own resolve rather than praying for Christ’s keeping?

The love behind the boast. Notice what Jesus doesn’t say. He doesn’t say, “Then you were never mine,” or withdraw the promise of verse 28. He tells Peter exactly what he will do, takes him into the garden anyway, dies for him, and has him named by an angel on the third day. The boast was hollow; the love behind it wasn’t, and Christ knew the difference.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Gethsemane Jesus takes Peter, James and John aside, becomes greatly distressed and troubled, and tells them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.” The Son of God truly felt overwhelming anguish as he faced the cross, and he is a Saviour who understands our deepest sorrow.

The garden. Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron. “Sit here while I pray” — the others are left behind.

The same three. He takes Peter, James and John — the three taken into Jairus’s house to see a dead girl raised (5:37) and up the mountain to see him transfigured (9:2). They have seen him at his most glorious; now they see him at his lowest. That is no accident. No one is fit to speak about the glory who hasn’t also seen the garden.

Overwhelmed. “He began to be greatly distressed and troubled.” Mark reaches for two of the strongest words he has — appalled, shuddering, distress with no bottom to it. And “began”: this isn’t a settled sorrow carried all week. It falls on him in the garden.

He told them. “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.” The Son of God, in the worst hour of his life, turns to three friends and tells them how bad it is. A certain kind of piety thinks that weakness. It isn’t in this Gospel. He asked for company and told them the truth. And his words echo the psalmist’s, “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5, 11; 43:5), where the Greek Old Testament uses the same word. He is praying the Psalms in his agony. “Even to death” means sorrow heavy enough to kill. Luke records what it did to his body: “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luke 22:44).

How can the Son of God be so distressed? Because he is truly man as well as God. His human soul shrank from the cup of God’s wrath, as any holy man would, and he said so. But his will was never set against the Father’s; he asked, and then submitted: “not what I will, but what you will” (v. 36). This isn’t a crack in the Trinity. It is the obedience of the Son, offered “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7).

Stay awake near me. “Remain here and watch” — the word of the parable, “stay awake” (13:34–37). He isn’t asking them to fix anything, only to stay awake near him. That is the plainest description of what friendship costs in someone else’s grief: you can’t fix it and aren’t asked to; you are asked not to fall asleep. A test: whose grief is Christ asking you simply to stay near this week?

He knows. Whatever you are carrying, he doesn’t look at it from a distance. There was a night when the Son of God was appalled and shaking and told his friends the sorrow was killing him — and he is the one you bring yours to.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Falling to the ground, Jesus prays that if possible the hour might pass, saying, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” Jesus shrank from drinking the cup of God’s wrath against sin, yet submitted to the Father’s will, so that we might be spared it.

He fell. Not knelt — fell; Matthew says on his face. The man who slept through a storm, faced down a legion and overturned the temple tables is on the ground among the olive roots.

A real request. “That, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him.” Mark gives the substance first, then the words. And note the condition: if it were possible. He isn’t demanding; he is asking whether there is another way, and the asking is real.

Abba. Mark keeps the Aramaic, as with “Talitha cumi” and “Ephphatha” — and this time it is the very sound of Jesus praying. “Abba” was the family word for father used in the home. It is sometimes over-translated “Daddy,” which is too small — grown men used it of their fathers — but it is unmistakably intimate, not the language of formal worship, and Jewish prayer very rarely if ever addressed God that way. He prays as a son at home, and in his deepest agony that is the word he reaches for. And he handed it on: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). A test: do you come to God in your trouble as a child to his Father?

The confession first. “All things are possible for you.” Before the request, the confession. He doesn’t ask whether God is able; he states that he is, and then asks — the reverse of how most of us pray in a crisis.

What is the cup? Not simply death. Reading Gethsemane as fear of dying leaves us a Lord less composed at his execution than many of his martyrs, who went to worse deaths singing. The cup is a fixed Old Testament image for God’s wrath: “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine… and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8); “you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath” (Isaiah 51:17); “Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath” (Jeremiah 25:15). That is what stands before him: not the nails, but God’s holy anger against the sins of all he came to save, to be drunk to the dregs. He isn’t afraid of pain. He is looking into the cup.

Not my will. “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” He doesn’t withdraw the request; he asks honestly for what he wants, then submits. Both are prayer: the asking isn’t unbelief, the submitting isn’t resignation. And it reverses Eden. In a garden a man knew the Father’s will and said, in effect, “Not your will but mine,” and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said, “Not what I will, but what you will,” and it was mended.

Your model and permission. When you pray about something God hasn’t taken away, this is your model and your permission. Ask plainly for what you want; he did. Then hand it over; he did that too. The cup didn’t pass, and he drank it — which is why nothing is left in it for those who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus finds the disciples sleeping and says to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Prayerful watchfulness prepares us for temptation, and Christ deals tenderly with our weakness even when we fail him.

Found asleep. He rises, walks back through the trees, and they are asleep. Mark’s reader was prepared for this by the parable of the master who comes home at night: “lest he come suddenly and find you asleep” (13:36). He came; they were asleep. The parable is acted out on the men it was told to.

“Simon.” He speaks to Peter by his old name — not Peter, the rock, but Simon, the name he had pulling nets out of the lake. It is the only time in Mark that Jesus calls him Simon, and it is deliberate, gentle and devastating. The man who said, “Even though they all fall away, I will not,” can’t stay awake.

One hour. Not the night — an hour. The smallest request, from a man overwhelmed with grief a stone’s throw away, and it was too much. But before using it against them, be honest about the circumstances. It was late; they had eaten a festal meal with wine and walked; and Luke kindly records that he found them “sleeping for sorrow” (Luke 22:45). Grief exhausts people. They weren’t indifferent; they were shattered.

Prepare before the test. “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” Two commands that belong together, and the reason is preventive: very soon they will be tested, and this hour is the preparation. They slept through the preparation and failed the test. That is the plainest practical lesson in the chapter: the battle is lost or won before the temptation arrives. The person who hasn’t prayed doesn’t fall in the moment; he fell in the hours before, when nothing seemed to be happening and there was no obvious reason to be on his knees. Gethsemane is where the courtyard was decided. A test: what temptation do you know is coming that you haven’t yet prayed about?

Willing spirit, weak flesh. “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Having named their failure, he explains it with a sympathy almost unbearable, given who is speaking. He grants that their intentions were real; Peter meant every word. “Flesh” here is human nature in its frailty — weakness, not wickedness. He isn’t calling them hypocrites; he is saying they are men.

He knows our frame. And the one diagnosing it is himself on the ground, his own flesh bearing a weight none of them can imagine. He knows exactly how weak it is. So this is comfort as well as warning: “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). Your Lord isn’t surprised by your weakness and doesn’t despise it. He has been more tired, more frightened and more alone than you will ever be, and he stayed awake for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes away and prays the same words again, and returns to find them sleeping again, their eyes heavy, not knowing what to answer him. Persistent, repeated prayer in anguish is right and good, and the disciples’ failure shows the honesty of the Gospel record and the need of grace.

The same words. “Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.” Don’t hurry past this; it says something about prayer many Christians have never been told. Some treat repetition as a failure of faith, as though asking twice meant you didn’t believe the first time, or prayer needed fresh and eloquent phrasing to be genuine. Jesus prayed the same request repeatedly in one hour, in the most important prayer meeting in history. Paul did the same about his thorn: “Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this” (2 Corinthians 12:8). And when words run out, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26).

Praying in Gethsemane. So if all you can do tonight is say the same desperate sentence over and over, you aren’t praying badly. You are praying as he prayed in Gethsemane. A test: have you given up asking God for something because you have asked before?

Heavy eyes. “Again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy” — a small human detail, the phrase you would use of yourself in the small hours.

Nothing to say. “And they did not know what to answer him” — the saddest clause in the paragraph, surely Peter’s own memory. They woke, he stood over them, and there was nothing to say; no excuse would work. Mark has recorded this before: at the transfiguration Peter blurted out a suggestion about tents, “for he did not know what to say, for they were terrified” (9:6). The same three men, in the two moments they saw most clearly who he was, both times with nothing to say.

Honest reporting. That is one reason this Gospel reads like testimony, not legend. No one inventing a founding story writes that its leaders slept through the crisis and had no answer when caught. Peter told it against himself for the rest of his life — and there is mercy in that too, because the church has never been able to pretend its first leaders were made of better material than the rest of us.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Returning a third time, Jesus says, “It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” Having submitted to the Father in prayer, Jesus goes willingly and steadily to meet his betrayer and his death.

The third time. “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest?” Three times he came back, three times they were asleep — and within hours Peter will deny him three times. The words can be read as a question or as a resigned statement (“sleep on now”); the Greek allows either. Either way, the tone has changed. He is no longer asking anything of them.

Settled. Something has happened in that prayer. He went into the grove appalled and shaking; he comes out settled, and every sentence from here to the cross has the same steadiness. The struggle was real, and it is over. He asked, he submitted, the answer was no — and he takes the no and gets up. A test: have you brought your hardest thing to God and left it with him, so that you can rise and face it?

The hour has come. “It is enough; the hour has come” — the very hour he prayed might pass from him (v. 35). It hasn’t passed; it has arrived. The whole Gospel has been walking toward it, and it doesn’t sneak up on him. He announces it.

Now happening. “The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.” He has said this in his predictions of the passion (8:31; 9:31; 10:33). Now the tense has changed: not “will be,” but happening.

Toward them. “Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” For half a second it sounds like escape — get up, we are leaving. It is the opposite. Torches are coming up from the Kidron (John 18:3), and he walks toward them. The disciples are drowsy, Judas is arriving with an armed crowd, and the man who has spent an hour on the ground begging for another way stands up and says, let us go and meet him. No one takes him; he goes: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

My betrayer. Notice the pronoun: not “the betrayer” but “my betrayer.” So Gethsemane ends with the sleepy disciples roused by their Lord walking toward the men who have come to kill him, having settled the matter in prayer while they slept.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas, one of the twelve, arrives with an armed crowd from the Jewish leaders, identifies Jesus with a kiss as the agreed sign, and they seize him. The deepest treachery uses the sign of love — and the Lord who could not be overpowered lets himself be taken.

One of the twelve. “Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve.” Mark says it a third time in the chapter. He can’t leave it alone, and neither should we.

Armed against an unarmed man. “A crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders” — an armed party sent by the council, and John adds soldiers with lanterns and torches (John 18:3). They come at night, into a garden, in force, to arrest an unarmed teacher who stood in the temple all week in broad daylight.

They needed a sign. “The one I will kiss is the man.” The arresting party couldn’t reliably pick him out at night, by torchlight, among Galileans dressed alike. That is believable realism, and it tells you Jesus didn’t look like anything in particular: no halo, nothing to distinguish the Son of God from the fishermen beside him. “Seize him and lead him away under guard” — securely. Judas knows what this man has done to crowds and storms, and takes no chances.

The kiss. “He went up to him at once and said, ‘Rabbi!’ And he kissed him.” A kiss was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher — respect, affection, belonging — and Mark’s verb here is the stronger form: he kissed him warmly. So the sign chosen to mark him for death was the sign of love. Scripture knows there is nothing worse: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9); “profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). And “Rabbi” — my teacher — not “Lord.” It is Judas’s last word in Mark, a title of respect emptied of its meaning.

He received it. Matthew records Jesus’ answer: “Friend, do what you came to do” (Matthew 26:50); Luke another: “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). He didn’t turn his face away or step back. He received the kiss. A test: is your outward affection for Christ matched by your loyalty when it costs?

Seized. “And they laid hands on him and seized him.” The Gospel turns. From here until the resurrection, Jesus is in custody, and everything is done to him: he is led, handed over, questioned, struck, flogged and crucified. The one who stilled storms, cast out a legion and raised the dead lets temple guards lay hands on him in the dark and take him away — because he chose to.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled." And they all left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bystander cuts off the high priest’s servant’s ear; Jesus rebukes the arresting party for coming against him like a bandit when he taught openly every day, and submits so the Scriptures may be fulfilled, and all the disciples flee. Christ’s kingdom isn’t advanced by force, and he goes to the cross alone, deserted by everyone.

The sword. Mark doesn’t name the swordsman. John, writing later, says it was Peter and the servant was Malchus (John 18:10). Be fair to Peter: eleven men are about to run, and one draws a weapon against an armed party. He wasn’t a coward, and whatever he got wrong tonight, he got it wrong bravely. He also got it wholly wrong. And Luke records Jesus’ last healing before the cross: “he touched his ear and healed him” (Luke 22:51). His last free act was to repair the damage his own disciple had done to a man who came to arrest him.

Does this forbid Christians to use force? Matthew records Jesus’ rebuke, “all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52), and John his reason, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Jesus forbids the sword to defend his kingdom or to stop the cross. He doesn’t abolish the state’s sword (Romans 13:4), nor the defence of life (Exodus 22:2). Christians may protect themselves and others; they may never advance Christ’s cause by force. A test: are you tempted to fight for Christ with the world’s weapons — anger, force, manipulation — rather than truth and love?

As against a robber. “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me?” The word means a bandit, an armed insurrectionist — the word later used of the two men crucified beside him (15:27). You have come out in force, at night, armed, as though I were a rebel.

A confession. “Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me.” He stood in their own building, in public, all week; they could have arrested him any day. They didn’t, because of the crowd (12:12; 14:2). So the swords, torches and night raid aren’t a security precaution but a confession. People who take a prisoner in the dark are telling you what they think of their case.

Let the Scriptures be fulfilled. With that he stops arguing and submits. Not “this is a miscarriage of justice,” though it is; not “my Father will vindicate me,” though he will — simply: this is what was written, it is happening, and I won’t stop it.

They all fled. “And they all left him and fled.” All: the eleven who said they would die with him, the three who couldn’t stay awake, Peter with his sword. “Left” is the verb Mark used when they left their nets to follow him (1:18). They left everything to follow him; now they leave him. “You will all fall away” (v. 27) is fulfilled within the hour — and he had already told them where to meet him afterward. From here he is alone; there isn’t a friendly face in the rest of the chapter.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young man wearing only a linen cloth follows Jesus, and when they seize him he leaves the cloth and runs away naked. Mark shows the disciples’ total desertion in one shameful picture, and many have thought the young man was Mark himself.

A strange detail. Two verses found in no other Gospel, which have puzzled readers ever since, because on the face of it they are pointless: an unknown person loses his clothes and runs; nothing depends on it. That is why many readers have concluded it is Mark himself. It is too specific and too embarrassing to be invented; no one puts an anonymous humiliation into a Gospel for its own sake. It looks like the signature of an eyewitness who wants to be in the record without being named.

A possible candidate. The church in Jerusalem later met at the house of Mary, Mark’s mother (Acts 12:12), where Peter went when released from prison, and some have suggested the upper room was there. If so, a young man in that household might have heard where they had gone, got up in the night with a linen sheet round him, and followed. Whether or not it was Mark, the text doesn’t say.

The desertion with a face. More important is what it shows. “They all left him and fled” (v. 50) — and now the desertion has a face: one person, caught in the torchlight, who would rather lose everything he was wearing than be taken with Jesus. That is what abandonment looked like from the inside: not a decision but a bolt. A test: what are you willing to lose rather than be associated with Christ — or to lose for his sake?

Two linen cloths. And watch the linen. The young man leaves a linen cloth and runs naked; in the next chapter Joseph of Arimathea buys a linen shroud and wraps the body of Jesus in it (15:46). A follower abandons his linen and flees, and his Lord is wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb.

Two young men. And there is a last bracket. The word “young man” appears only twice in Mark: here, fleeing naked in the dark; and on the first morning of the week, when the women find the stone rolled back and “saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe” (16:5). Mark brackets the passion with two young men: one who fled from Christ stripped and ashamed, and one seated in an empty tomb, clothed in white, announcing that he has risen. That is the gospel in two pictures — from shame to the news of resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the young man. Many have guessed he was Mark himself, but the text does not say.

parallels.desc: he who is stout of heart shall flee away naked in that day

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 53–72 — The Trial and the Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The council (vv. 53–65). He is taken to the high priest's house and the whole Sanhedrin assembles in the middle of the night. They look for evidence to justify a verdict they have already reached, and cannot find any that holds — the witnesses contradict each other, even about the temple saying. He says nothing at all. Then the high priest puts the direct question, under oath, and he answers it in full for the first time in this Gospel: I am — and adds Daniel 7 and Psalm 110 to it. The robes are torn, the sentence is passed, and men begin to spit at him.

The courtyard (vv. 66–72). And Mark cuts, in the same building, to the one disciple who followed. A servant girl looks at Peter across a fire; a second challenge comes; then the bystanders place his accent. Three times, escalating — a denial, a denial, and finally oaths and a curse.

Then a bird calls, and he remembers, and the strongest of the twelve goes to pieces.

Mark has interleaved the two scenes deliberately: upstairs, Christ confesses and is condemned for it; downstairs, Peter denies and is safe.
verseByVerse.theology:
The trial was illegal, and the record shows it. By the standards later codified in the Mishnah, capital cases were to be tried in daytime, in the temple's own hall, never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival, and a conviction could not be handed down on the same day as the trial — an acquittal could, but a death sentence required a night to pass first. This proceeding breaks all of it. It is held at night, in the high priest's residence, at Passover, with sentence passed at once.

How much of that code was in force in AD 30 is genuinely debated. But Mark's own account convicts them without any of it, in one sentence: the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death (v. 55). That is not a court. A court seeks the truth and then decides the penalty; this one had the penalty and went looking for grounds.

And I am is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of demons silenced and healed men hushed, and now, under oath, with nothing left to protect, he answers plainly. Egō eimi — the words of the burning bush (Ex. 3:14) — and then two texts fused: seated at the right hand of Power (Ps. 110:1), which he had put to them as a riddle two days earlier (12:36), and coming with the clouds of heaven (Dan. 7:13).

He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the high priest tears his garments (v. 63) — the formal gesture required of a judge on hearing blasphemy.

And it is worth knowing what the Law said about that particular man's clothes. The high priest was under a standing prohibition: he shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Lev. 21:10). The office was not permitted the ordinary signs of mourning.

So on the night the Sanhedrin condemned Jesus for blasphemy, the high priest of Israel broke the Law of Moses to do it. Every man in that room was more concerned with the letter of the law than anybody alive, and the one they killed for breaking it was the only one in the building keeping it.

Now: and then they spat at him and covered his face and hit him and said Prophesy! — a game, apparently, of making the blindfolded man name who struck him.

They did not know that he had prophesied, that afternoon and the night before, with total accuracy: that one of the twelve would betray him, that all of them would run, and that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed twice.

While they were demanding a prophecy, the last of those predictions was coming true below them, in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl.

verseByVerse.quote: And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is taken to the high priest, where the whole council gathers, while Peter follows at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard and sits warming himself with the guards. Following Christ at a distance, comfortable among his enemies, is the most dangerous place for a disciple to stand.

A night session. “They led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together.” The council assembled in the middle of the night — which takes organisation: messengers round the city, members roused from their beds. The arrangements were made in advance; they were waiting for Judas’s signal. John says they took him first to Annas, the former high priest and power behind the office (John 18:13). The high priest is Caiaphas, his son-in-law, who had already said “it is better for you that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50).

At a distance. Mark now starts the second thread, before the trial, so the two run side by side. “Peter had followed him at a distance” — the saddest description of discipleship in the New Testament. He hasn’t fled, and that should be said loudly, because Peter is easy to despise and doesn’t deserve it. The others are somewhere in the dark; one followed. But at a distance — close enough to see, far enough not to be associated. That is the most dangerous place in the world to stand: near enough to quiet your conscience, far enough to keep you safe. No one stays there long; it resolves one way or the other within hours.

Inside the courtyard. “Right into the courtyard of the high priest.” He gets inside; John says another disciple, known to the household, got him through the gate (John 18:15–16).

At the enemy’s fire. “He was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.” Every word is deliberate, and Mark will repeat it (v. 67). Sitting with the guards — not standing at the edge, but seated among the men who arrested his Lord an hour ago. Warming himself — it was a cold spring night, there was a fire in the yard, and Peter is at it with his hands out.

Two levels. Mark builds the picture: inside, Jesus stands before the council; below, in the same compound, Peter sits warm with the men who seized him. He hasn’t denied anything yet. He has simply taken a place at the enemy’s fire because it was cold and he wanted to see what would happen — and the next thing that happens is that the firelight falls on his face.

Your fire. There is a version of that fire in every Christian’s life: the place where you can be near Christ and comfortable at once, sitting with people who have no time for him and saying nothing, because it is warm and going home would cost something. No one is asked a hard question at a safe distance; they are asked at the fire. A test: where are you sitting comfortably and silently among those who scorn Christ?
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and whole council seek testimony to put Jesus to death but find none, because the many false witnesses don’t agree. The court was corrupt, its verdict fixed in advance — and even his enemies couldn’t find a true charge against the sinless Son of God.

Verdict first. “Seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death.” Mark convicts the court in one line. They aren’t seeking testimony, but testimony against him, to put him to death. The verdict is fixed and the evidence recruited to fit it. That is the exact inversion of a court, which establishes what happened and then decides the consequence. This body has the consequence and is shopping for the happening.

Irregular proceedings. The later Jewish law code (the Mishnah) says capital cases were to be heard by day, never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or feast, and that a guilty verdict had to wait until the next day, so the judges slept on it — though we can’t be sure how much of that was in force at the time. This hearing is at night, in a private residence, at Passover. But Mark doesn’t lean on any of that. His indictment is simpler.

They found none. “But they found none.” Quietly extraordinary. The supreme court of Israel, with every motive and the whole night, and presumably the means to find willing witnesses, couldn’t assemble a credible case. Three years of public ministry, much of it in the open before hostile experts who had followed him since chapter 2 precisely to catch him out — and they couldn’t find two men who agreed on any wrong he had done. That is no small evidence for the sinlessness of Jesus: the testimony of a hostile prosecution that had every reason to produce something and couldn’t.

Lies that didn’t match. “Many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.” Under the law that was fatal to the case: “A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime… Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15). And a false witness was to receive the penalty he sought to inflict (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). Yet no one in that room was charged with anything.

For your life. The innocent one stood condemned so that the guilty could stand acquitted. And when you are falsely accused, you follow a Lord who was, and who kept silent and trusted his Father. A test: when others misrepresent you, do you entrust yourself to God who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23)?
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, "We heard him say, 'I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.'" Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some testify falsely that Jesus said he would destroy the temple made with hands and build another in three days, but even their testimony doesn’t agree. The most effective lies twist true words, yet Jesus’ real meaning came true: in three days he rose as the new temple.

A lie made from truth. The best they can manage is a lie built from something true — which is how the most effective lies are made. He had said something like it, at the first cleansing of the temple: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” and John adds the explanation the witnesses dropped: “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19–21).

The alterations. First, the challenge becomes a threat. He said “Destroy this temple” — addressed to them. They report “I will destroy this temple” — a stated intention, turning a saying about his own death into a plot against the national sanctuary. Second, the picture is flattened into masonry. He spoke of his body; they present it as a claim about the building — as inflammatory a charge as could be made in Passover week. Jeremiah nearly died for prophesying against this house (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and Stephen will die on the same accusation (Acts 6:13–14). Take his real words, change one verb, remove the meaning: nothing invented, everything twisted.

Still how it is done. That is still the commonest way Christ and his people are misrepresented — not fabrication but selective reporting: a sentence lifted out, the context deleted, the qualifier dropped, and the thing reported still traceable to something actually said. A test: when you repeat what someone said, do you keep their meaning, or only their words?

Collapsed. “Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.” Even the best lie in the room couldn’t survive two people telling it. And this is crucial: he isn’t convicted of anything the witnesses said, because none of it stood up. The charge that kills him will come from his own mouth when the high priest asks who he is and he tells the truth.

Accidentally right. And the thing they mocked was about to come true. In three days there would be a temple not made with hands — his risen body — and the church has been built on it ever since: “in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21). The false witnesses were accidentally right, and nobody in the room noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest demands an answer to the charges, but Jesus stays silent; then asked, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” he answers, “I am,” and says they will see the Son of Man seated at God’s right hand and coming with the clouds of heaven. Jesus openly claims to be the Messiah, the divine Son and the coming Judge — at the moment the claim will cost him his life.

The trial failing. “The high priest stood up in the midst.” The case has collapsed, and Caiaphas moves into the middle of the room to rescue it, trying to get the prisoner talking: “Have you no answer to make?”

Silence. “But he remained silent and made no answer.” Mark says it twice, because the silence is the point. He doesn’t point out that the witnesses contradict each other, which might have ended the proceedings, or explain what he really said about the temple, which was entirely defensible. He says nothing. It fulfils Isaiah: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Every instinct in a wronged man is to explain. He won’t defend himself, because defending himself would have worked, and he had come to die.

The question of the Gospel. “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” — the question Mark has been asking since 1:1. “The Blessed” is a reverent way of avoiding God’s name; he means, are you the Messiah, the Son of God? Matthew says he put him under oath (Matthew 26:63).

“I am.” For chapters Jesus has silenced demons, hushed the healed and told disciples to say nothing, because the title would be misunderstood, a crowd might crown him, and the cross had to define it. Now there is nothing left to protect: he is bound, the crowd can’t reach him, no crown is on offer. And at the moment it can only cost him his life, he says it plainly. The words are the same he spoke on the water in the dark (6:50), and they may echo the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14).

Throne and judgment. “You will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” He fuses two texts: Psalm 110:1, the psalm he had put to these men as a riddle (12:36), and Daniel 7:13, the one like a son of man given everlasting dominion. A bound prisoner tells the court about to condemn him: you will see me on the throne, and you will see me coming as judge. The dock and the bench are about to change places.

When would they see this? Some take it as Christ’s vindication after his death — resurrection, ascension and the judgment on Jerusalem — since in Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom. Others take it as the final coming, when “every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7). The more likely reading holds both together. From his resurrection Jesus is enthroned at God’s right hand, and those who condemned him saw the signs of it; the coming with the clouds will be seen by all at his return, when these judges stand before their Judge.

For your life. Everyone present understood him perfectly; that is why the next verse happens. And the same Jesus will be your Judge. A test: will you confess him now as he confessed himself then, whatever it costs?
verseByVerse.note: “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God.” Jesus’ “I am” is his plainest claim in Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest tore his garments and said, "What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?" And they all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest tears his garments, declares it blasphemy, and the council condemns Jesus to death; then some spit on him, blindfold and beat him, mocking, “Prophesy!” Jesus bore humiliation and contempt as God’s suffering Servant, and the claim that condemned him leaves no middle ground: he is either God’s Son or a blasphemer.

Torn garments. “The high priest tore his garments” — a formal gesture of horror on hearing blasphemy. The law forbade the high priest the ordinary signs of mourning: he “shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes” (Leviticus 21:10). Later tradition allowed judges to tear their garments at blasphemy. Either way, the irony stands: the most scrupulous men alive, experts in the law, are condemning the one man in the building who had kept it perfectly.

The one honest sentence. “What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy.” In a way Caiaphas doesn’t intend, it is the one true sentence spoken all night. No further witnesses are needed; the case is settled from the prisoner’s own mouth. And his logic holds: if Jesus isn’t who he said, this is blasphemy — a man claiming God’s throne and the judgment of the world. Caiaphas isn’t unreasonable; he is consistent, having already decided the claim is false.

Two options. There were never more than two options in that room, and there are only two now. Either the man in the dock is God’s Son, or he said the most blasphemous thing a human being ever said. No one who has read this trial can go on calling him merely a fine moral teacher. A test: which of the two do you believe — and does your life show it?

Condemned. “They all condemned him as deserving death.” Mark says it flatly. Whether every member was present is another question; Joseph of Arimathea, a member, hadn’t consented (Luke 23:51). But those present were unanimous.

Spat on and struck. Then the court, having passed sentence, does this. Spitting was the deepest contempt, a mark of public disgrace (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9), and Isaiah’s Servant received it: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). Covering his face and striking him is a game: blindfold him, hit him, and demand he name who did it (Luke 22:64). Israel’s religious leaders, playing a guessing game with a bound prisoner in the night. And he bore it for the very people mocking him.

“Prophesy!” The cruellest word in the chapter, and the most ironic. He had prophesied that very evening, with total accuracy: one of the twelve would betray him, and one had; they would all fall away, and they had. And one more thing was coming true at that moment, below them in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl warming her hands at the fire.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, "You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus." But he denied it, saying, "I neither know nor understand what you mean." And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Below in the courtyard a servant girl stares at Peter and says he was with Jesus the Nazarene; Peter denies it, claiming not to understand, and moves out to the gateway. Denial of Christ often begins with a small evasion to escape a moment’s discomfort, and God’s warnings come to us before we fall further.

Two men, one question. “As Peter was below in the courtyard.” Mark sets it side by side: above, Christ on trial, confessing who he is and struck for it; below, Peter at the fire, about to be asked the same kind of question. One says “I am,” and it costs him his life. The other will say, in effect, “I am not,” and it costs him everything else.

A servant girl. Look at who breaks him. Not a soldier, a council member, or the guards who saw him draw a sword hours earlier, but one of the high priest’s servant girls — among the lowest-status people in the household, with no power over him at all. The man who swore he would die with Jesus is undone by a servant.

The firelight. “Seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him” — fixed her eyes on him, the word Mark used when Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him (10:21). She peers across the fire, the light on his face, working out where she has seen him. And she can see him only because he sat down at that fire. In the shadows at the edge, no one asks you anything.

Association. “You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.” Not “you are a disciple” or “you believe his teaching,” but “you were with him” — association, nothing more. And “the Nazarene” is faintly contemptuous: that man from that village.

A fog. “But he denied it, saying, ‘I neither know nor understand what you mean.’” The first denial is less a flat lie than a fog — the answer of a man buying time, the sort of thing everyone has said. We imagine Peter’s denial as dramatic and unlike us. It began as an evasion at a fire: not “I renounce Christ,” but “I don’t know what you mean,” said to someone unimportant to make a moment go away. A test: where do you dodge a simple question about your faith to avoid an awkward moment?

A warning unheard. “And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.” He moves nearer the door, further from the light, closer to escape. And a rooster crows somewhere in the city. There is mercy here that almost no one notices: the first crow was a warning, given just as Jesus said, to a man who had been told hours earlier what it would mean. There was still time; two denials hadn’t yet happened. He heard it, and it meant nothing to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, "This man is one of them." But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, "Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant girl tells the bystanders Peter is one of them, and he denies it again; then the bystanders insist he must be, since he is a Galilean. One lie makes the next easier — and a disciple of Jesus is marked by what he can’t hide.

Widening pressure. “The servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, ‘This man is one of them.’” She hasn’t let it go, and now she is telling others. The first challenge was private; this one is public. And the wording has hardened: not “you were with him” but “he is one of them” — a group, a party.

Easier the second time. “But again he denied it.” Mark doesn’t even record the words, just the fact. The second lie is easier and needs less said. That is how it works, and it is the most practically useful thing here. The first denial makes the second cheap. Having said, “I don’t know what you mean,” he must now defend the first statement as well as himself, and the only way is to say it again more forcefully. A lie is a loan, and every later lie is interest. A test: is there a small dishonesty you are now defending with bigger ones?

His accent. “After a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, ‘Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.’” Now it is a group, and they have evidence: his accent. Galilean Aramaic sounded noticeably different from Jerusalem speech. Matthew makes it explicit: “Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you” (Matthew 26:73). Peter can deny knowing Jesus, but he can’t deny the sound of his own voice. Every sentence he speaks in his defence proves the case against him.

Marked by his company. He was recognisable — not by a badge or confession, but by what he couldn’t help: where he came from, how he spoke, the marks of time spent in that company. That is what following Christ should do to a person over time, and it is a mercy even when inconvenient. There ought to be something about a Christian that doesn’t switch off — a way of speaking, of handling money, of treating people — that others notice before anything is said. Peter’s accent was more faithful than Peter was.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he broke down and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter calls down curses on himself and swears he doesn’t know Jesus; immediately the rooster crows a second time, Peter remembers Jesus’ words, and he breaks down and weeps. Even a grievous fall need not be final: godly grief drives a believer back to Christ, whose grace restores him.

The bottom. “He began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear.” Not swearing in the modern sense, but two formal and terrible acts. He calls down a curse on himself — in effect, “May God strike me if I am lying” — and takes an oath, calling God to witness. So Peter calls on God, and invites God’s curse on his own head, to guarantee a lie about God’s Son. This is the man who said hours earlier, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” He was always in earnest. That is the horror of it.

“This man.” “I do not know this man of whom you speak.” He won’t say the name — not Jesus, not the Nazarene, but “this man,” putting all the distance into the sentence that grammar allows. And it is the exact opposite of the truth. He knew him better than almost anyone alive: he had seen him raise a dead girl, still a storm, feed thousands and shine on a mountain, and had confessed, “You are the Christ.” Above, Jesus says, “I am.” Below, Peter says, in effect, “I am not.”

The rooster. “And immediately the rooster crowed a second time.” God didn’t send an angel or thunder. He used the most ordinary sound in the world, part of every morning of Peter’s life, and timed it exactly.

He remembered. “And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, ‘Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.’” The remembering is the turn, and it is everything. Luke adds: “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61).

He wept. “And he broke down and wept.” Mark’s phrase is hard to translate; the ESV margin offers, “when he had thought about it, he wept.” Whatever its precise sense, the strongest of the twelve went to pieces in a courtyard in the dark.

Two betrayers. Two men failed Jesus terribly that night. Both were of the twelve; both had been warned to their faces; both did what he said they would. One went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5); the other went out and wept. The difference isn’t the size of the sin — denying him three times with oaths isn’t obviously lighter than selling him. The difference is what each did with the wreckage. Judas’s remorse drove him away from Christ; Peter’s grief drove him back. And on the third morning an angel says, “go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee” (16:7). Named — the one who denied him singled out to be told.

Can a denier be restored? Jesus said, “whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:33), and Paul, “if we deny him, he also will deny us” (2 Timothy 2:12). Those words describe a final, settled denial, by someone who won’t come back. Peter’s was a terrible fall, but not a final one. Jesus had prayed “that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), and it didn’t. A believer can fall badly; Christ keeps him from falling away for good.

A way back. So if you have failed him badly, don’t read this chapter and despair. Read what he said before any of it happened: “you will all fall away… But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” The tears in that courtyard weren’t the end of Peter but the beginning of the man who preached at Pentecost and wrote of standing firm — and who told this story against himself, with the numbers in it, so that everyone who has warmed their hands at the wrong fire would know there is a way back. A test: will you let your failure drive you to Christ in grief, not away from him in despair?

14.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane turns on it, and it is not the general dread of dying. Thousands of his own martyrs have gone to worse deaths singing; if the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have a Lord less composed than his servants.

The cup is a fixed Old Testament image and it means the wrath of God: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine... and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8); you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17); take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jer. 25:15). That is what stands in front of him in the dark, and it is why a man who slept through a hurricane is on the ground shaking. And he drank it — for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21) — which is precisely why there is nothing left in it for anyone who is in him.

And Gethsemane reverses Eden. In a garden a man was told the Father's will and said, in effect, "not your will but mine", and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended.

Abba (v. 36) is one of the Aramaic words Mark preserves, and the most significant: the ordinary family word a child used for his father at home. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. And it did not stay his — twice the New Testament says the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians (Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he handed over.

And I am (v. 62) is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of silencing demons and hushing healed men — and now, under oath, in chains, when it can only cost him his life, he answers plainly, in the words of the burning bush, and fuses Psalm 110:1 to Daniel 7:13. He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
14.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has opened his mouth, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure happens. No condition attached — not if you repent, not if you come back. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards, and the word he uses is a shepherd's word: I will go before you, out in front, the way a shepherd leads. And not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong — Galilee, where they were called off their boats.

Now: the angel at the empty tomb repeats it with one addition — go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). The one named in the failure is named in the restoration.

And the chapter ends with two men who betrayed him. Both of the twelve, both warned to their faces, both doing exactly what he said they would. One went out and hanged himself; one went out and wept.

The difference is not the size of the sin — denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. It is what each did with the wreckage. Remorse drove Judas away from Christ, to a rope. Grief drove Peter back.

So if you have failed him badly, notice where Peter was standing when it started: at a distance (v. 54), and then warming himself at the fire — near enough to keep his conscience quiet, far enough to keep his safety. Nobody stays there long. And notice that the man who told this story against himself, with the numbers in it, for the rest of his life, is the man whose memories became this Gospel.

15.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. <sup>2</sup>And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>3</sup>And the chief priests accused him of many things. <sup>4</sup>And Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.” <sup>5</sup>But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed. <sup>6</sup>Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. <sup>7</sup>And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. <sup>8</sup>And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. <sup>9</sup>And he answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?” <sup>10</sup>For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. <sup>11</sup>But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. <sup>12</sup>And Pilate again said to them, “Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” <sup>13</sup>And they cried out again, “Crucify him.” <sup>14</sup>And Pilate said to them, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him.” <sup>15</sup>So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. <sup>16</sup>And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. <sup>17</sup>And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. <sup>18</sup>And they began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>19</sup>And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. <sup>20</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. <sup>21</sup>And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. <sup>22</sup>And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). <sup>23</sup>And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. <sup>24</sup>And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. <sup>25</sup>And it was the third hour when they crucified him. <sup>26</sup>And the inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.” <sup>27</sup>And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>29</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, “Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, <sup>30</sup>save yourself, and come down from the cross!” <sup>31</sup>So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. <sup>32</sup>Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. <sup>33</sup>And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <sup>34</sup>And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>35</sup>And some of the bystanders hearing it said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” <sup>36</sup>And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” <sup>37</sup>And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. <sup>38</sup>And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. <sup>39</sup>And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>40</sup>There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. <sup>41</sup>When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. <sup>42</sup>And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, <sup>43</sup>Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>44</sup>Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. <sup>45</sup>And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph. <sup>46</sup>And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. <sup>47</sup>Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
15.overview:
Fifteen hours from the garden to the grave, and Mark tells it almost without adjectives.

At first light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular and hands him to Rome, because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry one out. Pilate asks one question, gets four words, and then nothing at all — and it astonishes him, because he has never seen a prisoner decline to save himself.

He knows the case is malicious; Mark says so plainly (v. 10). He tries the festival amnesty and the crowd, worked by the chief priests, asks for a murderer instead — a man called Barabbas, guilty of exactly the crime Jesus is falsely charged with. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning and, getting no answer, hands him over anyway, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Then a cohort of soldiers stages a coronation as a joke and gets every detail right; a pilgrim from Africa is pressed into carrying the beam and his sons end up in the church at Rome; and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words.

At noon the light goes out. At three he shouts the first line of Psalm 22 into the dark, and then shouts again and dies — and sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down, and a Roman officer who has watched him for six hours says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Before Pilate and the Mocking
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transfer (vv. 1–5). As soon as it is light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular, and hands him to Rome — because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry out an execution. Pilate asks one question and gets four words, and then nothing at all, and it astonishes him.

Barabbas (vv. 6–15). Pilate has read the situation correctly — he perceived that it was out of envy — and tries to release him through a festival custom. The chief priests work the crowd, and the crowd asks for a murderer. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning, what evil has he done?, gets no answer, and hands him over anyway.

The mockery (vv. 16–20). Then the whole battalion is called together for a game: a purple cloak, a crown twisted out of thorns, a reed, mock salutes and real spitting.

Every element of it is accurate. He is the King; he does receive homage; he will wear purple and a crown. A cohort of Roman soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got every detail right.
verseByVerse.theology:
Barabbas is the atonement acted out on a platform in Jerusalem.

Mark tells us exactly what he was: a rebel, in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection — guilty of precisely the crime Jesus is falsely charged with, and guilty in fact.

So two men stand before the crowd. One is guilty; the other is the Son of the Father and is innocent. The crowd is offered a choice, chooses the guilty man, and condemns the innocent one — and the innocent one dies in the guilty man's place, on the cross that had been prepared for him.

Nobody in Jerusalem understood what they were watching. But somewhere in that city, by nine o'clock that morning, there was a murderer walking around free, and the only reason he was free is that Jesus of Nazareth was on his cross.

That is the whole gospel, and it happened to one man literally before it happened to anybody else spiritually. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What evil has he done? (v. 14) — the right question, asked by the one man in Jerusalem with the authority to act on it, who then did the opposite.

Mark is careful to show that Pilate knew. He perceived that it was out of envy (v. 10). He tried the amnesty. He put the question twice. The Roman governor of Judea conducted a better assessment of the evidence than the Sanhedrin had, and reached the correct conclusion, and signed the order anyway.

Now: and the reason Mark gives is five words long — wishing to satisfy the crowd. Not conviction, not deception, not a legal error. He wanted the noise to stop, and his position was already precarious enough that a riot at Passover could have finished him.

That is the commonest failure of people in authority, and it has never needed a Roman governor to perform it. The doctrine not defended because of who would leave. The wrong not named because of whose son it was. The decision made by counting the room rather than weighing the case.

Pilate did not decide that Jesus was guilty. He decided that being right was more expensive than being popular — which is a different sin, and a far more available one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as soon as it was morning.

The fourth watch of the parable (13:35), and the last of the four. Evening at the supper, midnight in the garden, cockcrow in the courtyard, and now morning — and the disciples have slept or run through every one of them.

The chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council.

They meet again at first light, and the reason is almost certainly procedural. A capital verdict reached at night was irregular even by their own standards; a daylight session could be recorded as the proper trial.

So this is a formality performed to make an illegality look regular — and Mark, who has already told us they had the sentence before they had the evidence (14:55), lets the reader draw the conclusion.

And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate.

Bound. He was already in custody; the binding is for the transfer, and it is how you move a man through the streets.

Delivered him over — paradidōmi, the word Mark has been using since chapter 1. It is the word for Judas's betrayal (14:10), for what the Son of Man must undergo (9:31), and it will be used of Pilate handing him to the soldiers (15:15). Everyone in this chapter is handing him on to somebody else. Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands.

And why Pilate at all? Because the council could pass a religious sentence and could not execute one. Rome reserved capital punishment to itself in the provinces, and John records the council saying so plainly: it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death (John 18:31).

Which is why the charge has to change on the way. Blasphemy will not interest a Roman court for a second. So the accusation is translated into something Rome must act on — a man claiming to be a king.

And Pilate asked him, Are you the King of the Jews?

Note that this is the first thing out of his mouth, before any evidence is heard, which tells you what he had been told in advance.

And it is the only charge Rome cares about. Judea was a difficult province with a history of messianic risings; a claimant to a throne was a security matter. Pilate is not asking a theological question. He is asking an operational one: is this man a threat?

And he answered him, You have said so.

Four words, and they are neither a yes nor a no.

It is not evasion. It is a refusal to accept the frame. King of the Jews is Pilate's phrase, loaded with everything Rome feared — insurrection, a rival throne, tax revolt. Jesus will not deny the kingship, because he is the King. He will not affirm it in Pilate's terms, because in Pilate's terms it means something he has never claimed.

John gives the fuller exchange, and it is the same distinction: My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36).

And this is his last recorded answer to a question in this Gospel. From here, almost nothing — until a cry at three in the afternoon.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chief priests accused him of many things. And Pilate again asked him, "Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you." But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the chief priests accused him of many things.

Mark does not itemise them, and Luke does: we found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king (Luke 23:2).

Every one of those is false or twisted. He had told them explicitly to pay the tax (12:17) — the very men accusing him were in the room when he said it, and had marvelled at the answer.

Many things. The strategy is volume. If no single charge will hold, pile them up and hope the weight does the work.

And Pilate again asked him, Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.

And here is something worth noticing about Pilate: he is trying to help.

That is what this question is. A governor who wanted a conviction would let the accusations stand unanswered and move to sentence. Pilate is prompting the prisoner — say something, they are burying you — because he can see the case is thin and he would rather not do this.

Matthew adds that his wife sent word about a dream and told him to have nothing to do with this righteous man (Matt. 27:19). Pilate is not a man in the grip of conviction. He is a man looking for an exit.

But Jesus made no further answer.

And he will not take the exit he is offered.

Take the measure of this, because a single sentence would have done it. He could have said: I told them to pay the tax; ask them. He could have said: my kingdom is not of this world, and here are eleven witnesses that I have never armed a man. The case against him was so weak that a competent defence would have collapsed it in two minutes, and everyone in the room knew it.

He says nothing.

And it is a fulfilment, deliberately. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

So that Pilate was amazed.

He marvelled; he was astonished.

Consider what it takes to astonish a Roman governor at a criminal hearing. This man had presided over years of provincial justice. He had seen every kind of defendant: the pleaders, the bribers, the weepers, the men who cursed him, the men who invented alibis. Every single one of them fought.

He had never seen a man decline to save himself.

And that is the thing to carry out of this scene. The silence was not resignation and it was not despair. It was the most deliberate act in the room. He could have talked his way out — and the whole point was that he would not, because talking his way out was the one thing that would have left us where we were.

He kept his mouth shut so that ours could be opened.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. And he answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?" For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked.

A goodwill custom at Passover — the feast of liberation, so a prisoner is set free. It is attested nowhere outside the Gospels, which some have made an objection; but Roman governors did grant such amnesties, and a local custom in one province for one feast is exactly the sort of thing that leaves no other trace.

And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas.

Mark is precise, and every detail matters.

Among the rebels. Not a common criminal — a political prisoner, one of a group.

Who had committed murder in the insurrection. Mark says the insurrection, as though his readers knew which one. So there had been a recent rising, and Barabbas had killed somebody in it.

He is, in other words, guilty of exactly what Jesus is falsely accused of — sedition against Rome, a claim to overthrow the order. One of these two men actually did what the other is charged with.

And the name. Bar-abbas is Aramaic and it means son of the father. Some manuscripts of Matthew even give his first name as Jesus — Jesus Barabbas (Matt. 27:16–17).

So the choice put to the crowd, in the plainest possible terms, is between two men called son of the father. One is a murderer. The other is the Son of the Father.

And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them.

Note that the crowd initiates it. They have come for their prisoner, and they have somebody in mind.

And note also who this crowd is. It is not necessarily the crowd from Sunday. Those pilgrims are camped on the hillsides; this is early Friday morning, at the governor's residence, and the people present are those who could be assembled at short notice by men with influence. Verse 11 tells us who assembled them.

And he answered them, saying, Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?

Pilate makes his move, and it is a shrewd one. He offers the amnesty in a way that puts his preferred outcome first.

He is also, in that phrase, needling the priests. The King of the Jews is his title for him throughout — he uses it here, again in verse 12, and he will have it nailed to the cross in three languages, and refuse to change it (John 19:22).

For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.

And Mark tells us plainly what Pilate had worked out, which settles the question of his culpability.

Envy. Not concern for public order. Not theological outrage. The priests wanted him dead because the crowds hung on his teaching (11:18; 12:37), because his authority made theirs look like what it was, and because he had walked into their temple and turned the tables over.

A Roman politician recognised professional jealousy when he saw it, because he had seen a great deal of it.

So Pilate knows the charge is malicious, knows the man is innocent, and knows exactly why he is standing there. Everything that happens next happens with that knowledge in the room.
verseByVerse.note: Barabbas means “son of the father.” The “insurrection” was one of many uprisings against Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead.
