Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that it is. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), and that Christians meet on the first day not as a law but because it is the day of the resurrection. The apostles’ churches did so from the beginning (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2), and it remains a good and wise practice.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were saying to one another, Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?

The tense is continuous — they kept saying it, all the way there. This is the conversation on the road.

And it is entirely reasonable. They had watched Joseph roll it across on Friday (15:46). These are women carrying jars, on a path outside the city at dawn, and the one thing standing between them and the errand is a piece of stone they cannot move and have no plan for.

Note that they set out anyway. They had no solution and they went — which is worth something, because a more calculating person stays at home until the problem is solved.

And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back — it was very large.

Mark puts the size at the end of the sentence, almost as an afterthought, and it is exactly how somebody tells a story afterwards: and it had been moved — and it was enormous.

A blocking stone for a rock-cut tomb was a disc set in a channel, and the archaeology suggests weights of a ton or more. Getting it into place was downhill work for several men. Getting it out again was not.

And here is the first thing the resurrection does in this Gospel, and it is worth taking home.

The problem they had worried about the whole way had already been dealt with before they got there — and not as a favour to them. The stone was not moved so that the women could get in. Matthew is explicit that it was rolled back and sat on by an angel (Matt. 28:2), and the body was long gone by then; a sealed tomb was no obstacle to a risen Christ, who would walk through locked doors that same evening (John 20:19).

The stone was moved so that the world could look in.

But the pastoral point stands, and it is the plainest comfort in the chapter. They spent the walk on a difficulty that had already been settled. God had gone ahead of them in the dark, while they were still asleep and still grieving and still certain that nothing had changed.

Which is very often the shape of it. The thing you are rehearsing at four in the morning — the conversation you cannot see a way through, the obstacle you have no plan for — may well be dealt with before you get to it. It was still worth setting out with no solution. That is what they did, and the stone was already back.

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And entering the tomb.

They go in. A rock-cut tomb of this kind had a low doorway and an antechamber, with a shelf cut into the wall where the body was laid — so they stoop through and stand up inside a room built for the dead.

They saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe.

Mark says a young man. Matthew says plainly that it was an angel (Matt. 28:2–5), and the white robe and the reaction settle it; Mark simply describes what they saw.

Matthew has one angel, Luke two men and John two angels; the women and the times vary too. Each Gospel tells the story selectively, and none says there was only one. The women evidently came in more than one group and at slightly different times. The core is the same in all four: the women came first, the tomb was empty, and the message was that he had risen.

And now the bracket, which is one of the loveliest things in this Gospel and is easy to miss.

That phrase, a young man, occurs exactly twice in Mark.

The first time was in the garden, on the night of the arrest: and a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked (14:51–52) — perhaps Mark himself, putting his own worst moment into his own book without a name attached.

The second time is here: a young man, sitting down, dressed in a white robe, inside an empty grave, telling women that Christ is risen.

One fled from Christ stripped and ashamed in the dark. One sits in the place of death, clothed in white, with the news. Mark has bracketed the passion between them, and whether or not he intended every echo, the picture is the gospel: that is what happens to people between Friday and Sunday.

Sitting on the right side. A small detail with two things in it.

He is sitting, which is the posture of somebody whose work is finished and who is waiting. There is no urgency in that tomb. The crisis is over; an angel has sat down.

And the right side is the side of honour — the place the sons of Zebedee asked for (10:37), the place where Jesus himself now sits (v. 19).

And they were alarmed.

They came expecting a corpse and found a living stranger sitting where it should have been. Every reaction to the supernatural in this Gospel is the same, and it is never serene: the disciples in the boat (4:41), the crowd at the demoniac's healing (5:15), the three on the mountain (9:6).

Nobody in the Bible meets the power of God and finds it comfortable. Which is why the first word out of the angel's mouth is the one it always is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be alarmed.

The same word as the last verse, negated. He deals with their terror before he gives them the news, which is how heaven habitually opens a conversation — fear not is the first thing said to Zechariah, to Mary, to the shepherds, and to John on Patmos.

You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified.

Three things in that identification, and every one is nailed down.

Jesus — the personal name. Of Nazareth — the village, the human address, the ordinary provincial origin that made people take offence (6:3). Who was crucified — the manner of death, stated flatly and in the past tense.

There is no ambiguity here about who is meant or what happened to him. The risen one is the crucified one; it is the same man, and he still carries the identity. When he appears to Thomas he will still have the holes in him (John 20:27).

Christianity has never offered a Jesus who got past the cross. It offers a man who went through it and out the other side, and who is known by it forever — a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Rev. 5:6).

He has risen; he is not here.

Four words in Greek and they are the hinge of history.

He has risen — and the Greek is a passive: he was raised. Which is how the New Testament almost always puts it. God the Father raised him (Acts 2:24; Rom. 6:4) — the resurrection is the Father's public verdict on the Son, the answer to the cry from the dark, the reversal of the council's sentence. The court of heaven has overturned the court of Caiaphas.

He is not here. And that is the second half, and it is a claim about a physical location on a spring morning. Not his spirit lives on. Not his cause continues. The body is not in the room, and the room is one the women had personally watched him carried into (15:47).

See the place where they laid him.

And now the angel does something no religion has ever done: he offers evidence and invites inspection.

Look. Come here and look at the shelf. There is nothing on it.

The resurrection is not presented in this Gospel as a spiritual experience, a symbol, or a way of speaking about hope surviving death. It is presented as an event with an address, a date and a witness list, and the first thing anybody is told to do about it is to examine the physical evidence.

Paul stakes everything on the same ground: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Cor. 15:17). Christianity is the only faith in the world that can be disproved by producing a body — and nobody ever has, though a great many people in Jerusalem that spring had every reason to try.

The tomb was open, the location was known, and the authorities had soldiers. All they had to do was walk in and carry out the evidence.

The place was empty, and it still is.

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But go, tell his disciples and Peter.

The first commission of the Christian era is given to three women in a graveyard, and it contains two extra words that have done more for failing Christians than almost any other phrase in Scripture.

And Peter.

He was one of the disciples. The word covered him. There was no need to add anything.

Unless somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain that it no longer did.

Peter had denied him three times, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, with oaths and a curse on his own head — and had gone out and broken down (14:71–72). He had spent Saturday somewhere in that city with nothing to think about but that. As far as he knew, he was not merely ashamed; he was out. He had disqualified himself, publicly, in the worst hour of his Master's life, after boasting that he never would.

And the first message sent from the other side of the grave has his name attached to the end of it, as though the general term might not reach him. In effect: tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter.

Somebody wanted him to be in no doubt.

That he is going before you to Galilee.

And this is not new information. It is a quotation.

On the walk out to Gethsemane, before anybody had failed, Jesus had said: You will all fall away... But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats the sentence almost word for word.

Which means the restoration was promised before the betrayal happened, and the meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it.

Go before is a shepherd's picture — to walk out in front of the flock. He had quoted Zechariah about the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, and now the struck shepherd is out in front of them again.

Galilee. Not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong. Home — the lake, the boats, the towns where they were called off their nets in chapter 1.

He takes them back to the beginning to start again.

But Luke and John record appearances in Jerusalem, and Luke has Jesus tell them to stay in the city (Luke 24:49). The Jerusalem appearances came first, that Sunday and the week after; the meeting in Galilee followed (Matt 28:16; John 21); and they returned to Jerusalem to wait for the Spirit. Luke’s command to stay belongs to the end of the forty days.

There you will see him, just as he told you.

And the last clause is the angel's own comment, and it is gentle and slightly pointed: just as he told you.

He had told them. Repeatedly. Every element of this weekend had been announced in advance — the betrayal, the scattering, the denial, the death, the third day — and not one of them had held on to any of it.

So the message to the disciples on Easter morning is not a rebuke and it is not a reward. It is a reminder that he had said so, and that he keeps his word even when nobody believed it, and that he had made the arrangements for their restoration before they had even failed.
verseByVerse.note: Peter is named — the one who had denied him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them.

They run. And Mark's two words are strong: trembling — the physical shaking — and ekstasis, being out of one's senses, the word behind our ecstasy but with none of the pleasantness. They are undone.

And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.

And there Mark stops.

First, the sentence itself, because there is a superb irony in it and it is Mark's last word about human beings.

All through this Gospel, people who were commanded to be silent could not keep quiet. The cleansed leper was told to say nothing and went out and began to talk freely about it, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly (1:45). The Decapolis crowd was charged to tell no one, and the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it (7:36).

And here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

Obviously they told somebody eventually, or this account would not exist — the sense is that they said nothing on the road, to anyone they passed. But Mark chooses to end on it, and the effect is deliberate: the last thing recorded of the followers of Jesus is that they were too frightened to deliver the best news in the world.

And now the question this verse forces: does Mark really end here?

The oldest and best manuscripts stop at this word. And the word is gar — for — which is an extraordinarily abrupt thing to end a book with in Greek; it is a little like closing on because.

Three explanations are offered, and honesty requires saying that we do not know which is right.

The original ending was lost. The last leaf of an early codex is the likeliest thing in the world to be torn off. Tradition places Mark in Rome under Nero, when Peter was executed, and it is entirely possible he was interrupted.

He was prevented from finishing. A variation of the same.

Or he meant to stop here. And this reading has grown stronger the longer people have looked at it, because it fits everything else about Mark — the abruptness, the urgency, the refusal to tidy things up, the relentless honesty about the disciples.

Consider what an ending at verse 8 does to the reader.

The resurrection has been announced and not described. The appearances are promised — there you will see him — and not narrated. And the last human beings in the book fail to pass the message on.

Which leaves the story unfinished on purpose, and leaves it in the reader's hands. Mark opened his book by calling it the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1). If it ends at verse 8, then the whole sixteen chapters are only the beginning — and the rest is written by whoever picks it up.

The women were told to go to Galilee, which is where chapter 1 started. The book loops back to its own first page and points the reader at it.

And in the end, nothing whatever is lost. The resurrection is stated as fact in verse 6 by a messenger from God. The appearances are recorded in detail by Matthew, Luke, John and Paul — and Paul's list of witnesses (1 Cor. 15:3–8) was written down within about twenty-five years of the event, while most of them were still alive to be asked.

Mark's Gospel ends with three frightened women running away from an empty grave. What it does not end with is any doubt about whether the grave was empty.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts end the Gospel here, and brackets verses 9–20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What this passage is. Before verse 9 your Bible prints a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. It is the most significant textual question in the New Testament, and it is dealt with fully at verses 9–11 rather than hidden in a note, because a reader who meets it for the first time deserves a straight answer.

What it contains. A summary of resurrection appearances — to Mary Magdalene, to two men walking into the country, and to the eleven at table — with the disciples disbelieving every one of them until Jesus stands in front of them and rebukes them for it.

Then the commission: go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Then a promise of accompanying signs, including the two sentences about serpents and poison that a handful of churches have built a lethal practice on.

And then the ending. He is taken up into heaven and sits down at the right hand of God — which is exactly what he told the high priest would happen, on the night they condemned him for saying it (14:62).

And the last verse of Mark is the disciples doing the one thing the women in verse 8 could not.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (v. 16) can sound, read at speed, as though baptism were half of what saves you. Read closely it says something more careful.

Believing and being baptized are named together in the first half because in the New Testament they belong together — nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines to be baptized; the washing is the ordinary, public, commanded seal of the faith professed.

But look at the second half, which is where the sentence settles the matter. The condemnation clause is not whoever is not baptized. It is whoever does not believe. Baptism drops out of it entirely.

That asymmetry is doing deliberate work. What saves is Christ, received by faith; baptism is the sign and seal of that faith, not the ground of it. Which is why a dying thief with no water within reach could be told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

So take the verse whole and let it cut both ways: do not despise baptism, because your Lord commanded it and it is no empty ceremony — and do not lean your weight on it, because it was never the thing holding you up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them (v. 18).

On the strength of that sentence, a handful of churches — mostly in the Appalachian hills — have taken up handling rattlesnakes and drinking strychnine in their services to prove their faith. People have died doing it.

Now: two things must be said, and they are enough.

First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all. To build a practice on a passage the earliest manuscripts do not contain is unwise twice over.

Second — and this holds even reading the verse at face value — it describes what may happen to Christ's servants, not what they are to seek out. When a viper fastened on Paul's hand on Malta and he shook it off unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), it was an accident of ministry he neither courted nor expected, not a stunt to test God.

Deliberately reaching for a snake or a poison cup to prove one believes is precisely what Satan urged in the wilderness — throw yourself down — and precisely what Jesus refused, with the words you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12).

Faith trusts God. It does not dare him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a word of the content, the question in the brackets — because it is the biggest textual question in the New Testament and a reader deserves a straight answer.

What your Bible says. Immediately before verse 9 the ESV prints, in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. Other translations use a similar note or a horizontal rule.

The facts, laid out plainly.

The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both from the fourth century — end Mark at verse 8. So do the oldest Syriac, Armenian and Georgian versions.

Eusebius, writing in the early fourth century, says that the accurate copies known to him ended at verse 8, and that verses 9–20 were absent from almost all of them. Jerome says the same a century later.

Some manuscripts have a different, much shorter ending instead; a few have both, one after the other, which is what copyists do when they know of two and cannot decide.

And the Greek itself does not read like Mark. There are more than a dozen words in these twelve verses that appear nowhere else in the book, and the style is noticeably different. Most tellingly, verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time — from whom he had cast out seven demons — although she was named a few verses earlier (v. 1). That is not how a writer refers to a character he has been following all morning. It is how a different writer begins.

The honest conclusion. Mark very probably did not write these verses. They were added early — early enough to be known and read widely by the middle of the second century, since Irenaeus quotes verse 19 around AD 180 — but they are almost certainly not from his hand.

Some Christians defend the longer ending as Mark’s own. They point out that it is found in the great majority of manuscripts, that Irenaeus quotes it in the second century, and that it seems unlikely Mark meant to end with for they were afraid. But the oldest manuscripts and early writers who knew the evidence point the other way. So is it Scripture? The more likely answer is that it is an early and faithful summary added to Mark, not part of what he wrote. It can be read and taught, but nothing should be built on it that is not taught elsewhere in Scripture.

And now the thing that actually matters to you, which is whether any of this should unsettle your confidence in the Bible.

It should not, and here is why.

First, nothing has been smuggled in. Every substantial thing in this passage is taught plainly elsewhere in Scripture. The appearance to Mary Magdalene is in John 20. The two on the road are in Luke 24. The commission to all nations is in Matthew 28 and Acts 1. The ascension and the session at God's right hand are in Luke 24, Acts 1, Ephesians 1:20 and Hebrews 1:3. There is not a doctrine of the Christian faith that stands or falls here.

Second, this is what a reliable text looks like. We possess thousands of manuscripts of the New Testament — vastly more, and vastly earlier, than for any other document of the ancient world. The consequence of having so many is that we can see exactly where copyists differed, and the differences are catalogued and printed in the margin.

A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one prints the workings at the bottom of the page. The reason you know about this passage is the same reason you can trust the rest.

Third, be clear what is not in doubt. The empty tomb, the announcement of the resurrection, and the promise of the appearances are all in verses 1–8, in every manuscript there is. Nothing in this discussion touches them by a hair.

And so to the content itself.

He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.

Whoever wrote it got something exactly right, and it is worth stopping on.

The first person on earth to see the risen Christ was a woman out of whom he had thrown seven demons. Not Peter, not John, not his mother, not a priest — a woman with a past so wrecked that her deliverance needed a number attached to it.

That is a detail no one would invent, in a culture where a woman's testimony was not accepted in a court of law. It is in Matthew and John, and here, because it happened.

She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept.

Note the state of the disciples on Easter Sunday: mourning and weeping. Not waiting hopefully. Grieving.

But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.

And there is the first of three refusals in four verses.

Which is worth having, because it is entirely consistent with everything Mark has said about them for sixteen chapters. They did not believe the resurrection when they were told. They had to be convinced, against their will, by the man himself.

These are not people who were predisposed to believe. They are the hardest audience in the story.
verseByVerse.note: These verses are not found in some of the earliest manuscripts; the ESV prints them in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.

parallels.desc: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord
from whom seven demons had gone out

verseByVerse.quote: After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country.

This is Luke 24 in one sentence — the road to Emmaus, seven miles out of Jerusalem, the two disciples who walked and talked with him for hours without recognising him, and knew him at last when he broke the bread.

In another form is this writer's way of accounting for the failure to recognise him, which Luke explains differently (their eyes were kept from recognizing him, Luke 24:16). Something about the risen body was both continuous and changed; Mary made the same mistake in the garden and took him for the gardener (John 20:15).

And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them.

The second refusal. Two more witnesses, and the eleven still will not have it.

Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table.

The third appearance, and it takes the Lord in person to end the matter. They are at a meal — which is where the risen Christ keeps turning up: at Emmaus, in the upper room where he asks for a piece of fish, on a beach in Galilee cooking breakfast.

And he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart.

And there are the two words the reader of this Gospel has met again and again.

Hardness of heart is the phrase used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5), and of the disciples in the boat who had carried the baskets and understood nothing (6:52; 8:17).

So the last thing the risen Christ does before commissioning them is tell them off. Not congratulate them for surviving the weekend. Not commiserate. He rebukes them, because they had been told plainly, three times, and had refused to believe three separate sets of eyewitnesses.

Because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.

And now hold two things together, because the passage puts them side by side and they explain each other.

These men were not credulous. That is the point being made, and it is a considerable one. The apostles are frequently accused of having been primed to believe in a resurrection — of wanting it so badly that they talked themselves into it. Every account we have says the opposite. They dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person, and even then Matthew records that some doubted (Matt. 28:17) and John gives us a whole week of Thomas refusing.

And he sends them anyway. That is the second thing, and it is the more astonishing. In the very next verse, this group — a company of men who had run away in a garden, denied him in a courtyard, spent the weekend weeping, refused three reports and just been rebuked to their faces for hardness of heart — is handed the gospel and told to take it to the whole creation.

He does not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation.

The commission, and every phrase widens it.

Go. The movement is outward, and it always has been. The Old Testament pattern was largely centripetal — the nations would come to Zion, to the mountain of the LORD (Isa. 2:2–3). Now the direction reverses and the people of God are sent out.

Into all the world. To eleven men in a room in Jerusalem, most of them from one lakeside district of one small province of one empire. Between them they had no money, no organisation, no standing and no education to speak of, and one of them had denied him to a servant girl the previous Friday.

Proclaim. The verb is the herald's word — kēryssō, to announce publicly what a king has decreed. A herald does not workshop the message or improve it. He carries it.

To the whole creation. And this is the widest phrase in the sentence, and it is worth pausing on. Not merely to all people — to the whole creation. It is the same scope Paul reaches for: the creation itself groaning in labour, waiting to be set free from its bondage to decay (Rom. 8:21–22), and God's purpose to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth (Eph. 1:10).

The rescue is not merely of souls out of a doomed world. It is the beginning of the repair of everything.

Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

And now a sentence that needs care, because read at speed it can sound as though baptism were half of what saves you — and a great many anxious people have stumbled here.

Why the two are named together. In the New Testament, believing and being baptized belong together as a matter of course. Nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines the water; the washing is the ordinary, public, commanded seal of the faith professed. To speak of an unbaptized Christian would have puzzled the apostles, not because the water saves but because a believer who refuses the sign is refusing his Lord's plain command.

And now look at the second half, which settles the matter.

The condemnation clause is not whoever is not baptized will be condemned. It is whoever does not believe will be condemned.

Baptism drops out of it entirely.

That asymmetry is deliberate and it is decisive. If baptism were part of what saves, its absence would be part of what condemns — and the sentence carefully does not say so. What saves is Christ, received by faith. Baptism is the sign and seal of that faith, not the ground of it.

Which is why a dying thief, nailed up with no water within reach and no possibility of getting to any, could be told: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read this verse as teaching that baptism is part of the means by which God saves, and they point to Peter’s Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins (Acts 2:38) and Ananias’ be baptized and wash away your sins (Acts 22:16). But in those verses, as here, baptism is joined to repentance and faith as their outward sign; forgiveness is given to faith (Acts 10:43), and the washing is the picture of it. The dying thief, who was never baptized, went with Christ to paradise (Luke 23:43).

So take the verse whole, and let it cut both ways.

Do not despise baptism. Your Lord commanded it, it is no empty ceremony, and a professing Christian who has never been baptized should stop reading and go and speak to his elders about it this week.

And do not lean your weight on it. If your confidence before God rests on something that was done to you at a font, you are resting on the sign and not on the thing signified — and it was never the thing holding you up.

verseByVerse.quote: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And these signs will accompany those who believe.

Five signs are listed, and the first thing to notice is the verb: they will accompany. They are not the point; they come behind. And verse 20 says the same, that the Lord confirmed the message by accompanying signs. The message goes first; the signs come after and attend it.

In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues.

Both are recorded in Acts — Paul at Philippi (Acts 16:18), and Pentecost and after (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6). And the name matters: in my name. The authority is borrowed, never possessed, which is the lesson the disciples learned badly at the foot of the mountain in chapter 9.

They will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.

Also recorded — Paul on Malta (Acts 28:8), and the elders anointing the sick in James 5:14, which is the ordinary provision Christ has left in every congregation.

Do these signs continue today? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe they do: the promise is to those who believe, with no end date given. But the verse goes on to say that the signs confirmed the message the apostles preached (v. 20), and Hebrews describes the same thing as past: God bore witness by signs and wonders to those who first heard the Lord (Heb 2:3–4). Paul calls them The signs of a true apostle (2 Cor 12:12). The more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic age and ceased with it. The new tongues were the real languages of Acts 2. God still heals in answer to prayer as he pleases; but a church should seek his word, not signs.

They will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them.

And now the sentence that has done real harm, and it needs a plain word.

On the strength of it, a handful of churches — mostly in the Appalachian hills of the United States, from the early twentieth century onwards — have taken up handling rattlesnakes and copperheads in their services, and drinking strychnine, to demonstrate their faith. People have been bitten. People have died, including pastors, some of them refusing medical treatment on principle.

Two things must be said, and they are enough.

First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all. The whole passage is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and to build a distinctive practice — a dangerous one — on a text the oldest copies do not contain is unwise twice over.

Second, even taken at face value, the verse describes what may happen to Christ's servants, not what they are to go looking for.

And Scripture supplies the illustration. Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, was gathering firewood when a viper fastened on his hand, and he shook it off into the fire and was unharmed (Acts 28:3–6). That is exactly what this promise describes — and note everything about it. He did not seek it, did not expect it, was not proving anything, and was engaged at the time in the humble business of collecting sticks for a fire to warm shipwrecked strangers.

It was an accident of ministry, not a demonstration.

And there is a deeper objection still, which settles it.

Deliberately picking up a snake or drinking poison in order to prove that one believes is precisely what Satan urged in the wilderness. Throw yourself down from here — and he even quoted a promise of protection to support it (Ps. 91:11–12).

And Jesus refused, with one sentence: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12).

That is the answer, and it applies far beyond serpents. There is a way of treating God's promises as dares — engineering a crisis to see whether he will come through, refusing the doctor to prove one has faith, taking a foolish risk and calling it trust.

Faith trusts God. It does not dare him. The two look superficially alike and they are opposites: one rests on his character, and the other demands that he prove it on our terms — which is the same demand the chief priests shouted at the cross, and he would not come down for them either.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.

The ascension in one sentence, and it is worth taking apart, because it is the last thing this book says about Jesus.

Was taken up. The Father receives him. Luke gives the scene at length — the Mount of Olives, the cloud, the two men in white asking why they are standing there looking up (Acts 1:9–11).

And sat down at the right hand of God.

And now put this beside a night, a few weeks earlier, in the house of the high priest.

Bound, mocked, spat on, with the case against him in ruins and the sentence already decided, he had been asked a direct question and had answered it plainly: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven (14:62).

They tore their robes and condemned him for it.

And here, at the end of the book, in one flat sentence: he sat down at the right hand of God. Exactly as he said, in the words he used, within weeks of being executed for saying them.

And the sitting is itself the doctrine. Priests in the temple never sat down — there were no chairs in the holy place, because the work of sacrifice was never finished. Hebrews makes the point directly: every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Heb. 10:11–12).

He sat down because it was done.

And they went out and preached everywhere.

And so the book ends with a sentence about the disciples — and it is the exact reversal of verse 8.

There, three women ran from a tomb and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. Here, the same terrified company goes out and preaches everywhere.

Something happened in between, and it is not a change of temperament. The only thing that turns that group into this one is the risen Christ standing in the room. Men who would not believe three separate reports and had to be rebuked to their faces went out and told the world, and most of them died for it, and not one of them ever recanted.

While the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.

The last clause of the Gospel of Mark, and there are two things in it.

The Lord worked with them. He has just sat down in heaven, and he is working alongside them on earth in the same sentence. That is not a contradiction; it is the whole shape of the Christian era. Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20).

Which means the going out was never the disciples carrying on a work he had finished. It was, and is, his work, done through people who had recently proved themselves entirely unreliable.

And now look back at the first line of the book.

The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1).

Mark called sixteen chapters — the baptism, the demons, the storms, the bread, the blind man who saw walking trees, the confession at Caesarea Philippi, the cup in the garden, the cry in the dark, the torn curtain, the empty grave — the beginning.

The beginning. And it has not stopped since. The centurion's confession was picked up by a church in Rome and carried out along the roads of an empire, and by tribes and languages that did not exist when Mark was writing, and it reached the room you are sitting in.

The Lord is still working with them. He is still confirming his own message. And the man who was appalled and shaking in a garden, and who shouted into three hours of darkness that his God had forsaken him, is sitting down — because the work is finished, and the last of them will be brought home.

16.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible? The facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament — Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at v. 8, as do the oldest Syriac, Armenian and Georgian versions. Eusebius and Jerome both report that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts carry a different, shorter ending; a few carry both. And the Greek does not read like Mark: more than a dozen words appear nowhere else in the book, and v. 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named twice.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these verses, though they were known and read by the middle of the second century.

And here is why that need not unsettle anybody. Nothing has been smuggled in: every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere — Mary Magdalene (John 20), the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission (Matt. 28; Acts 1), the ascension and session (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 1:3). No doctrine stands or falls here. And the reason you know about it at all is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them; this one prints the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest can be trusted. Nothing in the discussion touches vv. 1–8, which are in every manuscript there is.

Does Mark end at v. 8? The last word is gar — for — an extraordinarily abrupt way to end a book, rather like closing on because. Three explanations are offered and we do not know which is right: the last leaf of an early codex was lost; the author was interrupted (tradition places him in Rome under Nero); or he meant to stop there. The third has grown stronger the longer people look at it, because an ending at v. 8 leaves the resurrection announced and not described, the appearances promised and not narrated, and the story unfinished in the reader's hands. Mark called his book the beginning of the gospel (1:1) — and the women are sent to Galilee, where chapter 1 began.
16.examples:
Then: and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid (v. 8).

There is a superb irony in that sentence, and it is Mark's last word about human beings. All through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet — the cleansed leper went out and began to talk freely about it so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly (1:45); the Decapolis crowd was charged to tell no one, and the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it (7:36).

And here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

Now: and the last verse of the chapter is the exact reversal — they went out and preached everywhere. The same frightened company. Something happened in between, and it was not a change of temperament.

These were not credulous people. They dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person and rebuked to their faces for unbelief and hardness of heart (v. 14). Every account we have says the apostles were the hardest audience in the story, not the softest.

And he sent them anyway — a company of men who had run from a garden, denied him in a courtyard, spent the weekend weeping and refused three separate eyewitness reports. He did not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.
